ABSTRACT

In recent years, the intersection of biomedical signal processing and communication technologies has significantly accelerated healthcare innovations, particularly in real-time health monitoring systems. This paper presents the core principles of biomedical signal processing, focusing on techniques for signal acquisition and preprocessing that are essential in improving data quality and reliability. Effective signal acquisition is a key challenge, as physiological signals—such as ECG, EEG, and EMG—are often affected by noise and artifacts from internal and external sources. Ultimately, this study demonstrates how advancements in electronics and communication engineering are driving significant progress in biomedical signal processing, leading to better health outcomes and more efficient patient care. Additionally, the paper examines the critical role of advanced filtering techniques in reducing noise and enhancing signal clarity, which is particularly important in wearable medical devices.

1.0 INTRODUCTION

The healthcare industry has undergone a profound transformation over the past few decades, largely driven by technological advancements that have reshaped patient care and outcomes. One of the most significant innovations in this revolution is the integration of biomedical signal processing and communication technologies, which has enabled the development of real-time health monitoring systems. These systems harness the power of electronics and communication engineering to continuously track, analyze, and interpret physiological signals, providing a wealth of data that can improve diagnosis, treatment, and patient management. The motivation behind this integration lies in the desire to enhance the accuracy, timeliness, and accessibility of healthcare services, particularly through innovations such as wearable devices and remote patient monitoring. By leveraging advanced signal acquisition techniques, preprocessing methods, and machine learning (ML) algorithms, these technologies can address key challenges such as noise reduction, data quality enhancement, and personalized health insights. The role of communication technologies, including the integration of IoT (Internet of Things), is critical in ensuring seamless data transmission and enabling real-time monitoring, thereby facilitating better decision-making and early intervention. This paper explores how these cutting-edge advancements in biomedical signal processing and communication technologies contribute to improving the efficiency of health monitoring systems, while highlighting their potential to reduce the burden on healthcare systems globally. Ultimately, this integration offers a promising pathway toward next-generation healthcare solutions that can enhance the quality of care, empower patients, and reduce healthcare costs. (Rangayyan et al., 2024)

This chapter discusses different preprocessing techniques, including filtering, normalization, and artifact removal, are thus crucial to ensuring the accuracy of subsequent analyses. A major highlight of this study is the application of advanced ML algorithms to classify physiological signals. The use of ML in biomedical signal processing allows for the identification of subtle patterns in complex datasets, enabling early detection of diseases and more accurate diagnostic decisions. Central to this process is feature extraction, where essential characteristics of signals are identified and extracted to optimize the performance of ML models. Feature extraction methods such as wavelet transforms, time-frequency analysis and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) are instrumental in improving model accuracy and efficiency.

Filters like adaptive noise cancellation and wavelet denoising are employed to isolate meaningful physiological information from background noise, making these devices more reliable for continuous monitoring.

Emerging trends, such as the integration of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, are transforming healthcare delivery by enabling real-time remote health monitoring and data transmission (JARIAL et al., 2024). IoT-based systems facilitate continuous tracking of vital signs and deliver personalized care by leveraging vast amounts of patient data. This convergence of biomedical signal processing, IoT, and personalized medicine promises to reshape the healthcare landscape by enhancing patient outcomes, improving care delivery, and reducing healthcare costs.

1.1 The Role of Biomedical Signal Processing in Healthcare

The healthcare industry has witnessed a profound transformation over the past few decades, driven largely by technological advancements. Among the most significant innovations is integrating biomedical signal processing and communication technologies, which have enabled real-time health monitoring systems. These systems leverage the power of electronics and communication engineering to continuously track, analyze, and interpret physiological signals, offering immense potential for improving patient care and outcomes. Biomedical signals, such as Electrocardiograms (ECG), Electroencephalograms (EEG), and electromyograms (EMG), provide critical information about the body’s internal state. However, these signals are often contaminated by noise, artifacts, and other interferences that can compromise the accuracy and reliability of health monitoring systems (Khang et al,. 2024).

1.2 Challenges in Signal Acquisition and Preprocessing

Signal acquisition is one of the most crucial stages in the biomedical signal-processing pipeline, as the integrity of the collected data directly impacts the accuracy and reliability of the entire health monitoring system. The effectiveness of biomedical signal acquisition systems depends not only on the quality of sensors and hardware used but also on the system’s ability to filter out unwanted noise and artifacts that can distort physiological signals. As the field advances towards miniaturized, wearable devices, maintaining high-quality signal acquisition becomes increasingly challenging due to constraints such as limited power, small form factors, and the presence of environmental noise. These challenges are further complicated by the non-stationary nature of many biomedical signals, where characteristics such as amplitude and frequency may change over time.(Anwer et al., 2024)

To address these obstacles, researchers have developed a range of advanced preprocessing techniques. Signal filtering, normalization, and artifact removal are essential for enhancing signal quality, but they must also be tailored to the specific characteristics of the signal and the noise sources. Adaptive noise cancellation (ANC) plays a vital role in this context, as it can dynamically adjust to varying noise patterns, particularly in non-stationary environments, allowing for effective removal of noise while preserving the integrity of the signal. Moreover, feature extraction methods help identify the most relevant components of the signal, enabling the extraction of meaningful information for subsequent analysis, even in the presence of noise or interference. Together, these preprocessing techniques ensure that the signals used for analysis are both accurate and reliable, forming a solid foundation for health monitoring systems. Failure to effectively address these preprocessing challenges—such as poor noise rejection or inadequate feature extraction—can undermine the entire diagnostic process, leading to inaccurate assessments or delayed interventions.

1.3 The Integration of ML and Communication Technologies

In recent years, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing biomedical signal processing, offering a significant leap forward in the analysis of complex physiological data. ML algorithms, such as support vector machines (SVM), random forests, and deep learning techniques like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have shown exceptional ability to identify subtle patterns within large datasets that would be difficult to detect manually. These algorithms have demonstrated remarkable success in automating the classification of physiological signals such as ECG, EEG, and EMG, making it possible to predict a range of diseases with higher accuracy and efficiency. For example, SVMs have been applied in detecting arrhythmias from ECG signals, while deep learning models like CNNs are increasingly used for early detection of brain disorders through EEG signals. These ML techniques not only enhance diagnostic decision-making but also enable personalized healthcare delivery by tailoring treatment plans based on an individual's unique physiological profile.

Additionally, techniques such as wavelet transform, time-frequency analysis, and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) have significantly improved feature extraction, enhancing the quality and relevance of the data used in machine learning models. These methods allow for better handling of non-stationary signals and improve the accuracy of disease predictions, as they extract more meaningful features from complex signals. In real-world applications, ML-powered systems are already being used to predict cardiovascular events, detect early signs of neurological diseases like epilepsy and Alzheimer’s, and identify mental health conditions through continuous monitoring of physiological signals.(Adebayo et al,. 2024)

The integration of these ML-based systems with the rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) and the evolution of 5G and upcoming 6G networks is transforming healthcare delivery. IoT-based systems now enable continuous, remote monitoring of patients, transmitting real-time physiological data to healthcare providers. This constant flow of data, paired with ML algorithms, allows for timely detection of potential health issues and real-time intervention. The advancements in wireless communication and data transfer, particularly through high-speed 5G and future 6G networks, have made it possible to track vital signs, monitor chronic conditions, and provide personalized care more efficiently. This not only reduces the need for in-hospital visits but also significantly improves patient outcomes by enabling proactive healthcare (Olaleye et al., 2024). For instance, patients with chronic heart conditions can now receive continuous ECG monitoring via wearable devices, with ML algorithms predicting potential complications and alerting healthcare providers before serious issues arise.

2.0 FUNDAMENTALS OF BIOMEDICAL SIGNALS

Biomedical signals are electrical signals that are generated by biological processes and can be measured to assess the physiological state of the human body. These signals are fundamental to healthcare monitoring and diagnostics, as they provide real-time insights into bodily functions and help in detecting abnormalities that might signal underlying medical conditions.

The measurement of these signals is a critical component of health monitoring systems, and their accurate acquisition, preprocessing, and analysis are essential for effective diagnosis and treatment (Bhatele et al., 2023). In this section, we will examine three key types of biomedical signals commonly used in health monitoring systems: Electrocardiogram (ECG), Electroencephalogram (EEG), and Electromyogram (EMG). Additionally, we will explore the characteristics of these signals and the challenges faced in their acquisition.

2.1 Types of Biomedical Signals

2.1.1. Electrocardiogram (ECG)

The ECG is one of the most widely used biomedical signals to monitor and evaluate the electrical activity of the heart. It records the heart's rhythm and electrical impulses as waveforms that provide information about heart rate, the timing of each heartbeat, and the presence of any abnormalities, such as arrhythmias or heart attacks (Ukil et al., 2022).

  • ● Signal Characteristics: The ECG signal consists of P waves, QRS complexes, and T waves, each corresponding to different stages of the cardiac cycle (atrial depolarization, ventricular depolarization, and ventricular repolarization).

  • ● Challenges in Acquisition: The ECG signal is susceptible to interference from various external sources such as power line noise and electromagnetic interference. Additionally, motion artifacts from the patient (such as body movement) can distort the signal, making it difficult to obtain accurate readings in ambulatory settings.

2.1.2 Electroencephalogram (EEG)

An EEG records the electrical activity of the brain by measuring voltage fluctuations resulting from ionic current flows within the neurons. It is primarily used to assess brain function, diagnose neurological conditions like epilepsy, sleep disorders, and brain injuries, and monitor brain activity during surgeries (Chaddad et al., 2023).

  • ● Signal Characteristics: EEG signals are categorized into different frequency bands, including delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma waves, each associated with different states of brain activity, such as sleep, relaxation, or cognitive tasks.

  • ● Challenges in Acquisition: EEG signals are extremely low in amplitude, which makes them susceptible to various sources of noise, including muscle activity (electromyographic noise) and electrical interference. Furthermore, the signals are often affected by the patient’s movement or the placement of electrodes, making signal acquisition a delicate process.

2.1.3. Electromyogram (EMG)

The EMG records the electrical activity produced by skeletal muscles. It is used to assess muscle function, diagnose neuromuscular diseases, and evaluate muscle response during physical activities or rehabilitation exercises (Boyer et al., 2023).

  • ● Signal Characteristics: The EMG signal consists of a combination of motor unit action potentials (MUAPs) and the electrical activity from muscle fibers. The signal’s characteristics depend on muscle fiber type, muscle contraction force, and the location of the electrode.

  • ● Challenges in Acquisition: The EMG signal is vulnerable to interference from nearby muscles, electrical noise, and skin impedance. The placement of electrodes is crucial for accurate signal detection, and proper skin preparation is necessary to minimize noise and improve the signal-to-noise ratio.

2.2 Characteristics and Challenges in Data Acquisition

The acquisition of biomedical signals is a critical step in health monitoring systems, as it directly influences the quality and accuracy of subsequent analyses. Biomedical signals, such as ECG, EEG, and EMG, are inherently complex and can be influenced by various internal and external factors, making their acquisition both challenging and essential. One of the key characteristics of these signals is their low amplitude, which often requires sensitive equipment to capture accurate data (Arooj et al., 2022). For instance, the ECG signal, which records the electrical activity of the heart, is typically measured in millivolts, and small variations in signal strength can represent significant health changes. Similarly, EEG signals from the brain are typically weak, requiring precise signal acquisition technologies to detect and differentiate between various brain states. Another characteristic is the non-stationarity of biomedical signals. These signals can vary over time due to physiological changes or external factors, making it difficult to maintain consistent data quality during acquisition. This non-stationarity requires advanced techniques in signal processing to handle variations and ensure that the acquired data is accurate for diagnostic purposes. For example, EEG signals can fluctuate due to changes in brain activity, while EMG signals may be influenced by muscle fatigue or movement artifacts. A major challenge in signal acquisition is the presence of noise and artifacts (Xiong et al., 2022). Physiological signals are often contaminated by various types of noise, including electromagnetic interference, motion artifacts, and powerline noise. These external interferences can distort the signal, leading to inaccurate readings. Electromyographic signals (EMG), for example, are particularly susceptible to movement artifacts, as the placement of sensors can be influenced by muscle contractions or environmental vibrations. Similarly, EEG signals may be contaminated by electrical noise from nearby equipment or by patient movement. Overcoming these challenges requires the use of advanced filtering and signal conditioning techniques to isolate the true physiological signal from the noise. Furthermore, sensor placement and sensor reliability also pose significant challenges in the acquisition process. The positioning of sensors, especially for wearable or portable devices, can affect the accuracy of the measurements (Ayerbe et al., 2022). Improper electrode placement can lead to poor signal quality or the introduction of additional noise. Additionally, sensor drift or malfunction over time can compromise long-term monitoring. To address these issues, researchers and engineers continuously innovate in the design of non-invasive, wearable sensors that are more robust and accurate in diverse real-world conditions

3.0 SIGNAL ACQUISITION AND PREPROCESSING

Signal acquisition and preprocessing are fundamental stages in the process of biomedical signal processing. These stages ensure that raw physiological signals, such as ECG, EEG, and EMG, are accurately captured and cleaned for further analysis. The quality of signal acquisition and the effectiveness of preprocessing directly impact the reliability of health monitoring systems (Lu et al., 2023). This section will explore sensor technologies, common noise sources and artifacts, and preprocessing techniques, including amplification and Analog-to-Digital Conversion (ADC), which play a critical role in ensuring high-quality data for real-time monitoring.

3.1 Sensor Technologies and Data Acquisition Circuits

The acquisition of biomedical signals begins with the use of various sensors and data acquisition circuits designed to detect and measure physiological activity from the human body. Electrodes are the most common sensor type for biomedical signal acquisition. For instance, ECG signals are typically captured using Ag/AgCl electrodes placed on the skin, as they offer high conductivity and low skin impedance, ensuring the accuracy of heart signal measurements. EEG signals, on the other hand, are detected using electrodes placed on the scalp. These electrodes can be either wet (with a conductive gel) or dry, with dry electrodes gaining popularity for their ease of use, particularly in wearable applications. EMG signals are captured through surface or intramuscular electrodes, depending on the specific requirements of muscle activity measurement (Lynch et al., 2022). In terms of data acquisition circuits, these sensors are connected to amplifiers and analog front-end (AFE) circuits, which are responsible for boosting weak biomedical signals to levels suitable for processing. Low-noise amplifiers (LNAs) are employed to amplify the signals without introducing additional noise, while the AFE ensures that the analog signal is filtered, amplified, and prepared for conversion into a digital format. Wearable sensors have become increasingly important in continuous health monitoring, and these devices are designed to be lightweight, non-intrusive, and capable of operating for extended periods. Flexible and stretchable sensors are being developed to improve the comfort and performance of these wearable systems, making them more suitable for long-term monitoring (Chidolue et al,. 2023).

3.2 Noise Sources and Artifacts

Biomedical signals are often contaminated by various noise sources and artifacts, which can significantly degrade the quality of the acquired data. One of the most common sources of noise is power line interference, which introduces 50/60 Hz oscillations that can corrupt ECG and EEG signals. Additionally, electromyographic noise can occur in ECG and EEG recordings due to the electrical activity of muscles, such as those caused by eye movement or facial muscle contractions. This is especially problematic in wearable devices, where the patient’s motion can inadvertently generate noise in the signal (Iwamoto et al., 2022). Electromagnetic interference from nearby electronic devices, such as smartphones or medical equipment, can also distort the signal, making accurate signal processing more challenging.

Another major issue is motion artifacts, which occur when the patient moves during the signal acquisition process. For example, walking, shifting positions, or even normal breathing can create distortion in ECG, EEG, and EMG signals. The placement of electrodes is also crucial in reducing signal distortion, as skin impedance variations can introduce noise, especially in ECG and EMG signals (Ranjan et al., 2022). High skin impedance can cause weak or unstable signals, while low impedance can lead to excessive noise. Effective management of these noise sources is essential for ensuring reliable biomedical signal acquisition.

3.3 Preprocessing Techniques

Once the biomedical signals are acquired, preprocessing is essential for removing noise, amplifying weak signals, and preparing the data for further analysis. Signal amplification is one of the first steps in preprocessing. Since physiological signals are generally weak, amplifiers, particularly low-noise amplifiers (LNAs), are used to increase the signal strength without introducing additional noise. After amplification, the signals are typically passed through band-pass filters that allow only the frequency components of interest to pass through, removing unwanted high- and low-frequency noise.

Next, the analog signals are converted to digital form using analog-to-digital converters (ADCs). ADCs sample the analog signals at a specific rate, ensuring that the digital representation accurately reflects the original signal. The sampling rate is determined by the Nyquist criterion, which states that the sampling frequency must be at least twice the highest frequency component of the signal to prevent aliasing. The resolution of the ADC, typically measured in bit depth, determines how precisely the amplitude of the signal is represented, with higher bit-depth ADCs providing greater precision but requiring more power and resources (Werner de Vargas et al., 2023).

To further clean the signal, artifact removal techniques are applied. These can include methods such as wavelet transforms, which decompose the signal into different frequency components and allow for effective filtering of noise without affecting the underlying signal. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is another technique used to reduce signal dimensionality while preserving the most significant features, which can help eliminate noise in multichannel recordings. Kalman filtering, an adaptive filtering technique, is also useful for estimating the signal in real-time, particularly when noise characteristics vary dynamically.

Finally, normalization is often applied to adjust the signal amplitude and ensure that all components are within a consistent range, making them easier to analyze and compare. By employing these preprocessing techniques, biomedical signals are significantly improved, making them suitable for more accurate analysis, classification, and interpretation.

4.0 ADVANCED SIGNAL PROCESSING TECHNIQUES

Advanced signal processing techniques play a pivotal role in improving the quality and accuracy of biomedical signal analysis. These techniques are particularly important in real-time health monitoring systems, where the need for precise and timely information is crucial for patient care. This section explores some of the most effective advanced signal processing methods currently employed in biomedical signal analysis, including time-frequency analysis, nonlinear filtering, adaptive algorithms, and compressed sensing. Each of these methods provides distinct advantages in terms of handling complex biomedical signals, minimizing noise, and ensuring efficient data transmission for real-time applications (Zhang et al,. 2022).

4.1 Time-frequency Analysis

Time-frequency analysis is a fundamental technique in biomedical signal processing, as it enables the analysis of non-stationary signals—signals whose frequency content changes over time. This is particularly useful for biomedical signals such as ECG, EEG, and EMG, which exhibit varying frequency components over time. One of the most widely used methods for time-frequency analysis is the Wavelet Transform. The wavelet transform allows for multi-resolution analysis, where the signal is decomposed into components at different frequency scales, providing both time and frequency information simultaneously. This capability is particularly beneficial for identifying transient features in the signal, such as abrupt changes in ECG waveforms or spikes in EEG that could indicate irregularities or health issues. Wavelet-based methods, including Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) and Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), are employed to detect events at multiple time scales with high accuracy, making them suitable for real-time applications in wearable health monitoring devices (Pachori et al., 2023).

Another key technique is the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), which breaks down a signal into small overlapping segments and applies the Fourier transform to each segment. This method provides a frequency representation of the signal over time, but unlike wavelet transform, STFT uses fixed time and frequency resolutions. While it is less flexible than wavelet transform, STFT is still widely used due to its simplicity and efficiency in capturing the frequency content of stationary or quasi-stationary signals. Both wavelet transforms and STFT are commonly used in conjunction with filtering techniques to extract significant features for classification, anomaly detection, and disease prediction (Vuojamo et al., 2022).

4.2 Nonlinear Filtering and Adaptive Algorithms

Biomedical signals are often affected by complex, nonlinear noise and artifacts, which traditional linear filters may not effectively remove. As a result, nonlinear filtering techniques have gained increasing importance in biomedical signal processing. Nonlinear filters, such as the median filter and wavelet thresholding, are highly effective in removing impulsive noise and preserving sharp transitions in biomedical signals. For instance, median filtering is commonly used to eliminate spike noise in ECG signals without distorting the R-peaks or other important features of the heart's electrical activity (Satpathy et al., 2022).

Additionally, adaptive algorithms play a crucial role in real-time processing, where signal characteristics and noise conditions vary over time. These algorithms adjust filter parameters dynamically to minimize the error between the desired and actual signal. One of the most widely used adaptive algorithms is the LMS (Least Mean Square) algorithm, which adapts the filter coefficients based on the error signal, making it useful for applications where noise characteristics change unpredictably. Adaptive filtering is particularly effective in canceling out interference from power lines or other external sources, especially in environments where biomedical signals need to be recorded over long periods, such as during remote patient monitoring (Jin et al., 2023). Moreover, Kalman filters, which are based on statistical estimation, can be used for real-time prediction and correction of the signal, improving the accuracy of measurements by compensating for missing or corrupted data.

4.3 Compressed Sensing for Efficient Data Transmission

In the era of real-time health monitoring, especially in mobile and wearable devices, efficient data transmission and storage have become key concerns due to bandwidth limitations and power constraints. Compressed sensing (CS) has emerged as a revolutionary approach to address these challenges by enabling the acquisition of sparse signals at a lower sampling rate than traditionally required, without sacrificing signal quality. The core principle behind compressed sensing is that many biomedical signals, such as ECG or EEG, are inherently sparse in some transformed domain, meaning that they contain a limited number of significant components compared to the total number of samples (Sekar et al., 2022).

Through compressed sensing, these signals can be directly sampled in a compressed form, effectively reducing the amount of data that needs to be transmitted. This is achieved by leveraging the sparsity of the signal in a certain basis (e.g., wavelet or Fourier domains) and using optimization algorithms to recover the full signal from a small number of measurements. In practical terms, this reduces the need for high sampling rates and large storage capacities while maintaining signal fidelity. Compressed sensing is particularly useful in the context of wearable medical devices, where low power consumption and efficient data transmission are crucial for continuous, long-term monitoring (Ma et al., 2023). It also reduces the burden on wireless communication channels, enabling faster and more reliable transmission of health data, which is vital for real-time applications, such as remote monitoring and telemedicine.

Moreover, the integration of compressed sensing with other advanced techniques such as ML further enhances its potential by allowing for more efficient feature extraction and signal reconstruction. The combination of compressed sensing with ML algorithms enables real-time anomaly detection and disease prediction with minimal computational and bandwidth requirements.

5.0 APPLICATIONS AND CASE STUDIES

The rapid advancements in biomedical signal processing have paved the way for innovative applications in real-time health monitoring. These applications are revolutionizing healthcare delivery by enabling remote patient monitoring, enhancing wearable health devices, and improving the efficiency of smart hospital systems. This section explores three key applications of biomedical signal processing: remote patient monitoring, wearable health devices, and smart hospital systems. Each of these areas demonstrates how signal processing techniques are being leveraged to improve patient outcomes, optimize healthcare workflows, and ensure better management of chronic conditions (Paganelli et al., 2022).

5.1 Remote Patient Monitoring

Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM) is one of the most transformative applications of biomedical signal processing, especially in the context of telemedicine. RPM allows healthcare providers to monitor patients' vital signs and other physiological parameters from a distance, facilitating continuous care and reducing the need for in-person visits. Using wearable sensors and mobile technologies, patients can transmit real-time data such as ECG, heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation to healthcare professionals. Signal processing techniques are crucial in these systems for extracting meaningful information from the raw data, detecting anomalies, and providing timely alerts to both patients and healthcare providers (Shaik et al., 2023).

Advanced signal processing methods like adaptive filtering, wavelet transforms, and ML algorithms are integrated into RPM systems to enhance signal accuracy, reduce noise, and ensure the reliability of data transmission over wireless networks. For example, by processing ECG signals remotely, systems can detect arrhythmias or other heart conditions early, enabling healthcare providers to take prompt action. Similarly, EEG signals can be continuously monitored for signs of seizure activity, alerting caregivers before a potential seizure occurs. The combination of these technologies in RPM systems has been shown to significantly improve patient outcomes, especially for chronic disease management, elderly care, and post-surgical recovery (Tang et al., 2022).

Case studies like the Philips eICU program and AliveCor's KardiaMobile demonstrate the successful application of remote monitoring systems in real-world settings. These platforms leverage advanced signal processing and wireless communication to provide healthcare providers with real-time, actionable insights, enhancing patient care while reducing hospital readmissions.

5.2 Wearable Health Devices

Wearable health devices are rapidly becoming an integral part of personal health management, offering individuals the ability to monitor their health in real-time. These devices—ranging from fitness trackers to more sophisticated medical-grade wearables—use sensors to capture various physiological signals such as ECG, EMG, EEG, and accelerometer data. The data collected by these sensors is processed using advanced signal processing techniques to extract meaningful features, which can be used for both health monitoring and disease detection.

Wearables are particularly useful for continuous monitoring of heart health, detecting early signs of cardiovascular diseases, and tracking physical activity. For example, smartwatches with built-in ECG sensors can detect arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation, and provide users with the ability to share results with healthcare professionals remotely (Prieto-Avalos et al., 2022). AliveCor's KardiaMobile is a prominent case study in this field, offering a portable ECG device that allows users to perform an ECG test in just 30 seconds and send the results directly to their doctor. This real-time monitoring capability enhances early detection of heart conditions, enabling timely interventions before more serious complications arise. Similarly, wearable EEG headsets can monitor brain activity in patients with neurological disorders, such as epilepsy, and predict seizures through real-time signal processing of EEG data. This is particularly beneficial for patients who may not have easy access to frequent medical appointments. EMG-based wearables, such as those used in muscle rehabilitation, monitor muscle activity and provide valuable feedback for patients undergoing physical therapy or those managing musculoskeletal disorders.

The importance of advanced signal processing in wearable health devices cannot be overstated. Techniques such as real-time filtering, motion artifact removal, and feature extraction are essential to ensure the accuracy of measurements, especially when the device is worn during daily, dynamic activities. For example, wearables like the Fitbit, Apple Watch, and Oura Ring have made significant strides in this area by incorporating algorithms that minimize motion-related noise and improve signal clarity. These devices not only enable users to track their vitals, such as heart rate and sleep patterns, but also promote health awareness and early intervention by alerting users to potential health concerns, such as abnormal heart rates or irregular sleep cycles. These advancements in wearable technology are empowering individuals to take charge of their health, offering a proactive approach to disease prevention and management (Dai et al,. 2022).

5.3 Smart Hospital Systems

Smart hospital systems integrate cutting-edge technologies such as biomedical signal processing, the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and big data analytics to significantly enhance healthcare delivery within hospital settings. These systems are designed to continuously monitor patient health, optimize hospital workflows, and improve patient safety through real-time data collection and analysis. Biomedical signal processing plays a vital role in ensuring the accuracy and reliability of the data generated by a variety of hospital sensors, including vital signs monitors, infusion pumps, diagnostic equipment, and wearable devices. By applying advanced signal processing techniques, these systems can extract meaningful information from complex physiological signals, improving both clinical accuracy and response times.

In critical care settings like ICUs, smart hospital systems use advanced monitoring systems to continuously process signals such as ECG, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, and other vital signs. These systems are equipped with AI-driven algorithms that can detect early warning signs of patient deterioration, such as arrhythmias, septic shock, or respiratory distress. Upon identifying critical changes in patient conditions, the system automatically triggers alerts to clinical staff, enabling rapid interventions to prevent further complications. Machine learning (ML) algorithms also analyze historical and real-time patient data to uncover subtle patterns, predict adverse events, and assist in decision-making, reducing the likelihood of medical errors and improving clinical outcomes.

In addition to real-time patient monitoring, smart hospital systems leverage the IoT to interconnect various medical devices, enabling centralized monitoring and control. By creating a network of interconnected devices, the IoT allows for seamless communication between equipment and clinicians, ensuring that important data from multiple sources is synchronized and processed in real-time. For example, in a smart ICU, an array of devices continuously monitors patients' vital signs, analyzes trends over time, and shares the data with healthcare professionals via a centralized platform. This integration of IoT technology ensures that critical information is accessible at the point of care, enhancing clinicians' ability to make timely, informed decisions.

Furthermore, AI-driven analytics work synergistically with biomedical signal processing to enhance operational efficiency across the hospital. AI models can analyze large volumes of hospital data, from patient records to inventory management, to optimize resource allocation, streamline workflows, and reduce hospital bottlenecks. These systems can predict patient admission rates, manage staffing schedules, and monitor the supply chain, contributing to more efficient hospital operations. Ultimately, the integration of IoT with biomedical signal processing and AI is fundamental in creating a dynamic, responsive, and data-driven healthcare environment, where both patient monitoring and hospital operations are continuously improved to ensure better care and operational efficiency. (Kwon et al., 2022).

Case studies such as the Mount Sinai Health System in New York and the St. Gallen University Hospital in Switzerland have demonstrated the potential of smart hospital systems in improving patient outcomes. These hospitals have integrated biomedical signal processing techniques with IoT-enabled devices and AI to enhance monitoring, patient care, and operational efficiency.

6.0 EMERGING TRENDS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

The field of biomedical signal processing is evolving rapidly, driven by breakthroughs in Artificial Intelligence (AI), quantum computing, and advanced telecommunications technologies like 6G networks. These innovations promise to reshape how healthcare is delivered, improving both the quality and accessibility of care (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2023). This section delves into two of the most promising emerging trends in biomedical signal processing: the integration of AI and quantum computing in signal processing, and the role of 6G networks in transforming healthcare systems.

6.1 AI and Quantum Computing in Signal Processing

AI has already had a profound impact on biomedical signal processing, particularly through the use of ML algorithms that can analyze large, complex datasets in real time. AI-powered tools have enhanced signal classification, anomaly detection, and predictive modeling, enabling early disease detection and more accurate health monitoring. However, the integration of quantum computing into this space could revolutionize the way we process and analyze biomedical signals.(Mallow et al., 2022)

Quantum computing, with its ability to process vast amounts of data simultaneously, offers exponential improvements in computational power compared to classical computers. Quantum algorithms could enable the rapid processing of high-dimensional signal data, which would be particularly beneficial in areas such as genomic signal processing and multimodal sensor fusion. For instance, biomedical signal processing in EEG or ECG could benefit from quantum ML algorithms, enabling faster and more accurate classification of complex signals with lower computational overhead.

In particular, quantum-enhanced ML could be leveraged to improve signal feature extraction, anomaly detection, and predictive health analytics. Quantum computers can also handle large datasets with complex correlations, such as those encountered in multi-sensor and multi-modal health monitoring systems, where data from different sensors (ECG, EEG, EMG, etc.) must be fused to provide a holistic view of the patient's health status (Chauhan et al., 2022).

AI algorithms will likely evolve alongside quantum computing to enable quantum AI, which combines the strengths of quantum computing and machine learning. This hybrid approach will allow for real-time, highly accurate predictions of patient health conditions, improving the decision-making capabilities of healthcare providers and enhancing personalized medicine.

6.2 6G Networks for Healthcare

The advent of 6G networks is expected to revolutionize healthcare by offering ultra-fast, low-latency, and highly reliable communication capabilities. While 5G networks have already shown promise in supporting real-time health monitoring systems through faster data transmission and enhanced connectivity, 6G will take this to a new level, enabling an entirely new era of connected healthcare. One of the key features of 6G networks will be their ability to support massive device connectivity, which will be crucial for deploying large-scale Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) systems. These systems will enable continuous monitoring of patients through interconnected devices—such as wearables, smart implants, and remote sensors—all transmitting large volumes of biomedical data in real-time. 6G networks will facilitate this by providing extremely high bandwidth and Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC), ensuring that critical health data can be transmitted instantaneously with minimal delay. This is particularly important for remote surgeries or telemedicine applications, where real-time data streaming is essential for patient safety and surgical precision. (Srinivasu et al., 2022)

The improved data throughput and reduced latency of 6G networks will also make it feasible to transmit high-resolution, complex medical images and live biomedical signals, such as EEG or ECG data, from remote locations to healthcare providers or specialists. This enhanced communication capacity will enable remote diagnosis, allowing patients in rural or underserved areas to access medical expertise without the need for travel. Moreover, 6G networks will integrate AI and ML into the network itself, providing intelligent routing of data, predictive maintenance of medical devices, and even real-time decision support for healthcare providers (Ahmad et al., 2023) . The low power consumption associated with 6G will be crucial for the efficient operation of wearable health devices, which rely on long battery life for continuous monitoring.

One of the most promising applications of 6G in healthcare will be the development of smart hospitals, which leverage advanced network capabilities for seamless integration across all hospital systems. These systems will include smart medical devices, patient tracking, and automated healthcare workflows—all interconnected via the 6G network to ensure optimal resource utilization, patient safety, and real-time communication among healthcare providers. For example, in a smart hospital, real-time processing of patient signals will enable immediate action and remote monitoring, while AI and ML algorithms in the network can predict patient needs, optimize bed management, and even improve medical equipment management. (Amer et al., 2023)

In addition, 6G networks will play a transformative role in enabling immersive healthcare applications such as augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) for telemedicine. With the ultra-low latency and high throughput capabilities of 6G, AR and VR will be able to provide more effective and interactive telehealth experiences, from remote surgeries to rehabilitation and patient education. For example, in remote surgeries, surgeons can use AR to overlay critical patient information or 3D imaging onto their field of view, improving precision and reducing the risk of errors. VR will also enhance telemedicine by providing virtual consultations where patients and doctors can interact in a highly immersive, 3D environment, enhancing communication and ensuring better patient engagement. In the realm of rehabilitation, patients can use VR for guided physical therapy sessions, allowing them to perform exercises in a controlled, virtual space while receiving real-time feedback from healthcare providers. The combination of 6G’s capabilities with AR and VR in telemedicine will enable more complex and specialized healthcare applications that were previously impractical, offering a more immersive, efficient, and precise approach to remote healthcare. (Bhardwaj et al., 2022.)

Ultimately, the innovations in biomedical signal processing not only promise to improve patient outcomes but also to reduce healthcare costs, enhance patient satisfaction, and ensure a more efficient and equitable healthcare system. As these technologies evolve, they will continue to play a critical role in bridging the gap between technology and healthcare, driving the future of next-generation health solutions.

Chapter 4

Advancements and Emerging Trends in Deep Learning-Based Transformers for Medical Image Processing

ABSTRACT

The U-net Architecture is a U-shaped neural network developed from Fully Convolutional Networks FCNs in medical image segmentation. However, the traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), like the one in U-Net, poses challenges in addressing long-distance relationships relating to the subject matter hence making their applicability to several segmentation tasks somewhat restrained. To counteract this, extending Transformer modules into U-shaped designs has received considerable interest, as an approach to boosting feature extraction and segmentation effectiveness. This paper also presents an extensive analysis of U-Net and Transformer-related methods and sorts medical image segmentation models based on the position of the Transformer modules.

1. INTRODUCTION

It discusses that deep learning has brought significant changes in feature learning by allowing the neural network models to identify representations by its own. In this article, I consider this capability, which has been enhanced through the incorporation of gradient descent, as a catalyst for progress in a range of domains (Alhatami et al., 2024; Ali et al., 2023; Andrade-Miranda et al., 2023). In the field of computer vision, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have performed quite well, that they have become deeper in order to solve more challenging problems. The fully convolutional U-shaped network U-Net provided skip connections during down-sampling to recreate low feature detail while simultaneously acquiring global features, dramatically enhancing the segmentation efficiency. Since the success of U-Net, it became the base for medical image segmentation and it has finally inspired several derivatives tailored for specific medical applications(Asif et al., 2024a; Asif et al., 2024b;).

However, due to the intrinsic inductive bias of CNNs they are unable to model long range dependencies effectively thus hampering the performance of segmentation. This is a limitation that transformers, with their self-attention mechanism, do not have to overcome as they guard against long-range relationships. The Vision Transformer (ViT) continued the use of Transformer for computer vision by treating an image as a set of patches and processing patch tokens as sequences as in Natural Language Processing (NLP). In the following models like SETR and DETR, the role and possibility of using Transformers in vision tasks like segmentation and object detection were established(Azad et al., 2023; Bhatti et al., 2024; Bhatti et al., 2024;).

However, there are still some problems in employing Transformers for medical image segmentation, which are annotation challenges, highly imbalanced classes, low contrast, and less distinct boundaries in medical images. A small number of medical data also affects the quality of pre-training strategies for the Transformer models in this area. Therefore, it is crucial to find new solutions to apply Transformers in medical imaging(Bhatti et al., 2023; Bhatti et al., 2024).

Transformer has recently emerged as an innovative component for medical image segmentation within the U-shaped network topology; this paper systematically discusses the architectural features and design options for this model(Gao et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024;). We examine the strong and weak points of Transformer-based U-Net models, discuss how Transformer-based models can overcome the shortcomings of U-Net, and provide information about the use of Transformer-based U-Net for medical image processing tasks. Moreover, this paper present future direction towards the advancement of these hybrid model to revolutionize the medical image segmentation.

2. MEDICAL IMAGE SEGMENTATION

Medical image segmentation, a vital task in computer vision, focuses on pixel-level classification to precisely delineate target objects within medical images. These datasets are typically derived from advanced imaging modalities like MRI, CT, and ultrasound (Azad et al., 2023; Bhatti et al., 2024a). Traditional segmentation methods, such as thresholding, region-growing, and edge-detection techniques, offer simplicity and low hardware requirements but often depend heavily on manual tuning to achieve high-quality feature representation. In contrast, deep learning-based segmentation models automate feature learning with minimal manual input, delivering superior performance at the cost of significant computational resources for training(Bhatti et al., 2024b; Bhatti et al., 2023a; Bhatti et al., 2024c; Bhatti et al., 2024d; Bhatti et al., 2023b).

With advancements in GPU technology and memory capacity, training complex deep learning networks has become more accessible, driving their adoption in diverse applications, including medical image analysis. CNN-based segmentation models have been extensively used for tasks such as tumor detection, skin lesion analysis, and retinal vessel segmentation. Among these, U-Net has emerged as a cornerstone in medical image segmentation, particularly in computer-aided diagnosis and intelligent medical systems. U-Net’s design, featuring skip connections to combine low-level and high-level features, has demonstrated significant success across various medical domains (Bhatti et al., 2023c; Bhatti et al., 2024e).

Despite their strengths, CNNs face inherent limitations, including difficulty capturing long-range dependencies and a reliance on fixed-size convolution kernels, which restrict their generalizability. Additionally, the unique challenges of medical images, such as fuzzy boundaries, low contrast, and varying target sizes, demand effective extraction of global contextual information (Bhatti et al., 2024f; Bhatti, Tang, & Wu, 2023). The introduction of Transformers, leveraging a self-attention mechanism originally developed for NLP, addresses these challenges by enabling models to capture long-range dependencies and global context. This capability has driven the adaptation of Transformer-based architectures to medical image segmentation, opening new avenues for improved accuracy and robustness. This paper explores the evolution of segmentation techniques, emphasizing the transition from traditional methods to CNN-based approaches and the recent integration of Transformer models. We highlight the strengths and limitations of each paradigm, focusing on the role of U-Net and its Transformer-enhanced variants in overcoming the challenges of medical image segmentation.

3. U-SHAPED NETWORK

Medical image segmentation is one of the essential and challenging tasks in the medical field, further comprehensive identification and definition of the anatomical structures and pathological change from different medical imaging modalities as MRI, CT, and ultrasound (Bristi et al., 2023; Cao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023a). The U-Net architecture have turned out to be the perfect solution due to its unique design which make it perfect in capturing details and the bigger picture in an image. Basic U-Net structure is shown in Figure. 1.

Figure 1. U-Net architecture

A U-shaped Network (U-Net) architecture is commonly visualized as follows:

Components:

  1. 1. Encoder (Contraction Path):

    • o Series of convolutional layers followed by pooling layers.

    • o Extracts features while reducing spatial dimensions (downsampling).

    • o Captures the high-level context of the image.

  2. 2. Bottleneck:

    • o The central part of the U-Net where features are processed at the lowest resolution.

    • o Often consists of convolutional layers without pooling.

  3. 3. Decoder (Expansion Path):

    • o Series of upsampling layers followed by convolutional layers.

    • o Reconstructs the image resolution while refining segmentation details.

  4. 4. Skip Connections:

    • o Directly connect corresponding layers in the encoder and decoder.

    • o Preserve spatial information and fine details lost during downsampling.

a. Implementation of U-Net and Its Variants for 2D Applications

For multi-scale feature fusion, U-Net introduces encoder-decoder architecture, containing down-sampling for feature extraction, up-sampling to backing up for the missing information and skip connections. This integration enhances the ability of the model to include local and global features into consideration, making convergence to an optimum to be faster and an accuracy of medical image segmentation tasks to be higher(Chen et al., 2024; Chen, Lu, & Xie, 2023).

Since the introduction of U-Net, several modifications have been made based on the same. For example, U-Net++ introduced a concept of decreasing the difference in the feature maps of the encoder section and the decoder section. It achieves this by first introducing intermediate dense skip pathways through which the network can enhance the integration of the feature maps(Chen et al., 2023b; Cheng et al., 2023). This change makes the process of transition between different resolution levels more consistent, therefore provides better accuracy of the segmentation.

Another evolution to this is ResUNet which substitute the traditional convolutional layers of U-Net with residual blocks of ResNet. These residual connections resolve the vanishing gradient issue allowing the architecture to extend compatible with deeper networks without compromising a lot of performance(Cheng, Tang, Bhatti, & Li, 2024; Dong et al., 2023; Fahim, Fadil, & Bhatti, 2023; Fu et al., 2024). Building upon this, ResUNet++ includes Squeeze-and-Extraction (SE) Blocks after each residual block. These SE Blocks essentially use channel attention mechanisms which discard unwanted incoming features to the decoder. It improves the effectiveness of recombined multi-scale feature maps compared with the single-time concatenation procedure in the standard U-Net(Gao et al., 2024; Han et al., 2024a).

These improvements have ensured that U-Net and numerous derivatives are now vital resources in applications such as tumor detection, organ segmentation, and lesion delineation, where accuracy and speed are critical.

b. Application of U-net and its variants in 3D formulate

In 3D image segmentation, U-shaped networks have been extended to deal with volume data to overcome difficulties of 3D imaging modalities as MRI or CT scans. V-Net is one of the most well-known 3D adaptations as the authors remove 2D convolutional layers and apply the 3D convolutions to process the volume data. This is especially important for an accurate segmentation because this approach includes spatial dependencies in all three dimensions. Since there may be a considerable difference in the number of foreground and background classes typical for medical imaging, the authors of V-Net utilize Dice loss to improve the outcomes of segmentation(Han et al., 2024b; Hasnain et al., 2024a; Hasnain et al., 2024b).

Equally, 3D U-Net extends the original U-Net architecture by replacing the 2D operations with the 3D ones. This Flex offers high criterion and elastic characteristics fit well for semi-automatic and fully automatic feature a-segmentation as well. The application of 3D convolutions makes it possible for the network to get important representations from volumetric data and obtain a comprehensive understanding of the interior structures of the human body from the medical images (He & Bhatti, 2024; He et al., 2023a; He, Gou, & Wu, 2023; He et al., 2023b; He et al., 2023c; Huang et al., 2023a).

Its subsequent advancement, named nnU-Net, builds on that and states that data handling – preparation, normalization, denormalization, and specification of hyperparameters – is of equal significance to the deep learning algorithm. Due to a thorough optimization of each of these aspects related to particular datasets and tasks, nnU-Net has achieved a high level of segmentation accuracy with great efficiency, and these findings prove that a more general strategy goes beyond the architecture of the network(Huang et al., 2024a; Huang et al., 2024b; Joysoyal et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2023; Li & Bhatti, 2024; Li et al., 2023a). These 3D adaptations were originally developed and used for medical applications, but have since found their way into other industries including environment and geography. The ability to deal with 3D data has cemented the applications for U-shaped networks across a broad spectrum of use, guaranteeing its applications and value.

4. TRANSFORMER

Fusion of Transformer-based architectures on to U-shaped networks has been a paradigm shift for medical image segmentation, where Transformers excel at global dependency modeling, while U-Net excelled at hierarchical feature modeling(Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2023b; Liang et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Liu, Feng, Huang, & Bhatti, 2024). These hybrid architectures making use of the Transformer’s self-attention mechanism successfully incorporate both long-range dependencies and local context information, thus achieving superior segmentation accuracy in even hard tasks.

Figure 2. Transformers functioning according to need

a. Transformer as Encoder:

In case of a U-shaped network architecture, encoder component can be deemed worthy to extract the required features. Putting the Transformer in the encoder takes advantage of this self-attention to attain dependencies from the low resolution input image, in addition to hierarchical feature extraction which is familiar to convolution operations in convolutional neural networks.

TransUNet

Proposed by Chen et al in 2021, TransUNet is the first work in the Transformer U-shaped network domain, which focuses on medical image segmentation. The technique involves downsampling of image patches within the encoder and serially feeding them through conventional transformer blocks(Liu, Kaul, & Wang, 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2023; Nawaz et al., 2024a). This architecture takes advantage of the Transformer in understanding long-range relationships and enhancing segmentation performance, particularly for the feature map rate at which the SeedNet fails due to low resolution(Nawaz et al., 2024b; Nawaz et al., 2024c; Nawaz et al., 2024d; Nawaz et al., 2023). However, in the case of TransUNet we are experiencing large fixed size block sizes and high attention computation which could be optimized in the following way.

MedT

To overcome the issues related to the size of the dataset, the positioning embeddings of MedT have a gate mechanism included. This mechanism helps generalization ability of the model and makes it a good solution for various medical imaging tasks.

X-Net

X-Net is a dual-encoder-decoder network and the primary segmentation encoder is designed using the Transformers. Further, an auxiliary encoder-decoder based on the convolution performs image reconstruction as the proxy task thus enhancing the feature representation in the Transformer-based encoder(Nizamani et al., 2023; Noor et al., 2024; Pang et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2024a). This dual structure improves the capacity of the network to learn features relevant to its meaningful utilization.

LeViT-UNet

LeViT Vision Transformer is lightweight and fast and when deployed in the encoder portion of the LeViT-UNet model, bent on delivering high segmentation precision with relative low computational cost. It has been exceptionally good on Synapse data set, where it has been placed among the best models based on speed and accuracy(Peng et al., 2024b; Pham et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2024).

TransFuse

BiFusion Block connects CNNs and Transformers in TransFuse and combines their beneficial feature extraction abilities. It further uses a pre-trained model, the DeiT (Data-Efficient Image Transformer), to achieve parameter efficiency without a compromise on feature extraction capability.

Swin UNETR

This model is based on Swin Transformer trained with contrastive learning and random augmentation tasks on large scale CT dataset. Swin UNETR demonstrate the superiority of the pre-training strategy before fine-tuning for 3D medical image segmentation tasks since pre-training on non-target datasets(Reja et al., 2023; Roy et al., 2023; Shao et al., 2024).

b. Transformer in the Decoder Only

Limited use of the Transformer only in the decoder is aimed at enhancing the utilization of the features extracted by encoder.

Segtran

The compressed and expanded attention modules of Segtran are derived from the Set Transformer ISAB (Induced Squeezed Attention Block). The first decreases the effort to compute attention, whereas the second, based on single-head Transformers, improves feature differentiation(Sun et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024a). The semantic and the local continuity is also addressed in Segtran with the help of a learnable sine positional encoding.

This architecture brings performance gain in the second stage of segmentation which is decoding stage because high semantic and fine-grained details are important at this step.

c. Transformer in Both the Encoder and the Decoder

Training the Transformers both in the encoder and in the decoder can allow for the capturing of global context during the feature extraction phase and of further improving it during the reconstruction phase. But this endangers a huge number of retrievals to be made in many cases and often entails a vast amount of computational work.

nnFormer

nnFormer combines CNN and Transformer layers in its encoder and decoder systems in a theoretical way. Multi-scale supervision applied in it make sure that the features of the resolutions are precise. Since ImageNet pre-trained Transformer modules are utilized, the computation burden is reduced while segmentations are made more accurate in this manner(Tang et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023a).

D-Former

D-Former integrates dilated convolution with Transformer modules, which it incorporates local and global context in its architecture. On datasets similar to Synapse, this approach thus reached rather competitive performance while providing a correct segmentation of the input image(Wu et al., 2023b; Xu et al., 2024a; Xu et al., 2023a).

MISSFormer

The Medical Image Segmentation Transformer (MISSFormer) alleviates the problem of sequence length in the attention mechanism through matrix compaction of K and V. There is an emergence of a new skip connection known as the enhanced transformer context bridge that allows proper incorporation of low and high-frequency features. MISSFormer performs all the multi-organ segmentation tasks with relatively less amount of time compared to Swin UNet, though it yields a high level of accuracy(Xu et al., 2023b; Xu et al., 2023c; Yan et al., 2023).

MT Net

Reminder: MT Net effectively use external attention mechanisms for capturing inter-sample relationships and greatly enhancing the performance of segmentation.

PCAT-UNet

In PCAT-UNet, we incorporate convolutional self-attention within and between patches, to achieve a good compromise between global and local features.

d. Transitional Connections

In turn, connecting transformers to each other provides an opportunity to learn global relations from low-resolution feature maps at transitional connections between the encoder and decoder(Yang et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2023a; Yang et al., 2024b; Yu et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2024a).

UCATR

UCATR augments the classic Transformer architecture into the bottleneck stage of the U-Net for the extraction of global context from low-resolution images. skip connections, cross-attention mechanisms improve the segmentation quality by paying attention to important features.

TransBTS

The TransBTS family brings Transformers at the transition level. TransBTSv2 increases the dimensions of the feature space, and has a better parameterization of attention calculation and richer features than those in multiple stacking Transformers.

MS-TransUNet++

To cut the costs of the attention calculation, this model applies depth-wise convolutions, additionally, multiple skip connections help in feature recovery and accuracy of the segmentation.

e. Transformer in Skip Connections

Features related to skip connections can improve the integration of multi-modal features based on transformers situated in these connections. Transformers can better align two feature maps to improve fusion, and skip connections directly connect the encoder and decoder.

HTNet

HTNet incorporates Transformer modules into skip connections features deep and complex mechanisms known as RAPP (Residual Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling) as well as HCA (Hierarchical Context Attention). These modules improve the multi-scale contextual awareness for segmentation and global pixel interaction, further improving the segmentation result.

f. Transformer in the Output Block

The transformers in the output block further enhance the extremely local, highly detailed segmentation map.

RTNet

For DR segmentation, RTNet utilizes a Relation Transformer in the attention module to identify lesion-vascular relationships . Although being quite effective, addressing this issue resulted in the utilization of multiple attention modules that greatly increase the computational complexity of SWiMNet.

As has been noted in most Transformer-based U-shaped segmentation networks, the Transformer is commonly placed in the encoder section. This preference is justified by the Transformer’s ability to target contextual relations which are essential for feature representation. Whereas incorporating Transformers in the decoder helps in feature reconstruction, this positioning cannot achieve optimal usage of the model’s global dependencies(Zhang et al., 2024b). By applying Transformers at transitional stages or within the skip connections, there is the optimum of efficiency and performance. Transitional connections facilitate in capturing global relationships with low computational use because features maps are coarser. In the same manner, the addition of Transformers in skip connections provides better correspondence of encoder and decoder features for efficient feature integration. Depending on the task at hand then the appropriate position of the Transformer should be applied. Essentially, it is suggested to place the Transformer in the encoder for activities where fine-grained feature extraction is needed. Furthermore, feature integration is better achieved by using the Transformer in the decoder or skip connections for the tasks. There are future works that could be employed to employ the advantages of the transformer with lighter attention modules but the computational cost will be cheaper(Zhang et al., 2024c).

5. SEGMENTATION DATASETS

From the table 1, several datasets can be deduced to form a rich base upon which segmentation models can be enhanced especially in medical imaging and other areas. These datasets are designed to meet these requirements in a variety of applications such as organ segmentation, disease diagnosis and histology. For example, the BCV and The Segmentation Decathlon datasets include multi-organ segmentation tasks, which allow one to create models for a very wide range of problems. BraTS, TNBC, and LiTS datasets are Limited diseases such as brain tumor disease, new breast cancer, and liver tumor respectively, promote precision diagnostic accuracy and treatment methodologies(Zhang et al., 2024d). In histopathology applications such as GLAS and PanNuke, extracting Gland and nucleus is vital in cancer investigation. Also, retinal imaging datasets such as renew, drive, stare, chase_db1 are for the segmentation of the blood vessels and lesions that are essential for diabetic retinopathy analysis. Additional segmentation tasks including dermatological and gastrointestinal are also accomplished through ISIC and Kvasir that concern themselves with melanoma and polyp classifying, respectively. Altogether, these datasets stress the significance of domain-dependent resources to establish and assess state-of-the-art segmentation models which has an extensive impact not only in the health care field but in a number of other domains too.
