6. MAMBA BASED SEGMENTATION

Mamba-based segmentation is a process that moves beyond the simple usage of the Mamba formula into today’s method of deep learning(Aamir et al., 2018a). The Mamba algorithm, that originated from the morphological image processing, is effective for segmenting objects regarding geometric and structural features, and thus is most effective where the contact boundaries are most significant. This segmentation methodology is particularly outstanding in the analysis of those complex images that may have indefinite structures and unusual shapes; this is through the use of morphological operators including dilation, erosion, opening and closing to improve on the form and contours of objects. When incorporated into these deep learning platforms, operations developed with Mamba for segmentation will effectively link older image processing methods and more sophisticated neural network techniques(Aamir et al., 2019a; Aamir et al., 2018b).

Precisely, the use of Mamba-based segmentation has been well implemented in the application of medical imaging whereby precise boundary detection is crucial. For example, in tumor segmentation, the method improves the opportunity of precise detail on the edge of the tumor, which is important for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. When combined with CNNs or Transformer structures, Mamba-based segmentation can also perform global and local contextual analysis while maintaining the structural coherence of segmented regions. Moreover, its capability to combine with many a prior/pre- and post-processing methods like denosing or edge detection makes it desirable in complex imaging conditions.(Aamir et al., 2017a; Aamir et al., 2019b; Guan et al., 2021a; Guan et al., 2021b; Guan et al., 2021c)

Borrowing aspects of Mamba into U-shaped architectures such as U-Net or its derivatives adds morphological constancy to the architecture and brings improvements in segmentation using more forgivable boundaries. This is especially beneficial in large or more varied data sets especially for histopathology or multi-organ CT scans. Further, derived Mamba-based segmentation is much faster, if not real-time, it makes it possible to be used in applications such as surgical navigation or even automated diagnostic platforms. These features, in combination with the perfect ability to work in the multi-scale feature extraction make this method a perspective tool in the image segmentation(Aamir et al., 2023c; Aamir et al., 2019c; Guan et al., 2021d; Aamir et al., 2019d; Aamir et al., 2018c).

7. CHALLENGES AND PROSPECTS

7.1 Challenges

Transformers have been found to give excellent results in those applications where there are long dependency models. However, using them in medical image segmentation introduces certain difficulties that are based on the nature of the medical datasets and the complexity of the Transformers(Aamir et al., 2019e; Aamir et al., 2018d; Aamir et al., 2019f). These problems are significant to solve for deployment in medical imaging tasks, as indicated below.

  1. 1. Small Medical Image Datasets

The first is the lack of big annotated medical image datasets which are available for whatever ai is going to be trained on. Putting labels in the medical image also demands a lot of effort, takes a lot of time and is very expensive. This limitation is quite limiting since it limits the number of large datasets which are required for training of deep learning models. Transformers, especially, benefit greatly from large sample sizes since self-attention is used to effectively capture global dependencies. So, when we do not have wide and extensive sets of data, we then risk developing models that over-fit, thus may not be portable and efficient in other contexts (Guan et al., 2021e; Aamir et al., 2023d; Guan et al., 2021f). This issue requires the use of approaches like transfer learning or semi-supervised learning, or unsupervised learning to leverage small sample size.

  1. 2. Many images during diagnosis or treatment need high quality and, therefore, high resolution.

These medical images usually have high resolutions to provide clear images of the internal human anatomy particularly when distal limb parts are involved since they are used in diagnosis and planning processes in treatment. Actually conceived for natural language processing tasks, images should be serialized into sequences before being processed for Transformers. Owing to approaches like Vision Transformer (ViT) where images are transformed into patches, high-resolution medical images are seen as long sequences. These long sequences greatly enhance computational and memory requirements, because the computational cost of self-attention is proportional to the square of the sequence length. This challenge hinders the scalability of Transformers for medical imaging, especially for real-time learning, and so the hypothesis inspires the need to research better attention mechanisms.

  1. 3. Another factor responsible for poor health among women is that most of the women lack position information.

Positional information is critical in medical image segmentation because structures depend on the surrounding space. Specifically, while convolution based architectures such as convolutional neural networks CNNs have inherent positional relationships given by the local receptive fields, the base Transformer architecture described here does not. To overcome this, positional embeddings are incorporated within the input sequences to ensure that the model understands spatial relation. However, these embeddings are specific to the given dataset, and can be sensitive to the imaging modality. This variability, when coupled with other factors, can result in suboptimal performance which underlines the requirement for the creation of far more structurally invariant and generally applicable approaches to encoding positional information.

  1. 4. Specially, the self-attention mechanism only performs within patch calculation.

Since it is computationally expensive, stand-alone pixel-wise attention is generally not used, and attention is usually calculated between patches of images. Though this patch-based approach help to reduce computational load the drawback is that it loses the ability to model the fine-grained intra-patch relationship in the image as demonstrated in the ViT architecture. This drawback is especially intriguing for medical image segmentation since often, microaneurysms or other subtle structures may need pixel distinctions, whereas tumor edges are typically thin. Failing to account for such relations results in imprecise definition of small structures, or even loss of the boundaries, which directly impacts segmentation success. To this end, there remains a need for better approximations to fully recover the original pixels by using fully fledged hybrid models/ attention mechanisms/ or some refined kernel that can provide both faster convergence rate and accurate pixel by pixel estimation.

7.2 Prospects

Building on the advancements in hybrid networks combining Transformers and U-shaped architectures, several promising research directions and future prospects are outlined:

  • • Semi-Supervised and Unsupervised Learning: To meeting the scarcity of labeled data in medical imaging, Transformers can be used to obtain global representations from large-scale data by solving auxiliary tasks. Besides, it is possible to improve classification performance and generalization in the case of semi-supervised or unsupervised training through obtaining high-confidence pseudo-labels.

  • • Integration of Prior Knowledge: It is possible to incorporate the knowledge about shapes and positional priors that would allow the model to concentrate on important features while avoiding multiple fittings of essentially the same thing. This might entail the use of anatomical priors for more accurate representation of structural relationships into designs for better performance for medical image segmentation.

  • • Multimodal Image Fusion: In this way, features from one imaging modality can be complemented with information of features from another imaging modality. For example, the integration of T1-weighted MRI for the structural information visualization, while T2-weighted MRI for the lesion location can produce a better and more accurate segmentation.

  • • Optimized Sampling Methods: Standard subsampling and up-sampling in U-shaped network tend to discard useful high frequency information and create duplicate information. Enhancing better advanced sample methods within the deliberation procedure can monetarily assist in maintaining a richness of noteworthy aspects while simultaneously subduing model intricacy, thereby greatly enhancing model accuracy as well as computational speed.

The outlined research directions emphasize potential future improvements in terms of the design and performance of additional networks with U-shaped structures constructed on the basis of hybrid Transformers to produce promising and clinically beneficial medical image segmentation outcomes.

8. CONCLUSION

The transformers have become a workhorse in deep learning proving their merit in capturing the global context through attention mechanism. This strength is particularly useful in medical image segmentation as dispersed target regions and variability in anatomical shapes are difficult to handle. In contrast to CNNs who make use of local receptive fields and have difficulties capturing long-term dependencies, transformers are designed to learn relation between each point in the image and any other and therefore produce highly accurate and consistent segmentation in cases for which it is challenging.

However, when applied to medical image segmentation, Transformers have main challenges that are as follows: A main limitation is the need to train on large data sets because the self-attention operates on high dimensional space that demands large data for generalization. The key problem with medical image datasets is that they are usually relatively small because of the time and expense associated with annotation. This lack of data hinders transformers from fully exploiting their potential and capacity hence resulting to suboptimalized solutions in the course of solving a problem.

To this end, combining Transformers with U-shaped networks can be seen as moderate solution. U-shaped architectures which we describe in the case of U-Net networks are good at capturing complicated dependencies on local spatial scales due to their encoder-decoder design and skip connections. By combining U-shaped networks with Transformer modules, the resulting hybrid models can harness the strengths of both approaches: the global context modeling of Transformers and the local feature extraction of U-shaped networks. This integration helps to improve the given model concerning the case of proper segmentation where both the big picture and intricate details are critical.

In this paper, we have proposed Transformer-based U-shaped networks and have divided them based on positions of Transformer modules in a network. For example, integration of the Transformer in the encoder captures global relations while integrating it in the decoder attentively reconstructs the segmentation maps with context information. Hybrid designs that incorporate Transformers within the encoder, such as TransUNet, and in the decoder, like MISSFormer, indicate the benefits of such approaches. These models indicate enhanced performance on tasks including the multi-organ segmentation and lesion detection on seldom huge datasets. This paper has presented and analyzed networks and synthesizes the change that may be expected when integrating U-shaped networks with Transformers. They also surpass the drawbacks that originate from each of the arbitrary structures and unveil aspects for further advancement of medical image segmentations. This capacity towards modelling both global and local details makes the Transformer based U-shaped network a path for future investigation and has potential to revolutionise medical imaging diagnostics by enhancing its efficiency.

Chapter 5

Alzheimer’s Disease Detection Using CNN Model

Affaan Shaikh

https://orcid.org/0009-0004-7590-7456

Neuratia Labs, India

ABSTRACT

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a disease of the brain that slowly destroys memory and thinking ability. It is one of the most common forms of dementia in people over the age of 65 worldwide. Early detection of Alzheimer's disease helps medical personnel diagnose this disease, which certainly reduces the risk of death. Therefore, early detection of Alzheimer's disease is an important healthcare issue. In order to achieve accurate and timely diagnosis, and for detection of AD in its early stages, many Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine learning approaches have been proposed using data from brain imaging. AI and ML are used for many medical and health purposes, such as disease detection. In this chapter, the main focus is on the diagnosis and detection of Alzheimer's disease using CNN model. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a deep learning model specialized in detecting and classifying patterns in visual data, commonly used for tasks like image recognition, object detection, and classification.

1. INTRODUCTION

Neurodegenerative Diseases are the group of disorders that affect the brain and the nervous system. They can lead to problems with important functions such as breathing, thinking, talking, memory, balance and heart functions. It is a disease in which the nerve cells in the brain or peripheral nervous system lose their function over time and eventually die (Checkoway, Lundin, & Kelada, 2011).

These diseases are now increasing in the older population in recent years and its detection has become a challenging task for doctors and scientists. The most consistent risk factor for developing a neurodegenerative disorder, especially AD or PD, is increasing age (Tanner, 1992). Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) are three of the major neurodegenerative diseases (Checkoway, Lundin, & Kelada, 2011).

The World Alzheimer Report (2015) estimated that globally there were 46.8 million people living with some form of dementia. Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD) are the two most prevalent progressive neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) (Bharathi & Arunachalam, 2021).

Aside from Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), other notable neurodegenerative diseases include Huntington’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, and multiple system atrophy (Tysnes & Storstein, 2017). These diseases differ in their underlying pathophysiology and symptoms, but they all share the common feature of neuron degeneration (Swerdlow, 2007). AD and PD, for instance, are linked with the accumulation of abnormal protein aggregates (such as amyloid plaques and tau tangles in AD, and Lewy bodies in PD), which disrupt cellular function.

The causes of neurodegenerative diseases are multifactorial, involving genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors (Hardy & Selkoe, 2002). In addition to aging, which remains the most significant risk factor, genetic mutations (such as in the case of familial Alzheimer’s disease or Huntington’s disease) and environmental exposures (such as toxins or infections) have been identified as contributing factors (McGeer & McGeer, 2013). Studies have also highlighted the role of inflammation, oxidative stress, and impaired protein clearance mechanisms in the development of these diseases (Heneka et al., 2015).

The impact of these diseases on individuals and society is profound. Neurodegenerative diseases not only cause physical and cognitive disabilities in patients but also impose significant emotional, social, and economic burdens on families and caregivers. With the global aging population, the prevalence of these diseases is expected to increase, making early detection, diagnosis, and intervention even more crucial Zhou et al., 2020).

Recent advancements in diagnostic technologies, such as neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid biomarkers, and genetic testing, are helping to identify neurodegenerative diseases at earlier stages, providing hope for more effective treatment strategies. Additionally, research into novel therapies, including gene therapy, stem cell treatments, and targeted drug therapies, is underway, offering potential avenues for managing or even reversing the effects of these diseases in the future.

The need for further research into neurodegenerative diseases is critical, particularly in identifying early biomarkers, understanding disease mechanisms, and developing innovative treatment options to alleviate the suffering of millions of people globally (Tetzlaff, 2018).

2. LITERATURE REVIEW

Martinez-Murcia et al. (2019) utilized deep convolutional autoencoders for data analysis in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Tatiq and Barber (2018) suggested in their research that targeting modifiable vascular risk factors could prevent Alzheimer's, as these factors often coexist in the brain and share some modifiable risk factors. Williams et al. (2013) predicted cognitive functioning based on neuropsychological and demographic data using four different models: SVM, Decision Tree, NN, and Naïve-Bayes.

Mehmood et al. (2021) emphasised the early identification of Alzheimer's on magnetic resonance images through mild cognitive impairment detection using structured deep learning with multiple layers for brain tissue segmentation. EI-Latif et al. (2023) highlighted Alzheimer's disease as a neurodegenerative condition characterised by cognitive impairment and abnormal protein buildup in the brain, affecting millions worldwide.

Kavitha et al. (2022) described Alzheimer's Disease (AD) as a progressive neurological condition causing short-term memory loss, paranoia, and delusional ideas, often mistaken for the effects of stress or aging, impacting approximately 5.1 million people in the United States. Ahmed et al. (2018) discussed the increasing prevalence of Neuroimaging for Dementia, a chronic and progressive cognitive decline caused by disease or impairment, presenting a significant challenge in achieving accurate and timely diagnosis.

Patil et al. (2022) highlighted the natural deterioration of physical and neurological functions in individuals as part of the aging process, which can significantly impact some due to specific risk factors. KV et al. (2023) underscored Alzheimer's disease as a global health emergency affecting at least 6 million people globally and being a major contributor to dementia.

Checkoway et al. (2011) focused on neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and ALS, presenting growing health challenges. Molecular epidemiology was emphasized as a tool aiding understanding, diagnosis, and management of these conditions, guiding future prevention-focused research.

3. MACHINE LEARNING

Machine learning (ML) is a rapidly advancing subfield of artificial intelligence (AI) that focuses on enabling systems to learn and make decisions without explicit programming. By analyzing data and identifying patterns, ML algorithms can automatically improve their performance over time, making them highly versatile and effective in tackling complex problems across diverse domains. The performance of this system can improve the learning experience without any complicated programming (Bishop, 2006). These algorithms identify a unique feature or pattern in the given input data that contributes to better decision making. These algorithms are mainly used in applications related to medical images, computer vision, biometric recognition, object recognition, automation, etc (Bishop, 2006; Murphy, 2012).

There are three types of machine learning (Bishop, 2006; Murphy, 2012), such as supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. ML algorithms learn through experience and improve automatically. It finds techniques, trains models, and uses the learned approach to determine the output automatically (Alzubi, Nayyar, & Kumar, 2018).

ML is particularly transformative in medical and healthcare applications, where it is used for disease detection, drug discovery, patient monitoring, and personalized treatment plans. For instance, in the diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders like Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, ML can process large datasets of medical images, genetic information, and clinical data to identify early biomarkers, predict disease progression, and suggest treatment strategies. These capabilities have the potential to revolutionize healthcare by enabling earlier and more accurate diagnoses, which are critical for managing progressive conditions.

In addition to supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, other advanced ML techniques, such as semi-supervised learning and self-supervised learning, are gaining traction. Semi-supervised learning leverages both labeled and unlabeled data, which is particularly valuable in scenarios where labeled data is scarce or expensive to obtain, such as rare diseases. Self-supervised learning, on the other hand, uses the data itself to generate labels, significantly reducing dependency on manual annotation while improving efficiency.

Key advancements in ML include deep learning, which employs artificial neural networks to analyze complex and high-dimensional data. Deep learning has shown remarkable success in areas like natural language processing (NLP), image recognition, and autonomous systems. For example, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely used for analyzing medical images, while recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are effective for sequential data, such as patient monitoring or EEG signal analysis.

Choosing the right machine learning algorithm and tailoring it to the specific dataset and application is crucial to achieving optimal results. Techniques such as hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation, and ensemble learning can enhance model performance and ensure robust predictions. Additionally, integrating domain knowledge into the model design can improve its relevance and accuracy.

Challenges remain in applying ML to real-world scenarios, particularly in healthcare. Issues like data privacy, the need for large and diverse datasets, and interpretability of ML models require careful consideration. Transparent and interpretable models, such as decision trees or explainable AI frameworks, are essential for building trust with medical professionals and patients. Furthermore, ethical concerns, such as algorithmic bias and the potential for misuse, must be addressed to ensure fair and equitable use of ML technologies.

Looking ahead, the integration of ML with other emerging technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and edge computing, is poised to expand its applications further. For instance, wearable health devices powered by ML can provide real-time monitoring and alerts for chronic conditions, enabling timely interventions and improving patient outcomes. As research and innovation in ML continue to advance, its potential to drive breakthroughs in science, healthcare, and other fields becomes increasingly evident.

Choosing the correct existing machine learning algorithm and applying accordingly is crucial to obtain satisfying results.

Figure 1. Roadmap followed

The Machine Learning techniques (Reddy et al., 2020; Abdulsahib & Khalaf, 2021) were applied to Alzheimer's disease datasets to bring a new dimension to predict Disease at an early stage. The raw Alzheimer's disease datasets are inconsistent and redundant, which affects the accuracy of algorithms (Gadekallu et al., 2023; Salman, Khalaf, & Abdulsahib, 2019). Before evaluating machine learning algorithms, the data must be effectively preprocessed for analysis by removing unwanted attributes, missing values and redundant data sets. Creating a machine learning model requires splitting the data into training and test sets. In the following data preparation step, the training data were used to create a model, which was then applied to test data to predict Alzheimer's Disease (Gadekallu et al., 2023; Srinivasu et al., 2021; Khalaf et al., 2020). The model was trained using the training data and the test data was used to test the unseen data. Cross-validation was performed by splitting the data set into three subsets. The model predictions are made using one subset of the data (test data), and the model performance is evaluated using the other subsets (training and validation data). The data had been preprocessed, and we randomly divided it into an 80:20 ratio, with 80% going to training and 20% gone to testing (Khalaf et al., 2020; Abdulsahib & Khalaf, 2018). Figure 1 describes the system workflow for predicting Alzheimer's Disease at an early stage (Khalaf et al., 2020; Abdulsahib & Khalaf, 2018). Figure 2 shows the representation of data splitting.

4. CONVOLUTIONAL NEURAL NETWORK MODEL

4.1 Model Building

The proposed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model is designed with a layered architecture to process and analyze MRI images efficiently. The architecture comprises multiple layers, each serving specific functions to extract and process features for Alzheimer’s disease detection.

  1. 1. Base Model (6-layer CNN):

The base model consists of six primary layers:

  • o Conv2D Layer: Responsible for extracting features from the input images by applying convolutional filters.

  • o MaxPooling2D Layer: Reduces the spatial dimensions of the feature maps, retaining the most significant information.

  • o Flatten Layer: Converts the 3D feature maps into a 1D array for input to the fully connected layers.

  • o Activation Layer (ReLU): Introduces non-linearity to the model, enabling it to learn complex patterns.

  • o Dropout Layer: Helps prevent overfitting by randomly setting a fraction of the input units to zero during training.

  • o Dense Layer: Acts as a fully connected layer for decision-making and classification.

This model uses approximately 32 filters, each of size 3×33 \times 33×3, and the input to these layers consists of preprocessed MRI images.

  1. 2. Extended Model (15-layer CNN):

The extended CNN model is designed to enhance accuracy by incorporating more layers, allowing deeper feature extraction. It achieves superior results by processing the input data through all its bitwise filters. This architecture includes the following:

  • o 3 Conv2D Layers: Each with 32 filters of size 3×33 \times 33×3, processing the input images sequentially. These layers extract spatial hierarchies of features, such as edges, textures, and higher-order features.

  • o 5 Activation Layers (ReLU): After each Conv2D layer and dense layer, the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation is applied to introduce non-linearity and ensure computational efficiency.

  • o 3 MaxPooling2D Layers: Applied after Conv2D layers to reduce feature map size while preserving important information, with a pool size of 2×22 \times 22×2.

  • o 1 Flatten Layer: Converts the multi-dimensional feature maps into a 1D array suitable for fully connected layers.

  • o 2 Dense Layers: The first dense layer has 64 neurons and applies ReLU activation, acting as a feature aggregator. The second dense layer has 2 neurons with a softmax activation, performing binary classification (e.g., Alzheimer’s vs. Healthy).

  • o 1 Dropout Layer: Includes a 50% dropout rate to minimize overfitting by randomly disabling neurons during training.

4.2 Model Workflow

  1. 1. Input:

The model accepts MRI images with a predefined input shape of (INPUT_SIZE,INPUT_SIZE,3)(\text{INPUT\_SIZE}, \text{INPUT\_SIZE}, 3)(INPUT_SIZE,INPUT_SIZE,3). This shape accommodates RGB images, though grayscale images can also be preprocessed to fit this input structure.

  1. 2. Initial Feature Extraction:

The input is processed by the first Conv2D layer, where 32 filters of size 3×33 \times 33×3 are applied. This layer identifies low-level features like edges and corners. ReLU activation ensures that only positive feature values are propagated forward. A MaxPooling2D layer then downsamples the feature map, reducing its size to improve computational efficiency and mitigate overfitting.

  1. 3. Deeper Feature Extraction:

Two additional Conv2D layers follow, each extracting higher-level features from the images. These layers are also accompanied by ReLU activation and MaxPooling2D for downsampling.

  1. 4. Flattening:

After feature extraction, the output of the final MaxPooling2D layer is flattened into a 1D array by the Flatten layer, making it compatible with the fully connected layers.

  1. 5. Fully Connected Layers:

    • o The first dense layer with 64 neurons aggregates the extracted features into a meaningful representation.

    • o The Dropout layer, with a dropout rate of 0.5, reduces overfitting by deactivating 50% of neurons randomly during training.

    • o The second dense layer, with 2 neurons and a softmax activation function, generates probability scores for the two output classes, enabling binary classification.

The deeper architecture allows the model to capture complicated patterns and relationships in the data, resulting in higher accuracy. The added Conv2D and activation layers improve feature extraction, while the dropout layer effectively addresses overfitting issues.

4.3 Training And Testing

The training of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for Alzheimer’s disease detection involves a systematic and comprehensive approach designed to optimize performance while ensuring robustness. This process leverages an organized Support Vector Machine (SSVM) framework and propagates its sub-gradient through the network. Although training CNN models is inherently complex, advancements in methods and frameworks have recently facilitated this task. Below is a detailed breakdown of the process, merging and refining the descriptions for clarity and quality.

4.3.1 Training Process

  1. 1. Organized Framework and Sub-gradient Propagation: The training process begins with the utilization of the SSVM framework, which organizes the training pipeline systematically. By employing an approximate sub-gradient method and a quick derivation strategy, the optimization of the CNN model becomes feasible. These strategies ensure efficient propagation of gradients through the network, even for challenging MRI data.

  2. 2. Whole-image Training: To enhance inference performance, the CNN model is trained on complete MRI images, mirroring the testing conditions where the model processes entire images. This alignment ensures that the model learns to handle complete data effectively, improving its real-world applicability.

  3. 3. Iterative Refinement: Training involves a multi-stage iterative refinement process. The initial model is trained on a dataset comprising MRI images ranging from mild dementia to severe dementia. This dataset provides a baseline for performance evaluation, highlighting areas for improvement. Hyperparameters are then adjusted, and certain layers are modified based on these findings to improve the model's accuracy. This refinement continues iteratively until the desired performance metrics are achieved.

4.3.2 Testing Process

  1. 1. Evaluation on Hard Negative Samples: Testing includes challenging the model with hard negative samples to evaluate its robustness and reduce false positives. This is crucial in building a resilient model capable of handling ambiguous or complex cases effectively.

  2. 2. Five-stage Protocol: The testing protocol is designed to comprehensively evaluate the model's performance and ability to generalize. This involves:

    • o Baseline Evaluation: Initially, the model is trained and tested on the same dataset to establish a baseline for its performance. Metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score are assessed during this phase.

    • o Quality and Similarity Levels: The model is tested at four levels using images of varying quality and similarity. This helps evaluate the model’s adaptability and its capacity to handle diverse data characteristics.

    • o Calibration: Based on the results, the model is recalibrated by fine-tuning hyperparameters or modifying layers. This iterative adjustment focuses on improving the model's weak areas identified during baseline evaluation.

    • o Cross-dataset Testing: The refined model is tested on datasets with differing characteristics to measure its ability to generalize and learn from new data.

    • o Final Evaluation: After successive iterations, the model is evaluated on datasets with decreasing similarity to the training data, ensuring its robustness across diverse scenarios.

4.3.3 End-to-End Training Benefits

End-to-end training of CNN models has proven advantageous in various applications, including Alzheimer’s disease detection. By focusing on complete image datasets and iterative refinement, the model gains the following advantages:

  • • Optimized Inference Performance: Training on whole images ensures alignment with real-world testing scenarios, enhancing prediction accuracy.

  • • Generalization Capability: Cross-dataset testing fosters the model's ability to generalize across diverse MRI data, making it applicable in different clinical settings.

  • • Adaptability: Fine-tuning hyperparameters and modifying layers iteratively improve the model’s learning capacity and adaptability to new datasets.

4.4 Validation

Validation of a CNN model is a crucial step in assessing its performance and generalisation capabilities. Approval of a CNN model includes assessing its exhibition on a different dataset (approval set) to guarantee that it sums up well to unseen data. This interaction recognizes potential overfitting and gives bits of knowledge into the model's general adequacy. validation of a CNN model ensures that it generalises well to unseen data and helps in making informed decisions regarding model architecture and hyperparameters. It plays a crucial role in the development and deployment of deep learning models.

Validation can be explained using following ways:

  1. 1. Data Splitting:

    • ● The dataset is usually split into three subsets: training set, validation set, and test set.

    • ● The training set is used to train the model, the validation set is used to tune hyperparameters and assess performance during training, and the test set is used for final evaluation after model training.

  2. 2. Training the Model:

    • ● During training, the CNN model learns to map input data to corresponding labels by minimising a chosen loss function.

    • ● The parameters of the model are iteratively updated using optimization algorithms (Koushik, n.d.).

  3. 3. Validation during Training:

    • ● At the end of each training epoch (a complete pass through the training dataset), the model's performance is evaluated on the validation set.

    • ● Metrics such as accuracy, pre precision, recall and F1-score can be calculated to evaluate the performance of the model (Deepchecks, n.d.).

    • ● If the model meets the desired performance criteria on the test set, it can be deployed for making predictions on real-world data.

6. FLUTTER APPLICATION

Flutter is introduced as a compact User Interface (UI) tool intended to help cross-stage application improvement. By giving its own sources or options of interface parts, interface platforms instrument and quick advancement cycle, the structure intends to compare with local and cross-stage solutions. Flutter is a cross-platform framework aimed at developing high-performance mobile applications. In Flutter, every application is written using Dart. Google has developed and maintained a programming language called Dart (Tashildar et al., 2020).

Flutter adopts a highly efficient and versatile approach to cross-platform application development, enabling developers to create seamless, high-performing apps for multiple platforms with a single codebase. Developed by Google, Flutter provides its own set of application programming interfaces (APIs), a powerful rendering engine, and an array of foundational libraries to build visually appealing and functionally robust applications.

At the core of Flutter's architecture is its rendering engine, which eliminates the reliance on platform-specific UI components. Instead, Flutter directly renders its own user interface elements, such as buttons, text fields, and other widgets, ensuring consistency across Android, iOS, and other platforms. This approach enables Flutter to deliver a native-like look and feel, enhancing the user experience.

Flutter is built with a robust framework that includes its own graphics engine, Skia, which handles animations, graphics, and file management with precision. The rendering pipeline efficiently processes layout, painting, and compositing to deliver high-quality visuals and smooth animations. By avoiding overly complex layouts that require deep calculations for intricate widget trees, Flutter achieves a balance of simplicity, speed, and flexibility.

As an open-source software development kit (SDK), Flutter provides developers with the freedom to create apps that cater to the aesthetics and functionality expected by both Android and iOS users. Its pre-designed widgets follow Material Design and Cupertino standards, ensuring platform-specific familiarity while maintaining a unified development process.

In addition, Flutter's “hot reload” feature significantly speeds up the development cycle by allowing developers to see changes to the code in real time without having to restart the entire application. This boosts productivity and facilitates rapid iteration during the development process.

Flutter’s versatility extends beyond mobile app development, supporting web, desktop, and embedded applications, making it a one-stop solution for building scalable and dynamic applications across various platforms. This makes Flutter a preferred choice for developers aiming to create intuitive, high-performance, and visually consistent applications for diverse user bases.

6.2 Integration with the Model

The Flutter app provides a user-friendly interface for accessing the model's predictions, making it easy for farmers to use the system without any technical expertise (Shoaib et al., 2023).

Integrating the CNN model with the Flutter app involves several steps, including setting up a data server, creating APIs, and handling JSON data. Firstly, you need to deploy your ML model on a server that can handle inference requests from your Flutter app. This server can be hosted on cloud services like AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure. Once the model is deployed, you'll expose its functionality through APIs. APIs act as a bridge between the Flutter app and the ML model, allowing them to communicate seamlessly.

In terms of data flow, your Flutter app sends input data (such as user inputs or images) to the server through API requests. These requests typically include JSON-formatted data, as JSON is a lightweight data interchange format that is easy to parse and transmit. The server processes the input using the ML model, generates predictions, and sends the results back to the Flutter app in JSON format. The app can then parse the JSON response and display the predictions or take further actions based on the ML model's output.

This integration requires careful consideration of data formats, network communication, and error handling to ensure a smooth and efficient interaction between the Flutter app and the ML model deployed on the server. Additionally, proper security measures should be implemented to protect the data being transmitted between the app and the server.

Here’s a more detailed breakdown of the process:

  1. 1. Deploying the ML Model on a Server

To make the CNN model accessible to the Flutter app, you need to deploy it on a server. This process involves several steps:

  • • Model Preparation: Ensure your trained CNN model (e.g., built using TensorFlow, PyTorch, or Keras) is converted into a format suitable for deployment, such as TensorFlow SavedModel, ONNX, or PyTorch ScriptModule. Optimize the model for inference by reducing its size or increasing its speed using techniques like quantization or pruning.

  • • Choosing a Hosting Platform:

    • o Cloud Services: Platforms like AWS (SageMaker, Lambda), Google Cloud (AI Platform), Azure (Machine Learning Studio), or Heroku allow you to host your model.

    • o On-premises Server: If cloud services aren't an option, you can set up the model on a local or on-premises server using frameworks like Flask or FastAPI for Python.

    • o Edge Deployment: For lightweight models, deployment directly on mobile devices using tools like TensorFlow Lite or CoreML might also be considered.

  • • Creating a Backend Service: Develop a backend service to expose your model's functionality. Frameworks such as Flask, FastAPI, or Django can be used to build APIs that handle input data, run inferences using the model, and return the predictions.

    1. 2. Creating APIs for Communication

APIs serve as the intermediary between the Flutter app and the ML model. The key steps in creating these APIs include:

  • • Defining API Endpoints: Determine the types of requests your Flutter app will make, such as:

    • o Prediction API: Accepts input data (e.g., an image or text) and returns the CNN model's predictions.

    • o Status API (Optional): Reports the server's health and ensures the model is operational.

  • • Handling Requests:

    • o Input Data Formatting: Define the format for inputs (e.g., JSON for structured data or binary streams for image uploads).

    • o Output Data Formatting: Ensure the response is sent in JSON format, containing the prediction results and metadata (e.g., confidence scores or classes).

  • • Integrating Middleware:

    • o Implement middleware for logging, authentication, and error handling.

    • o Use tools like Postman to test the API endpoints thoroughly before connecting them to your Flutter app.

      1. 3. Setting up the Flutter App

The Flutter app needs to be capable of sending requests to the server and receiving the results. Here’s how you can do it:

a. Sending Input Data

Flutter provides libraries like http or dio to make HTTP requests. The steps include:

  • • User Input: Collect data from the user, such as an image captured using the camera or uploaded from the gallery.

  • • Preprocessing: If needed, preprocess the data (e.g., resizing images to match the CNN model's input dimensions or normalizing pixel values).

  • • Creating API Requests: Package the input data in the required format (JSON, base64, or multipart form data) and send it to the server using a POST or GET request.

import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:http/http.dart' as http;

Future<void> sendImageToServer(String imagePath) async {

var request = http.MultipartRequest('POST', Uri.parse('http://your-server.com/predict'));

request.files.add(await http.MultipartFile.fromPath('file', imagePath));

var response = await request.send();

if (response.statusCode == 200) {

var responseData = await response.stream.bytesToString();

print('Prediction: $responseData');

} else {

print('Error: ${response.statusCode}');

}

}

b. Receiving and Parsing Predictions

  • • JSON Response Parsing: Parse the prediction results returned by the API using Flutter’s built-in dart:convert library.

import 'dart:convert';

void parseResponse(String response) {

var data = jsonDecode(response);

print('Prediction: ${data['prediction']}');

}

  • • UI Updates: Use the parsed data to update the app’s UI, such as displaying the prediction label or charting confidence scores.

    1. 4. Handling Network Communication and Errors

Ensuring robust network communication is vital for a smooth user experience:

  • • Error Handling:

    • o Check for common errors like timeouts, server unavailability, or invalid inputs.

    • o Display user-friendly error messages for issues like poor network connectivity.

  • • Retry Mechanism:

    • o Implement retry logic for failed requests using libraries like dio_retry.

  • • Data Compression: Use compression techniques (e.g., gzip) to reduce payload sizes for faster transmission.

    1. 5. Ensuring Security

Protecting the data exchanged between the Flutter app and the server is critical:

  • • Encryption: Use HTTPS to encrypt data in transit.

  • • Authentication: Secure API endpoints with authentication mechanisms like OAuth, API keys, or JWT tokens.

  • • Input Validation: Prevent malicious inputs by validating data on both the client and server sides.

    1. 6. Optimizing Performance

For a responsive app:

  • • Minimize Latency: Deploy the server in a region close to your target users.

  • • Asynchronous Operations: Use Flutter’s async and await for non-blocking API calls.

  • • Batching Requests: Reduce the number of API calls by batching inputs when possible.

    1. 7. Testing and Deployment

  • • Testing:

    • o Simulate different scenarios such as high traffic, edge cases, and unexpected inputs.

    • o Use tools like JMeter or Postman for stress testing the server.

  • • Deployment:

    • o Continuously monitor the system using tools like CloudWatch (AWS) or Stackdriver (Google Cloud).

    • o Plan updates to the app and server carefully to maintain compatibility.

By following these steps, you can seamlessly integrate a CNN model with a Flutter app, enabling robust and efficient machine learning-powered functionalities.

7. RESULTS

The Alzheimer's disease detection application is designed to provide a simple yet effective tool for early diagnosis based on MRI scans, leveraging the power of machine learning. The app allows users to select an MRI image from their device's gallery, providing flexibility and ease of use. Once the image is chosen, the app processes the MRI data and uses a trained machine learning model to assess whether the scan indicates the presence of Alzheimer's disease.

At the core of the application is a Simple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a well-established architecture for image classification tasks. CNNs are particularly well-suited for processing visual data, such as MRI images, due to their ability to automatically detect patterns and features within the image. In this case, the CNN has been trained on a dataset of MRI images labeled with Alzheimer's and non-Alzheimer's cases. The model learns to recognize subtle differences in brain structures, such as shrinkage in certain areas, which are indicative of Alzheimer's disease.

The app is developed using Flutter, a popular framework for creating cross-platform mobile applications. Flutter's flexibility allows for the seamless integration of machine learning models with the app's user interface, making it easier to deploy the solution on both Android and iOS devices. Once the MRI image is uploaded into the app, it is passed through the CNN for inference. The model processes the image, extracting relevant features and generating a prediction. This prediction indicates whether the MRI scan shows signs of Alzheimer's disease or not.

The result is then displayed in the app’s user interface in a clear and user-friendly manner. If the model detects signs of Alzheimer's, the app will display a message indicating the likelihood of the disease, providing the user with an early warning. If no signs are detected, the app will provide reassurance, although it will still encourage further consultation with a healthcare professional for a definitive diagnosis.

Overall, the application aims to make the process of detecting Alzheimer's disease more accessible and efficient. By using a machine learning model integrated into a mobile app, the tool allows users to quickly assess MRI images, potentially catching early signs of the disease before more noticeable symptoms occur. This can lead to earlier intervention and better outcomes for patients (Sharma, n.d.). The simplicity of the app, combined with the power of AI, makes it an invaluable tool in the early detection and management of Alzheimer's disease.

8. ETHICAL AND SOCIETAL ISSUES

AI-driven diagnostic tools have the potential to revolutionize healthcare, but their adoption comes with critical ethical and societal challenges that must be addressed comprehensively. One of the primary concerns is accessibility, especially in underprivileged and rural areas. While these tools promise advanced diagnostic capabilities, their benefits can only be realized if they are affordable and accessible to those who need them most. Developing partnerships with healthcare providers, non-governmental organizations, and government initiatives can help deploy these technologies in rural clinics. Subsidies, open-source solutions, and innovative distribution strategies can ensure that the reach of AI tools is not limited to urban or affluent regions but extends to underserved populations as well.

Another pressing issue is bias in datasets, which can significantly affect the fairness and accuracy of AI-based diagnoses. Many AI models are trained on datasets that may not fully represent the diversity of global populations. This can result in skewed predictions that favor certain ethnic or demographic groups while disadvantaging others. For example, a model trained predominantly on data from urban, Western populations might underperform when diagnosing diseases in individuals from rural or developing areas. To mitigate this, it is crucial to curate balanced datasets from diverse global sources. By including data that reflects the varied genetic, cultural, and environmental factors of different populations, developers can create models that provide equitable and unbiased healthcare outcomes.

Data privacy is another critical consideration, as healthcare data is highly sensitive. Compliance with strict regulations, such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe, is essential to safeguard patient information. AI systems should be designed to anonymize patient data, ensuring that no personal identifiers are stored or used inappropriately. Moreover, secure protocols for data storage and processing must be implemented, utilizing encryption and other advanced security measures to protect against breaches. These safeguards are vital for building trust among patients and healthcare providers who rely on these tools.

The broader societal impact of AI diagnostics is also significant. On the one hand, these tools can alleviate the burden on overtaxed healthcare systems by providing faster and more accurate diagnoses, allowing medical professionals to focus on complex cases. For instance, AI models can quickly analyze imaging data or detect early signs of diseases that might be missed by human practitioners, improving overall efficiency. On the other hand, it is crucial to ensure that these technologies complement, rather than replace, expert medical opinions. Patients and providers must view AI as an aid to medical decision-making rather than a standalone authority. Maintaining this balance is essential for preserving trust in both AI and the medical profession.

Addressing these ethical and societal issues will not only enhance the adoption of AI diagnostic tools but also ensure that their implementation aligns with the core values of fairness, accessibility, and human-centered care.

9. CHALLENGES AND SOLUTIONS

9.1 Data Scarcity and Insufficient Labeled Data

Challenge: One of the major hurdles in implementing CNNs in medical imaging for Alzheimer’s disease detection is the scarcity of labeled data. High-quality labeled medical datasets are essential for training deep learning models, but these datasets are often small due to privacy concerns, cost of data collection, and the expertise required for labeling medical images. This lack of data can hinder the training and generalization capabilities of models.

Solution: To overcome this issue, researchers employed data augmentation techniques, including image transformations such as flipping, rotation, and scaling, to artificially increase the dataset size. Additionally, transfer learning was used by leveraging pre-trained models on large datasets (e.g., ImageNet) and fine-tuning them on smaller medical datasets. This approach allows the model to benefit from previously learned features, reducing the need for large amounts of labeled data (Litjens et al., 2017; Tajbakhsh et al., 2016).

9.2 Class Imbalance in Data

Challenge: In medical datasets like those for Alzheimer’s detection, class imbalance is a common problem. For example, early-stage Alzheimer’s images are less frequent compared to normal or advanced Alzheimer’s stages, leading to biased model training. This imbalance can cause the model to be biased towards the majority class, limiting its ability to accurately detect early-stage AD (Nithya et al., 2024).

Solution: Oversampling techniques such as Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) were used to generate synthetic samples for the underrepresented classes. Additionally, loss function modifications (e.g., weighted cross-entropy loss) were implemented to penalize the model more for misclassifying minority class samples, ensuring better balance in the learning process (Chawla et al., 2002; Buda et al., 2018).

9.3 Overfitting Due to High Dimensionality of Medical Data

Challenge: The high dimensionality of medical imaging data, such as MRI scans, often leads to overfitting in deep learning models. This occurs when the model memorizes the training data, rather than learning generalizable patterns, which reduces its performance on unseen test data.

Solution: To address overfitting, techniques like dropout layers and L2 regularization were implemented to reduce model complexity and prevent overfitting. Dropout randomly drops a fraction of the neurons during training to prevent the network from relying too heavily on any single feature. L2 regularization penalizes large weights in the network, further mitigating overfitting (Srivastava et al., 2014; Ng, 2004).

9.4 Model Interpretability in Medical Applications

Challenge: Deep learning models, particularly CNNs, are often criticized as “black-box” models because it’s difficult to understand the rationale behind their predictions. In medical imaging, such lack of interpretability can be a significant barrier to clinical adoption, where understanding how a model arrived at a decision is crucial for clinicians' trust and decision-making.

Solution: To improve interpretability, techniques like Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) were used to highlight regions of the MRI scan that the model focused on when making predictions. This visual explanation allows clinicians to understand which parts of the image contributed most to the model’s decision, thereby increasing transparency and trust (Selvaraju et al., 2017; Ribeiro et al., 2016).

9.5 Real-World Generalization and External Validation

Challenge: Although CNN models may achieve high accuracy in controlled research environments, they often face challenges in generalizing to real-world data. Variations in patient demographics, image acquisition techniques, and scanner models can lead to performance degradation when the model is applied outside the training set.

Solution: To enhance generalization, domain adaptation techniques were applied to make the model robust to data variations. This includes training the model on datasets from different hospitals or geographic regions, ensuring that it can handle diverse real-world conditions. Cross-validation techniques using data from multiple institutions were also employed to test the model's generalizability (Guan & Liu, 2021; Zhou et al., 2020).

10. CONCLUSION

The detection of Alzheimer's disease using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), specifically through Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), has emerged as a promising and innovative approach in the medical field. CNNs, a class of deep learning models particularly effective in processing visual data, have proven to be highly effective in analyzing medical images such as MRI scans to detect early signs of Alzheimer's disease. These models are trained to recognize patterns and anomalies in brain scans that could indicate the presence of neurodegenerative changes associated with Alzheimer's, such as atrophy in specific brain regions.

The literature review on Alzheimer's disease detection via AI and CNNs highlights a growing body of research exploring various methodologies, data sources, and model architectures. Many studies have demonstrated the potential of CNNs to improve diagnostic accuracy, reduce human error, and offer faster detection compared to traditional methods. The review likely outlines different approaches, such as using pre-trained CNN models on large medical datasets (e.g., ADNI, a well-known Alzheimer's database) and fine-tuning these models for specific detection tasks. It also likely discusses challenges such as dataset imbalance, computational resources, and the need for high-quality imaging data for training.

In practice, integrating the CNN model into a Flask-based website and a Flutter mobile app makes it accessible and user-friendly, which is critical for real-world applications. Flask, a lightweight web framework, allows for easy deployment of the AI model as a web service, enabling users to upload medical images, run predictions, and receive results through a simple interface. This is particularly beneficial for healthcare providers, clinicians, and even patients who require quick and reliable access to diagnostic tools. On the other hand, Flutter, a popular framework for building cross-platform mobile applications, offers a seamless and responsive user experience on both Android and iOS devices. By leveraging Flutter, the application ensures that users, regardless of their device preference, can access the Alzheimer’s detection tool with ease.

Together, this combination of CNNs, Flask, and Flutter not only exemplifies a practical application of AI in healthcare but also addresses the growing need for accessible, accurate, and fast diagnostics. The real-world application of this technology has the potential to significantly enhance early diagnosis and intervention for Alzheimer's disease, which is crucial in slowing disease progression and improving patient outcomes. Additionally, such AI-driven systems could reduce the workload on healthcare professionals, allowing them to focus on critical cases that require human expertise.

Overall, this integrated approach represents a substantial contribution to the ongoing efforts in using AI and machine learning to combat neurodegenerative diseases, aligning with the broader goals of improving public health through technological innovation. By providing easy access to early diagnostic tools, the project supports timely interventions, which could ultimately change the trajectory of Alzheimer's disease treatment and care.

Chapter 6

An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Tumor Detection and Segmentation in Brain MRI Scans

A. V. Kalpana

https://orcid.org/0000-0003-2289-4968

SRM Institute of Science and Technology, India

B. Bharathi

https://orcid.org/0009-0001-1068-996X

R.M.K. Engineering College, India

ABSTRACT

This chapter presents an automated biomedical image classification system, HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning with Fusion Brain Tumor Analysis), focused on brain tumors—abnormal cell growths in the brain or surrounding tissues that require early, accurate detection for effective treatment. The HBDL-FBTA employs pre-processing to enhance image quality, Swin-UNet-based segmentation for precise region delineation, and fusion-based feature extraction for robust feature acquisition. It uses Humpback Whale Optimization with Simulated Annealing (HSSA) for parameter tuning and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) for reliable classification. Simulations on benchmark datasets, including BraTS2017, demonstrate superior performance, achieving accuracies of 94.51% on ISIC 2017 and 95.38% on ISIC 2020 datasets. Future work will focus on evaluating computational complexity on large-scale datasets, integrating multi-modal imaging data, and developing interpretable deep learning models to enhance clinical adoption and reliability.

1. INTRODUCTION

A wide variety of methods and strategies are used in the vast field of biomedical image analysis to extract, process, and interpret pertinent information from biomedical images (S. Nazir et. al, 2023). It plays a crucial part in clinical practice, medical research, and healthcare administration (M. Obayya et.al, 2022). The duties of automatically labeling or classifying medical images according to their content are referred to as biomedical image classification (S. Chakraborty et. al). Due of the abundance of medical imaging data and the potential for Deep Learning (DL) techniques to assist medical professionals in identifying illnesses and making treatment decisions, the field has attracted a lot of attention recently (M. Di Giammarco et. al, 2022). Medical image analysis seeks to provide radiologists and doctors with instruments for efficient diagnostic and therapeutic procedures (J. Yang et. al, 2023). Medical imaging tools such as CT, MRI, and X-ray can provide anatomical and functional information on diseases and anomalies inside the body without causing any damage (J. Zhu et. al, 2023). Processing is necessary to retrieve meaningful data from medical images since they contain flaws, artifacts, and confounding information (if any exist) (F. Li et. al, 2023). Medical applications have benefited greatly from the contributions of image processing techniques; for example, image-guided surgery, segmentation of images, and registration of images are widely used in medical diagnosis and treatment (S. Maqsood et. al, 2023). DL approaches significantly outperform human professionals in certain domains, such as medical imaging. Massive datasets are used by DL algorithms to forecast complicated tasks.

In tasks involving picture interpretation in Computer Vision (CV), the DL approach has achieved a significantly greater degree of accuracy (A. Shrivastava et. al, 2022). The most efficient type of neural networks for information analysis in a grid-form architecture are convolutional deep neural networks (CNNs) (D. Sharma et. al, 203). The most effective method for medical imaging analysis in recent years has been the DL model, particularly Deep CNN (DCNN) (S. Dash et. al, 2023). When it comes to picture classification tasks, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) perform significantly better than other Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies and can often outperform human domain experts. Concern over the use of AI technology for imaging segmentation and classification in biomedical applications has grown (K. VanHorn et. al, 2022). Although encoder-decoder converter methods are advised, CNN is a more contemporary paradigm for picture classification and segmentation (S. Patel et. al, 2022) (Aamir et al., 2019).

Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning - Fusion based Brain Tumor Analysis (HBDL-FBTA) is presented in this paper. The pictures are first preprocessed and segmented using the Swin-UNet model by the HBDL-FBTA approach. The Xception and Residual Network (ResNet) models then perform the merger of several DL-based feature extractors. Additionally, a Hybrid Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) with Adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (APSO) called HWOA_APSO was used to choose the best hyperparameters for the DL models. The recognition and classification of biomedical images was finally accomplished by utilizing the gated recurrent unit (GRU) method. The HBDL-FBTA algorithm's superior performance is demonstrated by a comprehensive simulation examination.
