Through its revolutionary impact on patient care, diagnosis, and treatment, artificial intelligence (also known as AI) is redefining the healthcare sector. AI analyzes vast amounts of medical data, such as imaging tests, patient records, and scientific literature, using sophisticated algorithms as well as machine learning approaches to produce insightful results that improve clinical decision-making. In order to enhance patient outcomes, machine learning models are especially good at finding patterns in data, forecasting the course of diseases, and creating individualized treatment regimens.

Radiology, pathological conditions, and dermatology are among the medical imaging specialties that have been greatly impacted by AI-powered tools. These tools help doctors identify anomalies more accurately and efficiently by enabling very accurate image identification. Another essential AI technology is Natural Language Processing (the NLP), which makes it easier to analyze medical literature and keeps medical practitioners abreast of the most recent findings. Virtual assistants who offer patients real-time health advice and support are also powered by NLP.

AI improves healthcare delivery in addition to diagnostics by speeding up drug discovery procedures, enabling remote patient monitoring, and using predictive analytics for population health management. AI-driven solutions can improve total healthcare efficiency by identifying at-risk individuals, forecasting future health trends, and allocating resources optimally. AI in healthcare has obstacles despite its revolutionary potential. Important issues that demand attention include data privacy concerns, the necessity of strong legal frameworks, and the significance of combining physician experience with AI capabilities. To overcome these obstacles and guarantee the safe, moral, and successful application of AI, cooperation between AI developers, medical practitioners, and legislators is crucial.

The growing importance of AI in healthcare is reflected in the global market. The market is expected to develop at an outstanding compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 30.6% from 2022 to 2032, reaching a size of USD 280.77 billion by 2032. This quick expansion highlights the growing use of AI-powered technologies to improve healthcare systems throughout the globe, opening the door to more individualized patient care and quicker, more accurate diagnosis.

2. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORKS

An intelligent method for dividing CXR and MRI pictures into abnormal and normal classes for the initial identification of HD, COVID19, and AD that relies on ensemble DNN is examined by Pradhan et al. (2023). CNN was used in the presented method to automatically extract features from photos, while LSTM was used as the final classifier. Additionally, the Hill-Climbing Algorithm (HCA) is used to fit the other parameters while identifying the best possible value for the CNN and LSTM hyperparameters, such as the CNN filter dimensionality and the LSTM unit counts. A novel encoded-decoded structure called DOLG-NeXt is examined by Ahmed et al. (2023), who incorporate three key enhancements over the UNet-based variants. The authors primarily use the ConvNeXt phases driven by SE-Net as an embedded backbone to effectively extract features. Secondarily, the authors retrieve fine-grained contextual feature representation by using DOLG feature components from the decoded. For the classification of biomedical images, Barzekar and Yu (2022) investigate a novel CNN structure called C-Net, which is made up of the concatenation of several networks. Six networks make up the first two components of the architecture, which help with feature extraction to create an inner network for benign and malignant picture classification. Mansour (2022) presents AIFM-CRC, a novel AI-based fusion technique for CRC classification and analysis. Additionally, a classification method for identifying the existence of CRC was the WOA-tuned deep SVM algorithm.

In recent research by G. Habib et. al (2020), a novel deep CNN method for classifying brain tumors was introduced. By using TL to some extent for data distillation, a revolutionary CNN technique could save the requirement to be trained from start, wasting days or weeks. Additionally, weights were created using the Gaussian initialization strategy and subsequently the ReLu activation function in order to increase the trained acceleration using different optimizer approaches. Diagonal Bilinear Interpolated Deep Residual Network (DBI-DRSN) is a novel deep feature extraction and classification method for biomedical pictures created by Assad and Kiczales (2020) . The DBI-DRSN approach classifies the features using the DRSN approach's fine-tuning and incorporates a balance of information or features using the DBI pre-processing approach.

Pang et al. (2019) describe a new fused CNN that combines shallow and deep layer characteristics in the given DNN structure to create an even more accurate and highly effective classification for biological images. Using biomedical pictures, Alanazi et al. (2022) investigate an intelligent DL-allowed oral squamous cell carcinoma detection and classification (IDL-OSCDC) method. GF is used as the pre-processed step in the proposed IDL-OSCDC technique to remove noise content. Additionally, OC detection and classification were done using a DBN approach based on enhanced GOA (EGOA). The EGOA technique was used to perform the hyper-parameter tweaking of the DBN algorithm, which improves the classifier results.

The application of the red foxes heuristic optimization algorithm (RFOA) for diagnostic segmentation of images is suggested by Jaszcz et al. (2022). With the innovative fitness function and the emphasis on equation modification, the heuristics' operation was modified for the analysis of 2D images. To overcome these difficulties, the Harris Hawks optimised convolution networks (HHOCNN) is employed by S.Z.Kurdi et.al (2023). To reduce the rate of false tumor recognition, the brain magnetic resonance (MR) picture was preprocessed, and noisy pixels were removed. The malignant area is then located using the candidate region approach. A lightweight deep learning technique for human gait identification is presented by Khan et al. (2022). Two light pretrained models are first examined and improved in terms of adding more layers and freezing some intermediate layers. The moth-flame optimization approach improves the discriminatory correlation analysis, which can be used to complete the fusion process.

There is a significant research gap in the areas of feature extraction and hyperparameter tuning in the field of medical picture classification. Even though DL algorithms have produced excellent results in this field, feature extraction techniques specific to medical picture characteristics can yet be improved (Guan et al., 2021). The discriminatory strength of a classification model may be enhanced via fusion-based extraction of features, which combines data from various DL techniques. Furthermore, the model performance for the medical picture classification task may be further enhanced by the methodical adjustment of hyperparameters, including those pertaining to network design and optimization strategies. The majority of current literature does not concentrate on applying metaheuristics for hyperparameter optimization. In the end, closing this research gap could lead to more reliable and accurate categorization methods, which would improve clinical evaluation and planning of treatment in the medical industry. As a result, the creation and development of the fusion-based feature extraction procedure using the ResNet and Xception models has been the main emphasis of this work. Additionally, the HSSA can be used to do the hyperparameter tuning procedure.

3. THE PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning-Based Fusing Model for Brain Tumor Analysis) method is a complete framework for automated biomedical classification of images that is presented in this article. The HBDL-FBTA approach's main objective is to precisely evaluate and categorize biological pictures for illness diagnosis, tackling important issues in contemporary healthcare diagnostics. The framework is methodically created, combining several sophisticated stages that complement one another to improve dependability and performance.

To guarantee uniform and high-quality inputs, pre-processing is the initial step, during which raw biological images are enhanced and noise-removed. In order to reduce mistakes and inconsistencies in later processing, this step is essential. After pre-processing, particular regions of interest across the images are isolated using Swin-UNet-based segmentation. By utilizing the Swin Transformer model's capacity to capture combined global and local picture features, the Swin-UNet architecture provides remarkable segmentation precision. Only the most pertinent portions of the image are examined further thanks to this segmentation.

In the subsequent stage, two cutting-edge deep learning models, Xception and Residual Network (ResNet), are used to perform fusion-based feature extraction. The framework captures complex patterns and variations in the biomedical pictures by combining the strengths of different models to extract a wide range of useful features. The framework's representational capability is greatly increased by this fusion technique, which makes it possible for it to distinguish between intricate disease features. For hyperparameter optimization, the HWOA_APSO is used to maximize the performance of the deep learning models. By methodically adjusting the settings, this metaheuristic optimization technique makes sure the models perform to their best ability. The framework is more reliable and scenario-adaptive because to the addition of HSSA, which also improves accuracy and computing efficiency.

The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm is used for classification in the last stage. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), of which GRU is a variation, excel in processing temporal and sequential data. The GRU algorithm effectively and remarkably accurately diagnoses and classifies diseases by examining the retrieved features. A comprehensive and reliable analysis of biomedical pictures is ensured by this multi-layered technique, which combines segmentation, feature extraction, optimization, and classification.

Figure 2 shows the HBDL-FBTA framework's comprehensive process, which includes each of these stages. The suggested approach shows great promise to transform biomedical image analysis by fusing cutting-edge deep learning techniques with creative metaheuristic optimization. Its potential as a potent instrument for improving diagnostic precision and efficiency in healthcare applications is highlighted by its capacity to provide accurate and trustworthy disease classification.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for automated biomedical image classification using the HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Meta Heuristics plus Deep Learning-Based Fusing Model for Medicinal Image Analysis) technique. The primary goal of the HBDL-FBTA technique is to accurately assess and classify biological images for the diagnosis of illness, addressing significant problems in modern healthcare diagnostics. The structure is carefully constructed, including multiple advanced phases that enhance performance and dependability.

Figure 2. The proposed HBDL-FBTA Framework

Pre-processing is the first stage to ensure consistent and high-quality inputs, where raw biological images are improved, and noise is eliminated. This phase is crucial to minimizing errors and inconsistencies in subsequent processing. Following pre-processing, Swin-UNet-based segmentation is used to separate certain regions of interest within the images. Using the ability of the Swin Transformer model to collect both local and integrated global picture features, the Swin-UNet architecture achieves exceptional segmentation accuracy. This segmentation ensures that only the most relevant areas of the image are subsequently analysed.

The next step is fusion-based feature extraction using two state-of-the-art deep learning models, Xception and Residual Network (ResNet). The framework combines the strengths of various models to extract a wide range of valuable information, capturing intricate patterns and variations in the biological images. This fusion strategy significantly improves the representational capability of the framework, allowing it to discriminate between complex illness features.

The HWOA_APSO is used for hyperparameter optimization in order to optimize the deep learning models' performance. This metaheuristic optimization strategy ensures that the models operate as efficiently as possible by systematically modifying the settings. The use of HSSA enhances accuracy and processing efficiency while making the framework more dependable and scenario adaptive.

The Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) algorithm is used for classification as the last step in the suggested methodology. GRU is an advanced type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that excels at processing and evaluating temporal and sequential input. In contrast to conventional RNNs, GRU uses gating mechanisms—such as update as well as reset gates—to mitigate the vanishing gradient issue and efficiently manage and maintain pertinent information over time steps. Because of this, GRU is incredibly effective and strong for jobs requiring comprehension of temporal relationships or patterns over time.

The GRU algorithm is essential for accurately and reliably diagnosing and classifying diseases in the framework of biomedical image analysis. GRU can identify intricate patterns and relationships in the data by examining the attributes that were extracted in the earlier phases of the process. These patterns and relationships may be suggestive of particular medical disorders. More accurate classifications are a result of the algorithm's capacity to concentrate on crucial sequential information, which guarantees that minute but crucial aspects in the data are successfully recorded.

The result of a multi-layered strategy that combines segmentation, feature extraction, optimization, and classification is this classification step. In biomedical pictures, segmentation identifies areas of interest, feature extraction extracts significant attributes from these areas, and optimization optimizes the system for optimal performance. Lastly, by utilizing the structured pipeline, the GRU-based categorization offers a thorough and reliable analysis. This comprehensive approach guarantees that biological image analysis is accurate, dependable, and able to support precise medical diagnosis.

Each of these steps is included in the entire process of the HBDL-FBTA framework, which is depicted in Figure 2. The proposed method, which combines innovative metaheuristic optimization with state-of-the-art deep learning algorithms, has the potential to revolutionize biomedical image processing. Its ability to deliver reliable and precise illness classification highlights its promise as a powerful tool for enhancing diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in healthcare applications.

Dataset

The BRATS2017 (Brain Tumor Segmentation 2017) sample serves as a prominent benchmark for the study and segmentation of brain tumors. The dataset consists of 285 MRI scans of brain tumors, each featuring four distinct MRI modalities: T1-weighted (T1), T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1ce), T2-weighted (T2), and Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR). These modalities offer supplementary information, facilitating a thorough analysis of cerebral tissues and neoplastic areas. Each MRI scan is accompanied by masks that delineate three essential tumor sub-regions: the Enhancing Tumor (ET), signifying the actively proliferating tumor area; the Non-Enhancing Tumor Core or Necrosis (NET/NCR), illustrating inactive or necrotic tissue; and Edema (ED), which denotes adjacent swelling or fluid accumulation. The dataset facilitates segmentation assessment across three tasks: Whole Tumor (WT), encompassing all tumor regions; Tumor Core (TC), which contains Enhancing Tumor (ET) and Non-Enhancing Tumor/Non-Critical Region (NET/NCR); and Enhancing Tumor (ET), concentrating on the active tumor region as shown in Figure 3.

Figure 3. Samples of Glioma and No Glioma

Data augmentation techniques are employed to improve model performance and generalizability by artificially enlarging the dataset through the introduction of differences in the original images (Aamir et al., 2023). Prevalent augmentation techniques encompass rotation, to simulate diverse orientations; flipping, for anatomical symmetry; scaling, to identify tumors of varying dimensions; translation, for positional discrepancies; intensity modifications, to accommodate variations in MRI acquisition parameters; and elastic deformations, which replicate natural anatomical distortions. These methods, together with the normalization of pixel intensities across modalities, provide resilient feature learning and reduce overfitting (Aamir et al., 2022). The integration of the BRATS2017 dataset with data augmentation establishes a robust basis for training sophisticated brain tumor segmentation models, enhancing diagnosis, treatment planning, and patient outcomes.

Fusion-Based Extraction of Features

To extract feature vectors from the segmented images, two feature extractors are fused in this phase. In the Xception model, depthwise separable convolution took the place of separable convolution (M. T. Aziz et. al, 2023). An “extreme” version of the Inception architecture called Xception performs better on ImageNet data than InceptionV3 and significantly outperforms it on huge datasets with 17,000 classes. Depthwise Separable convolution requires less compute than separable convolution. As a result, Xception requires less parameters than other CNN variations. The depthwise 2D convolutions used less memory and performed more slowly than standard 2D convolutions. Notably, it achieves excellent computing performance with a comparable number of model parameters as Inception. The presence or lack of nonlinearity after the initial function. By compressing and filtering input space, nonlinearity was suggested in the Inception architecture; however, Xception does not.

In this work, deep feature extraction was done using the ResNet18 version. There are eighteen layers in it. The ResNet18 architecture, which has 11,511,784 trainable parameters, was first pre-trained on the thousand classes found in the ImageNet datasets. Enabling a large number of convolutional layers is the primary goal. The network's performance deteriorates or becomes saturated because of vanishing difficulties. The network performance deteriorates when there are more layers because a vanishing gradient occurs, and the constant multiplication produces a gradient that is even smaller than the previous one. To solve the gradient vanishing problems, a novel idea known as “skip connection” was presented in this paper. By utilizing the previous layer activation, the skip connection fixes the gradient disappearing issues. By compressing the network, skip connections enable the network to learn more quickly than before.

Classification Based on GRU

Lastly, the classification of images is done using the GRU technique. The LSTM modules are reconstructed by the GRU network while maintaining their quality (Obayya, M et. al, 2023). The reset gate (JT) and the update gate (BT) are the two distinct gates found in every GRU cell. The GRU infrastructure is shown in Figure 4. The GRU network is used to tackle the issue of a long-dependency typical RNN network because it differs from the LSTM network.

GRU Framework

Following the extraction of important features from the pictures, we apply a GRU, a specialized type of neural network, to the temporal analysis of brain MRI data. GRUs are similar to an improved version of traditional Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which were first proposed by Ref.42. They have the ability to identify links and patterns in data sequences. Update and reset gates are useful aspects of GRUs that aid in improved information management. We leverage the ability of a GRU with 1024 units to understand time-varying changes in brain MRI images in our design. This improves our ability to detect and categorize brain cancers. Because of its faster training and simpler architecture, the GRU outperformed other RNNs, such as LSTM, in capturing dependencies. An input gate and a forget gate are two essential parts of the LSTM type of RNN architecture. These elements are essential for controlling the network's information flow. While the forget gate chooses which information should be erased, the input gate chooses which input data is kept in the memory cell. GRUs are crucial to many Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, including speech recognition, machine translation, and language modeling. They are also a crucial component of our methodology, which enables the model to more accurately and effectively identify and classify brain tumors.

Combining the advantages of the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) with Adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (APSO), the Hybrid WOA_APSO Algorithm is a state-of-the-art optimization method. By combining these two strategies, the algorithm improves the resilience and efficiency of the optimization process by utilizing the adaptive nature of APSO and the exploration and exploitation capabilities of WOA.

The humpback whale's bubble-net hunting technique served as the model for the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA). It effectively explores and exploits the search space by imitating their spiral and surrounding swimming movements. WOA uses mathematical models and control parameters like b, P, L, and m to alternate between global search (exploration) and local refining (exploitation). This equilibrium guarantees that WOA may both fine-tune solutions around the most well-known positions and diversify the search space to avoid local optima.

The conventional Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), which is based on swarm intelligence, is improved upon by Adaptive Particle Swarm Optimization (APSO). By constantly modifying its parameters, such as acceleration coefficients and inertia weight, in response to the swarm's performance, APSO adds adaptability. This flexibility helps the algorithm avoid premature convergence and enhances the optimization process overall by balancing local refinement with global search.

These two methods are combined in the Hybrid WOA_APSO Algorithm to produce a more reliable framework. First, the fitness of the population of search agents (particles and whales) is assessed after they are randomly initialized in the search space. The agents' positions are updated during the WOA phase in response to the encircling and spiral movements of WOA. APSO's processes are used to adaptively update particle locations and velocity during the APSO phase. The hybrid algorithm makes sure that the global best solution is refined using the best solutions from both WOA and APSO by incorporating these updates.

Until the maximum number of iterations is reached or the answer converges to an ideal value, this iterative process keeps going. In addition to improving the algorithm's capacity for exploration and exploitation, the hybridization guarantees quicker convergence by avoiding standstill. The global best position, which represents the best possible solution to the issue, is the end result. Because of its great adaptability, the Hybrid WOA_APSO Algorithm has been used to solve a number of real-world issues, including biomedical image processing, resource allocation, feature selection, and path planning. It is an effective tool for resolving intricate optimization problems in a variety of domains because of its capacity to strike a balance between exploration and exploitation while retaining adaptability.

4. RESULTS AND DISCUSSIONS

Confusion metrics, which divide accurate and inaccurate predictions into four different categories, were used to assess the system model's efficacy (Figure 3):

When both the anticipated and actual results are favorable, this is known as a true positive (TP);

When a forecast indicates a positive result but the actual result is negative, this is known as a false positive (FP); When the predicted consequence and the observed outcome are both negative, this is known as a true negative (TN);while a predictor makes a mistake and predicts a negative outcome while the actual result is positive, this is known as a false negative (FN).

The accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score are among the measures used to assess the performance of the suggested model. These metrics, such as True Positive, True Negative, False Positive, and False Negative, are computed using the information in the confusion matrix and demonstrate the model's development.

Three different metrics were used to evaluate the model's performance, and they are listed below:

The proportion of correct forecasts to all predictions is known as accuracy.

$Accuracy = ~\frac{TP + TN}{Total~Predictions}$

The term “specificity” describes a model's innate ability to correctly locate and categorize samples that are negative within a given dataset;

$Specificity = ~\frac{TN}{TN + FP}$

The capacity of a model to detect positive samples is known as sensitivity.

$Sensitivity = ~\frac{TP}{TP + FN}$

This section uses brain tumor datasets from Kaggle to validate the biomedical image classifier results of the HBDL-FBTA approach. In radiology and medical imaging, these datasets are frequently utilized for the classification and study of brain tumors. The Brain Tumor Image Segmentation (BRATS) 2017 and BRATS 2020 datasets are two well-known datasets that we take into consideration for this work. As part of the Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge, the BRATS 2017 dataset was made available with the goal of improving automated brain tumor identification using computer vision and machine learning methods. Gliomas, meningiomas, and pituitary tumors are among the various types of brain cancers that can be identified by MRI scans. To aid in precise categorization and analysis, ground truth annotations are included for every image, highlighting tumor locations and features. In a similar vein, the Brain Tumor Segmentation Competition 2020 inspired the creation of the BRATS 2020 dataset. The goal of this dataset is to enhance the identification and classification of brain cancers, specifically glioblastoma and low-grade gliomas and shown in Figure 5. It has an extensive and varied collection of MRI scans, including sequences like FLAIR, T1-weighted, and T2-weighted images. To enable thorough model evaluation, the dataset is separated into several subsets, such as training, validation, and testing sets.

5. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This paper introduces a unique automated biomedical image classification system called HBDL-FBTA (Hybrid Bio-inspired Deep Learning with Fusion Brain Tumor Analysis). The principal aim of the HBDL-FBTA algorithm is to proficiently evaluate biological pictures for the detection and classification of illnesses. This thorough methodology incorporates many sophisticated computational stages, guaranteeing elevated efficiency and precision in biological picture categorization.

The HBDL-FBTA approach comprises a sequence of functional phases that operate synergistically to accomplish its objectives. A pre-processing phase is utilized to improve image quality and diminish noise, which is essential for precise analysis. This is succeeded by a Swin-UNet-based segmentation technique that utilizes cutting-edge deep learning (DL) architectures to accurately delineate regions of interest in biomedical images. A fusion-based feature extraction module is employed to integrate diverse feature types, facilitating the extraction of robust and differentiated characteristics from the segmented images. A Humpback Whale Optimization with Simulated Annealing (HSSA)-based parameter tuning mechanism is subsequently employed to enhance the parameters of the classification model for improved performance. A Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based classification model is employed to assess the retrieved characteristics and categorize the biological images with great reliability.

To assess the efficacy of the HBDL-FBTA system, comprehensive simulations were performed utilizing two benchmark datasets: BraTS2017, which are prominently employed in dermatological and biomedical image analysis research. The simulation results demonstrate the enhanced efficacy of the proposed HBDL-FBTA methodology in comparison to traditional deep learning methods. The model attained maximum classification accuracies of 94.51% on the ISIC 2017 dataset and 95.38% on the ISIC 2020 dataset, illustrating its capability for precise disease diagnosis. Future study and development of the HBDL-FBTA technique is promising. A crucial aspect is assessing the model's computational complexity on extensive, real-time datasets, which may yield insights into its scalability and efficiency in practical applications. Furthermore, subsequent research may investigate the amalgamation of data from several imaging modalities, including MRI, CT, and X-ray, to improve the precision and reliability of classification tasks. This multi-modal strategy possesses considerable potential for enhancing diagnosis accuracy in intricate circumstances. Furthermore, initiatives aimed at creating interpretable deep learning models, such as methods for producing saliency maps or visual elucidations, may enhance transparency, cultivate trust, and expedite the clinical integration of these automated systems in healthcare.

ABSTRACT

Classification of brain tumors has emerged as a major issue medical diagnostics. In this research, we propose a model that integrates both CNN and Vit architectures, combined with an attention-based feature fusion mechanism to improve MRI data classification. The proposed model successfully integrates the capability of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in capturing localized features and that of Vision Transformers (ViTs) in capturing global contextual information. Multi-scale feature extraction is performed using DenseNet-201, followed by tokenization and embedding transformation for input into ViTs. The attention-based feature fusion enables the proposed network to dynamically integrate features at different granularities and enhance the model’s capability to classify High-Grade Gliomas (HGG), Low-Grade Gliomas (LGG), and non-tumor regions. Experimental results demonstrate superior accuracy of 97%, sensitivity, and specificity across modalities, showcasing the model's robustness and efficiency in automated brain tumor diagnosis.

1. INTRODUCTION

Classifying brain tumors is vital for devising appropriate treatment plans, enhancing prognoses of patient, and enabling more targeted therapeutics. Accurately identifying tumor types is challenging due to their complex and diverse nature. Advanced imaging techniques like MRI provide detailed insights into tumor structure, location, and characteristics, forming the basis for reliable classification methods, as depicted in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Different tumor types with annotations: Row 1.Glioblastoma, Row 2.Lower Grade Glioma, Row 3. Meningioma, Row 4. Metastasis

This diversity has complicated the accurate diagnosis and treatment plan thereafter. For clinicians, it is essential to be able to differentiate among tumor types, gliomas, meningiomas, and metastatic lesions. Classification of these tumors is crucial (Rao & Karunakara, 2021) because patient management is based on the biological behaviour, treatment protocols, and prognoses as given in Table I. However, dependence on a traditional diagnostic approach relying solely, or mostly, on the radiologist's expertise brings with it limitations that include subjective interpretation and inter-observer variability at best. Therefore, within these limits, advanced artificial intelligence techniques offer great potential.

Biological Behaviour

Treatment Protocols

Prognosis

Gliomas

Originates from glial cells; can be highly invasive, often infiltrating surrounding brain tissue.

Surgery, followed by radiation and chemotherapy, depending on grade and location of the tumor.

Variable; high-grade gliomas (e.g., glioblastomas) often have poorer prognosis, while low-grade gliomas have better outcomes.

Meningiomas

Typically, slow-growing and benign; originates from the meninges (brain and spinal cord linings).

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing the field of medicine. It offers immense potential to improve diagnostic accuracy, speed, and convenience across various medical specialties. AI is increasingly integrated into radiology, pathology, and other fields to aid in early disease detection staging, assessment of disease progression, and surgical planning. One of the primary benefits lies in assisting with diagnosis based on complex data, which helps healthcare professionals to identify intricate patterns that may be difficult for the human to detect (He et al., 2023).

One significant use of AI is identifying and evaluating conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and neurological disorders, at an initial stage. For instance, in oncology, AI algorithms are being used in the demarcation of tumours, tumour grading and in the assessment of the response to therapy (Khan, Nasim, Ahmad, & Masood, 2024). Similarly, AI assisted image analysis has a very important role in Neurology for diseases like Alzheimer’s, Multiple sclerosis and Brain tumors. AI systems are designed to interpret MRI, Computed Tomography (CT) scans, and other such imaging modalities with very high accuracy, aiding the radiologists in identifying the areas of interest and also minimises diagnostic variability.

Although AI is currently focused on diagnosis, it holds significant potential for treatment and progress tracking. In cancer radiotherapy, accurately identifying tumor boundaries is essential to optimize treatment effectiveness and protect healthy tissue. Advanced deep learning algorithms for segmentation enhance the precision of tumor boundary detection, supporting clinicians in designing more effective treatment strategies.

1.1 Challenges of AI-based Brain Tumor Classification

Classification of brain tumours using AI technology also poses several challenges due to the wide variety of tumour types, the complexity of brain anatomy, and variations in the imaging techniques. Brain tumors are categorized as primary or secondary. Secondary tumors develop from other parts of the body and spread to the brain while primary tumors originate from the brain tissue. These tumors exhibit substantial heterogeneity in appearance, size, location, and behaviour, complicating classification efforts. Early-stage tumors often resemble normal tissue, making it difficult to distinguish from healthy regions.

Figure 2 represents an organized breakdown of each primary challenge and its related factors in AI-based brain tumor classification.

Figure 2. Challenges in AI-based brain tumor classification

Classification is further complicated by the brain’s structure; with so many areas that are only slightly different from each other, making it challenging to find where the normal tissue ends and where the abnormal tissue starts, particularly in the early stages of the tumor. Further, the differences in sequences obtained from MRI also affects the development of the model because each of the sequences contains crucial information about the tumor. Some tumors, for example, need a contrast-enhanced MRI for tumor grade assessment, while others need an fMRI to understand how the tumor will affect the brain (Zhang, Xu, Tian, Jiang, & Ma, 2021). Other barriers are as well identified by data limitations and constraints. Classification requires large annotated datasets; however, these are scarce due to the tedious and expensive process of acquiring expert labels especially in rare tumor phenotypes. This scarcity however causes AI models to be not very generalizable and introduces this possibility of bias.

Despite the advances, there are few more issues including data privacy, the problem of obtaining large and well-annotated datasets, and model interpretability (Tang, He, Liu, & Duan, 2022). Medical imaging data is considered to be sensitive and must be handled with great care in order to comply with the data protection regulations and protect the patients’ privacy. Additionally, AI models need large volumes of well-annotated data to produce accurate results, and obtaining such data can be difficult, especially for rare conditions. Another crucial factor in developing AI is making them to be interpretable and transparent, so that health care practitioners can comprehend and trust the outcomes of these models to make correct clinical decisions.

1.2 A Contemporary Research Landscape

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Vision Transformers (ViT) are two of the most critical architectural frameworks defining modern trends in computer vision and medical image analysis. Derived from natural language processing transformers, ViTs essentially re-interpret image processing; Images are segmented into patches of a predetermined size and are processed similarly to sequences of words, or embeddings. This approach enables global contextual modeling through self-attention mechanisms, allowing simultaneous consideration of relationships across entire image spaces. Like traditional CNNs, which utilise localized convolution operations to process the images, ViTs are capable of capturing long range dependencies with unprecedented efficiency that has not been observed heretofore. Hence, these novel architectures are particularly well-suited for recognizing complex patterns in medical images.

Although challenged by the transformer architectures, the CNN architecture remains primary in feature extraction and the patterning determination process. With this hierarchical design at its core, utilizing the power of convolution and pooling operations, they continue to outperform the field in recognizing the scaled patterns of local spatial hierarchies and for detecting complex features in images. In recent research, the modifications of such general CNN structures, such as dilated convolution, SE blocks, and normalization layers, have become applicable to contemporary deep learning ecosystems.

The current research direction is gradually transferring to the combined architecture of ViT and CNNs that can complement each other. Researchers are exploring fusion techniques where local feature extraction and context perception are interactive. The goal of these hybrid models is to overcome the limitations of the individual architectures, establishing more robust, flexible neural networks. Their design allows for increasingly complex visual recognition challenges in diverse domains such as medical diagnostics and perception systems.

1.3 Feature Fusion: Concepts and Techniques

Feature fusion is a widely used technique that integrates data from multiple sources or representations to enhance model performance. In this context, the desired robustness and accuracy of predictions (Kittler, Hatef, Duin, & Matas, 1998) can be improved by exploiting complementary information to construct a more informative representation. Early, late, and hybrid fusion are several types of feature fusion.

Early fusion occurs at the feature level where several features are combined before being passed to the model. In this case, the model benefits by starting its learning process from the combined data. For instance, in the medical imaging application, early fusion might involve the fusion of MRI and CT health features’ representation (Li, Jiang, Zhang, & Zhu, 2023). Late fusion, on the other hand, occurs after models have been developed and trained on different features whereas early fusion occurs prior to the models being built. Each model provides the probability over the classes, which are combined, for instance by averaging, voting, or stacking. Late fusion enables models to specialize in various features but lacks a way of optimally utilizing all the complementary information that can be derived from the raw data (Ahmed, Dada, & Samaila, 2023).

Early fusion and late fusion can be blended to integrate features at different stages of the modelling phase. This approach can be beneficial for complex tasks, such as classifying brain tumors, where both high- and low-level features are necessary (Xie et al., 2022; Batool & Byun, 2024). With a strategic fusion approach, models can extract a richer set of features in more challenging domains, thus improving their prediction accuracies.

1.4 Feature Fusion: Synergizing Architectural Capabilities in Medical Image Analysis

Combining both CNN and ViT using feature fusion presents a plausible solution to address the drawbacks of each in medical image analysis. CNNs are optimized for adopting the spatial organization of local details, hence useful in identifying minute details such as texture or lesion. On the other hand, ViTs are adept at modelling global dependencies by leveraging self-attention mechanisms, enabling them to understand broader contextual relationships across an image.

Patients’ medical images including MRI, CT, histopathological images that are to be diagnosed, need local cues as well as global context cues. Feature fusion of CNN and ViT architectures combines these strengths, enabling enhanced feature extraction and interpretation. It is especially useful for tasks such as multi-class tumour classification, disease localisation, and detailed anomaly detection to which the global and local nature of the images seems crucial.

Benefits of integrating CNN and ViT include increased diagnostic accuracy, enhanced generalization across different datasets and a reduced risk of overfitting in complex models. Moreover, this synergy streamlines feature hierarchies, making the models more efficient.

Key advantages of feature fusion include:

  • • Complementary Information: Different model architectures excel at capturing different types of information. CNNs effectively extract local spatial features while ViTs model long-range dependencies well. These complementary features enable a more complete interpretation of input data.

  • • Reduced Overfitting: Feature fusion can reduce the likelihood of overfitting, which is an issue that often arises when using deep learning algorithms. By incorporating features learned from all these combined sources, the model becomes more robust to variability and noise.

  • • Enhanced Performance: Feature fusion improves the performance of deep learning algorithms consistently. Models can achieve higher accuracy, sensitivity and specificity results by using strengths of various architectures.

  • • Improved Interpretability: It can also enhance interpretability of deep learning models. Through visualization of the fused features, one can better understand how the model has arrived at the decision, and which aspects played a crucial role in leading the final prediction.

2. LITERATURE REVIEW

Brain tumor classification has gained significant attention in recent years, driven by advancements in deep learning techniques. Several approaches, including CNNs, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, and hybrid models, have been analysed in this section.

Aamir et al. (2022) proposed a multiscale CNN framework along with data augmentation and sliding window testing to reduce bias and prevent overfitting. Khan et al. (2020) developed an automated MM-Brain Tumor classifier utilizing deep learning, where VGG16 and VGG19 architectures were employed for precise feature selection. Contrast stretching was applied to enhance tumor visibility, and feature selection was conducted to reduce computational load. However, the study encountered several challenges, including the high similarity in tumor structures of certain types, the impact of low contrast in T1-weighted images on feature extraction, and the inherent complexities of multimodal classification.

Mohsen et al. (2017) utilized CNN, discrete wavelet transform (DWT) for feature extraction and principal component analysis (PCA) for dimensionality reduction, classifying MRIs into four broad categories. Their approach achieved classification accuracy comparable to traditional CNNs, with less equipment and faster computation. However, the study's limitations include the small dataset size and reliance on T2-weighted images, restricting its broader application.

Ari and Hanbay (2018) proposed an Extreme Learning Machine with Local Receptive Fields (ELM-LRF) for classifying MR images as benign or malignant. The main limitation is the small dataset, consisting of images from only 16 patients. In Srinivas et al. (2022), authors discussed the use of deep transfer learning techniques in classifying brain tumours based on MR images. VGG-16 yielded the best performance results after intensity normalization and re-sizing preprocessing the data. Badjie and Ülker (2022) developed a deep learning-based architecture that leverages pre-trained networks, fine-tuning them for tumor classification to effectively detect and differentiate various tumor types in MRI scans.

Mehrotra et al. (2020) evaluated various models including AlexNet, GoogLeNet, ResNet 50, ResNet 101, and SqueezeNet. However, they used only 696 MRI image samples which may not generalize well especially in large scale applications. Hao et al (18) introduced an innovative active learning framework leveraging transfer learning to minimize annotation costs. The performance yields an AUC of 82.89% on the test dataset and with augmentation all labelling costs are reduced by 40% mark.

Ali (2023) introduced ViT-BT, a Vision Transformer-based model designed for brain tumor classification. The ViT-BT framework enhances classification performance by first pre-training the Vision Transformer model and then fine-tuning it using specialized MRI brain tumor datasets with an accuracy of 98%. Reddy et al. (2024) implemented a variant of vision transformer for automatically classifying multiple classes of brain tumor from the MRI scan images. Several pre-trained models were compared in the study, with the FTVT-l16 model performing best with a test accuracy of 98.70%.

Tummala et al. (2022) proposed an ensemble of ViT models for tumor classification. Pretrained ViT models on ImageNet were fine-tuned and utilized for the classification task. The proposed model achieved an accuracy of 98.7%. Goceri (2023) leveraged advantages of CNN and ViT to develop a novel architecture for glioma classification through the effective integration of feature-combining modules. Experimental results demonstrated the approach's efficacy in classifying four glioma subtypes from histopathological images, achieving an accuracy of 96.75%.

Karagoz et al. (2024) introduced a self-supervised technique to address the issue of limited availability in datasets. The dual CNN & Vision Transformer approach is pre-trained and fine-tuned. Synthetic MRI imagery is used to balance datasets by augmenting them, thereby increasing classification efficiency and reducing overfitting. This model demonstrated excellent performance as well as generalization capability to other databases but the usage of fake images indicates that there may be some biases inherent to the generated synthetic images.

Asiri et al. (2023) introduced the FT-ViT model, a fine-tuned Vision Transformer leveraging image processing and deep learning techniques to classify tumors. The framework comprises multiple stages, including data preprocessing, patch extraction, feature concatenation, selection, learning, and fine-tuning. Trained on the CE-MRI dataset, which includes 5,712 brain tumor images, the FT-ViT achieved 98.13% accuracy. DeepTumorNet (Asiri et al., 2023) is a hybrid deep learning model designed for brain tumor classification. The architecture integrates a modified GoogLeNet with leaky ReLU activation. The results demonstrated that the model outperformed comparable methods, achieving an accuracy of 99.67% and a recall of 100%.

Vimala et al. (2023) utilized EfficientNets to classify brain tumors using the Figshare dataset. EfficientNetB2, fine-tuned with additional layers and Grad-CAM visualization for interpretability, outperformed other models. Dixon et al (2024) proposed a hybrid architecture combining ViT and CNNs for robust brain tumor classification. The framework integrates texture, structural, and deep features, leveraging Haralick features, local binary patterns, and ViT-derived features. Evaluations demonstrate superior performance on diverse brain MRI datasets. Aloraini et al. (2023) proposed a hybrid model for brain tumor classification, combining CNNs for local feature extraction and transformers for global feature attention. The model achieves average accuracies of 96.75% on the BraTS 2018 dataset and 99.10% on the Figshare dataset. Tabatabaei et al. (2023) proposed a two-branch parallel model combining a Transformer Module (TM), and CNN for brain tumor classification. Using a cross-fusion strategy, local and global features are integrated to enhance accuracy. The lightweight iResNet architecture outperformed other CNN variants, achieving 99.30% accuracy.

As indicated in the literature review, there are improvements for classification of brain tumours (Verma et al., 2023; Garg et al., 2024), however the studies present several issues that restricts the effectiveness for broader uses. One common issue identified is the limited or unbalanced datasets, as cited in Ari and Hanbay’s (2018) and a similar case in Mehrotra et al (2020). These limitations impair transferability and reliability of the models, particularly within the clinical practice where numerous patient groups and imaging modalities are used. Further, the inclusion of synthetic data for augmentation as done in Karagoz, Nalbantoglu, & Fox (2024) pose some biases. Though synthetic data is beneficial since it can minimize the impact of small dataset; however, it will not always reflect real-world situations, thus the model’s efficiency declines when tested on other datasets.

There are also major issues regarding the computational and training issues. Approaches by (Reddy et al., 2024; Tummala et al., 2022) need substantial computational resources for pretraining and fine-tuning, so they are not practically viable in resource constrained settings. In addition, many hybrid models such as DeepTumorNet (Asiri et al., 2023) are prone to overfitting due to the highly fine-tuned parameters and a limited amount of data. This may decrease the model’s ability to generalize to the other datasets or other clinical applications.

The literature highlights some of the major difficulties in feature extraction, which have a direct relationship on the performance as well as the efficacy of the models used in brain tumor classification. One of the major challenges is that the structures of different types of tumors do not vary significantly, which poses a challenge to the models to discern in between them well. Additionally, low contrast in T1-weighted images poses a significant obstacle, as it hampers the extraction of meaningful features necessary for accurate classification. Multimodal classification is also inherently difficult because information derived from the various imaging modalities has to be combined and interpreted by the model. The aforementioned challenges imply that misclassifications are more likely to happen when the models are used in real clinical practice. This underscores the need to develop sophisticated feature extraction methods and reliable data fusion approaches.

The work shows the potential and limitations of Transfer Learning (TF), Vision Transformers (ViT), and ViT-CNN integrated models in brain tumour classification. TF models, often starting from VGG16 or ResNet, work well with feature extraction but fail at identifying tumor features when the size of the set of images is relatively small or unbalanced. It has been found that the use of ViTs is appropriate of large amounts of data and gets high accuracy but consumes a lot of computational power and does not capture local details. The ViT-CNN hybrids have better performance than the ViT and CNN approaches; however, they are complicated and may overfit on small datasets.

3. REVIEW OF APPROACHES IMPLEMENTED IN BRAIN TUMOR CLASSIFICATION

3.1 DenseNet-210

For the proposed hybrid model, DenseNet-201 serves as the primary CNN architecture. Figure 3 illustrates the detailed structure of DenseNet-20. The most distinctive feature of DenseNet-201 is connectivity, which implies the concatenation of the previous layer’s features with all the subsequent layers. This connectivity structure enhances the flow of information which makes DenseNet-201 appropriate for extracting complex features in different applications. Let x0 represent the input to the network, and f1,f2,f3,…fl-1,fL denote the output from each of the L layers in the dense block. The input to layer l is the combined output from the earlier layers:

fl=H([x0, f1,f2,f3,…fl-1]) (1)

where H(⋅) represents the composite function applied in layer l, which typically includes operations like Batch Normalization, ReLU activation, and convolution.

Figure 3. Architecture of DenseNet-201

The structure of DenseNet is made of dense block and transition layers. A dense block has many convolutional layers, and each layer is connected with all other layers through dense connectivity. In this case there are transition layers between the dense blocks which assist in down sampling the feature maps using average pooling. Additionally, the growth rate, which determines the number of new features added by each layer, is kept relatively low to ensure computational efficiency while preserving model performance.

The output of DenseNet-201 features is passed through a Multilayer Perceptron with two fully connected layers, each containing 512 neurons each. These layers are interspersed with BN (Batch Normalization) to increase the stability of the learning process. Leaky ReLU is used as the activation function, defined as:


$$f\left( z \right) = \left\{ \begin{matrix} {z~z > 0} \\ {\alpha z~z \leq 0} \\ \end{matrix}\operatorname{} \right.$$
(2)

where α prevents dead neurons and is constant, allowing neurons to handle negative inputs.

3.2 Vision Transformer

The Vision Transformer represents a shift from conventional paradigms in computer vision to the currently popular Transformer models in natural language processing. In 2020, researchers at Google Brain developed ViT, applying the self-attention mechanism of Transformers to image data, in contrast to the standard sequence data used in NLP. This approach addresses the limitations of CNN such as restricted global context awareness. Thus, ViT became a notable architecture, particularly in large-scale image classification, achieving significant results and marking a new era in research.

ViT differs fundamentally from CNNs in the way it processes images. Traditional CNNs work hierarchically by extracting more and more abstract features from the localized receptive field to understand the image content. In contrast, ViT treats images as a sequence of fixed-sized grids. This is similar to how NLP models treat sentences as sequences of words. In this innovative approach, the input image is segmented into image patches. Each of them is linearly transformed into a one-dimensional vector through a learnable embedding layer. These embedded patches effectively act as tokens to be processed by Transformer models similar to word tokens in NLP.

The key component of ViT as shown in figure 4 is the encoder which forms the backbone of the model. Each block contains a self-attention mechanism and then a feedforward neural network with the addition of residual connections and layer normalization. The self-attention mechanism evaluates the dependencies of the patches adaptively, focusing on the critical regions of the image. This enable ViT to learn long-range contexts and capture global information, while avoiding the need for many parameters, as is the case of traditional CNNs’ convolutional kernels.

Figure 4. Architecture of Vision Transformer

To preserve the spatial structure of the image, ViT adds learnable positional embeddings on the patch embeddings. This is because the Transformer models are naturally order-agnostic by default and do not inherently understand token layout. The model keeps the spatial structure by using positional embeddings to know the position of every patch in the image. When combined with the self-attention mechanism, these embeddings make ViT learn to capture the local and the global spatial structures, and thus perform even better in learning spatial patterns.

This concept, originally introduced in the BERT model for NLP tasks, serves as a global representation of the entire image in ViT. As the image is processed, the CLS token interacts with all other patches via the self-attention mechanism, collecting features that represent the overall content of the image. Once the image passes through the final Transformer encoder layer, the CLS token is passed through a linear classification layer, where it is used to generate the model's final prediction. By incorporating both local and global features, this approach enables ViT to effectively analyse and classify images.

The computational power and the large datasets deemed necessary for training ViT models effectively are substantial. Unlike CNNs that have certain built-in biases such as spatial hierarchies and local patterns (e.g., edges and textures), ViT is not affected by these inherent biases. For this reason, ViT models require pretraining on large datasets such as ImageNet-21k or JFT-300M to learn high quality representations. Then they can be fine-tuned using task specific datasets to perform well. This pretraining-finetuning approach of ViT enables it to generalize better and often outperforms CNN models in large-scale classification tasks.

Despite these advantages, the computational complexity of ViT is a big issue. However, the self-attention mechanism is highly resource intensive, scaling quadratically with the number of patches, which is especially significant given that ViTs work well with high-resolution images. The model needs to compute all patch interactions, resulting in quadratic memory and processing power scaling. However, while these high demands are required for ViT in resource limited settings they can be impractical. In order to address these challenges, researchers have developed solutions including sparse self-attention as well as these hierarchical Transformer architectures, which come at a reduced computational cost but maintain strong performance.

The rise in popularity of Vision Transformers has led to the development of various hybrid architectures that merge advantages from both fields of CNNs and transformers. Models like the Swin transformer and DeiT (Data-efficient Image Transformers) combine the power of local feature extraction achieved through the CNN structure with the global context-awareness of transformers. Conventional models provide a regional fit, making hybrid models appropriate for small datasets. For instance, Swin transformer models utilize hierarchical structuring to process images at varying resolutions to make it far less computationally expensive without compromising accuracy. These improvements help address the limitations of ViT and make these models more practical for real-world use.

4. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

This work proposes a hybrid architecture with a novel attention-based feature fusion mechanism to classify the MRI of the BRaTS dataset into three categories.

The contributions of this work are:

  1. 1. Novel Hybrid Architecture: A hybrid framework that integrates the advantages of CNN and ViT is proposed. It aims to capture and integrate both global and local information from images.

  2. 2. Attention driven Feature Fusion Module: A novel feature fusion mechanism is proposed that combines features at various granularities using a cross-attention mechanism. This allows the module to seamlessly integrate global contextual patterns with localized details through the cross-attention mechanism. This dynamic fusion process also adjusts the importance of features while simultaneously increasing the variety of captured information, without merely including other features.

The proposed method consists of three interconnected components as shown in figure 5.

Figure 5. Hybrid CNN-ViT architecture with attention-based feature fusion mechanism

  1. 1. CNN-Based Multi-Scale Feature Extraction:

This component employs DenseNet-201 to generate feature maps at three distinct spatial scales: features at the coarse level (global structural patterns), medium level (intermediate anatomical details), and fine level (localized and textural information). The module produces detailed and diverse representations by extracting features across multiple scales.

  1. 2. ViT Feature Refinement:

The attention mechanism in these transformers enhances CNN-derived features with contextual information, resulting in structured and high-quality feature map representations.

  1. 3. Cross-Attention Feature Fusion Model:

This mechanism enables interaction between feature maps of different scales from the three ViTs, optimizing the feature maps with refinements and consolidating the integrated results into a single feature map. The cross-attention mechanism uses the information from the coarse, medium, and fine feature levels to yield a unified multi scale representation tailored to be used in classification.

The following section will detail each component of the architecture, elucidating its architecture and function in the overall system.

4.1 CNN-Based Multi-Scale Feature Extraction

DenseNet-201 is designed to have dense connectivity across its layers. This structure enhances the flow of gradients during backpropagation and improves feature reuse. The model is organized into several dense blocks, with each block extracting features at different levels of abstraction. For brain tumor classification, we aim to extract fine, medium, and coarse features from these blocks to capture various spatial patterns and structures in brain images.

The reasons for choosing DenseNet-201 as the CNN Component are as follows:

Dense Connectivity: Within each dense block, every layer utilizes feature maps from all preceding layers, enabling an efficient mechanism for feature reuse. This approach captures subtle and nuanced features, which are crucial for precise diagnosis.

Feature Preservation: Unlike traditional CNNs which suffer from feature loss, DenseNet-201 maintains and combines features from earlier layers throughout the network. This characteristic is crucial in medical imaging, where early-stage feature details can be as important as high-level semantic features. The dense connectivity allows for comprehensive feature preservation and aggregation.

Parameter Efficiency: Despite its depth (201 layers), DenseNet-201 achieves remarkable parameter efficiency. The dense connectivity pattern reduces the need for redundant feature maps, resulting in a more compact model. This is particularly beneficial for medical image classification, where model complexity and computational requirements must be balanced with precision.

Multi-Scale Feature Extraction: DenseNet-201's architecture naturally supports multi-scale feature extraction. The dense blocks capture features at different levels of abstraction, ranging from low-level texture details to high-level semantic representations. This multi-scale approach is ideal for medical image analysis, where tumors and pathological conditions can manifest in various subtle ways.

DenseNet-201, with its dense connections, parameter efficiency, and multi-scale feature extraction capabilities, provides high-quality hierarchical feature maps that are ideal for a hybrid CNN-ViT architecture. When combined with the Vision Transformer’s long-range dependency modeling, this setup leverages the strengths of both paradigms, making it highly effective for challenging tasks like brain tumor classification.

Extraction of Fine Features (Dense Block 1)

Dense block 1 is responsible for extracting fine features, which includes low-level details and small anatomical structures. The input image, denoted as X0, passes through the initial convolution layer before being processed by the dense block layers. Each convolution operation within this block takes the output from all previous layers, enabling the model to capture increasingly complex patterns. Mathematically, the output of the ith convolutional layer within Dense Block 1 is represented as:

Yi=σ(Wi∗Xi−1+bi) (3)

where Wi is the convolution kernel, bi is the bias term, ∗ denotes the convolution operation, and σ is the non-linear activation function (ReLU). After processing through all layers in Dense Block 1, the output feature map, denoted as Ffine, represents the fine-grained details.

Extraction of Medium Features (Dense Block 2)

After extracting fine features from Dense Block 1, the next step is to capture medium features. These features are abstracted from the fine-level details and represent intermediate anatomical patterns, such as larger structures or patterns within the brain. The output from Dense Block 1, denoted as Ffine , is passed to Dense Block 2, where additional layers further process the features. The mathematical representation of this transition from Dense Block 1 to Dense Block 2 is as follows:

Fmedium=fblock(Ffine) (4)

where fblock refers to the operations performed within Dense Block 2, including additional convolutional layers and batch normalization. The resulting output Fmedium contains medium-level features, which abstract away finer details and begin to capture larger anatomical structures. These medium features are essential for identifying intermediate tumor characteristics and structures that span across smaller regions in the image. Additionally, these features can also help detect relationships between different brain regions which are essential for accurate tumor diagnosis.

Extraction of Coarse Features (Dense Block 3)

Dense Block 3 captures the coarse features, which represent the highest level of abstraction in the feature extraction process. These coarse features are global, large-scale patterns that encompass significant structures, such as the entire tumor or other broader brain regions. The output from Dense Block 2, denoted as Fmedium is passed to Dense Block 3 for further processing. The mathematical transition from Dense Block 2 to Dense Block 3 is represented as:

Fcoarse=fblock(Fmedium) (5)

where fblock represents the operations within Dense Block 3, including further convolutions and batch normalization. The resulting output Fcoarse contains coarse features, which are abstracted and provide a global understanding of the brain's structures. These coarse features are essential for recognizing the overall tumor region, its size, and its relationship with other parts of the brain. The coarse features provide the model with context about the tumor's location within the brain, which is critical for making final classification decisions.

Table II summarizes the dimensions of output at different stages of the DenseNet-201 architecture for an input size of 240×240×4. After the first convolution layer and pooling layer, the spatial dimensions are halved. Output size after initial convolution and pooling is 120×120×64 where 64 is the number of filters/channels. This serves as input to the first dense block.

4.2 ViT Feature Refinement

The integration of Convolutional Neural Network with Vision Transformer represents a critical computational challenge in modern computer vision architectures. This transformation requires a sophisticated approach to convert hierarchical feature maps into a tokenized format compatible with transformer-based models. This section proposes a systematic approach for such transformation, with a focus on handling features at multiple granularities to enable hierarchical representation learning.

4.2.1 Mathematical Formulation of Feature Map Transformation

Let the CNN-extracted feature map at granularity level g {fine, medium, coarse} be denoted as be Fg , represented mathematically as:


Fg ∈ Rwg × Hg  × cg  
(6)

where H represents the height, W the width, and C the number of channels of the feature map. ViTs require tokenized inputs, where each token corresponds to a fixed-length vector. This necessitates:

  1. 1. Flattening of spatial dimensions height (Hg) and width (Wg) into a single dimension.

  2. 2. Projection of the resulting tokens into an embedding space of dimension d, which aligns with the ViT input specifications.

4.2.2 Tokenization and Embedding Transformation

Tokenization and embedding transformation are critical steps that adapt image data into a format suitable for processing by transformer architectures. The steps involved in this process is detailed below.

4.2.2.1 Flattening CNN Feature Maps.

The spatial dimensions Hg×Wg are flattened, converting the feature map Fg into a matrix Fgflat as:

Fg ∈ Rwg × Hg  × cg   (7)

For a feature map Fg∈R64×16×16F,flattening produces Fgflat∈R256×64 (i.e., 256 tokens, each of dimension 64).

4.2.2.2 Linear Projection to Embedding Space.

Flattened feature map Fgflat is projected into a lower-dimensional space using a learnable linear projection matrix Wgproj and the bias term bgprojas given in (8)

Eg=
Fgflat
⋅
Wgproj
+
bgproj
(8)

Where Wgproj∈ RCg×d: Linear projection matrix that reduces Cg-dimensional tokens to d- dimensional embeddings. bgproj∈Rd:Bias term added to each token embedding.

The resulting token embeddings Eg are given by:


Eg  ∈ R(Hg.Wg)Xd 
(9)

4.2.2.3 Processing Tokenized Features with Vision Transformers.

The tokenized embeddings Eg  are processed through a dedicated ViT block for each granularity level g:


Fg ′ = ViTBlock(Eg )
(10)

where Fg ′′ represents the refined features. Each ViT block consists of:

  • • Multi-head self-attention (MHSA) layers for capturing long-range dependencies.

  • • Feedforward layers for non-linear transformations.

The independent processing of Eg  at different granularities enables the model to extract multi-scale representations critical for downstream tasks.

4.3 Cross-Attention Feature Fusion Model

The proposed fusion technique addresses the challenge of effectively integrating multi-granularity feature representations. The model begins with three distinct feature maps extracted from different levels of granularity as shown in figure 6.

Figure 6. Multi Scale Feature Extraction using DenseNet-201

Let F1 ′, F2 ′, F3 ′ represent feature maps extracted from coarse-, mid-, and fine-level ViTs, respectively. These feature maps, obtained after tokenization and embedding transformation, are of varying spatial resolutions and semantic granularity. To enable effective fusion, all feature maps are projected into a common feature dimension d:


Fi′

$$W_{i}F_{i~} + ~b_{\begin{matrix} {i~} \\ ~ \\ ~ \\ \end{matrix}}~$$
(11)

Wi ∈ RdXd′ where Wi and bi are learnable projection parameters, and d′ is the original feature dimension.

4.3.1 Cross-Attention Blocks

To fuse information, three cross-attention blocks are defined, where each feature map alternates as the query while the remaining two serve as keys and values. The Cross-attention Feature fusion is depicted in figure 7.

Figure 7. Cross-Attention Feature Fusion

Q1=F1′WQ, K2=F2′WK, V2=F2′WV, K3= F3′WK, V3=F3′WV

where WQ Wk, Wv ∈Rd×d′ are learnable projection matrices for queries, keys, and values. The cross-attention output is computed as:

Residual connections and layer normalization are applied to each cross-attention output to stabilize training and enhance feature representation,

4.3.3 Concatenation and Fully Connected Fusion

The residual outputs from all three blocks are concatenated:


Fconcat = Concat[F1res ,F2res ,F3res]
(16)

The concatenated features are then passed through a multi-layer perceptron to generate the final fused feature representation:


Ffused = MLP(Fconcat)

Algorithm: Attention Based Feature Fusion

Inputs:

  • • F1 ′, F2 ′, F3 ′ : Feature maps from ViTs at coarse, mid, and fine granular levels, with sizes B×N ×d1, B×N2×d2, B×N3×d3.

  • • d′: Common feature dimension for fusion.

Output:Ffused: Fused feature map.

1 1. Initialization:

5. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND RESULT

5.1 Experimental Setup

Models were implemented using Python-based libraries and executed on a desktop equipped with a CPU-Intel Core i9-13900K CPU alongside a GPU - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090. A deep learning-based classification framework was developed for analyzing MRI using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The framework performed multiclass classification to categorize tumors into four distinct types. The implementation utilized Python-based deep learning libraries, specifically Keras with TensorFlow backend, within the Anaconda environment.

5.2 Dataset

The BraTS 2015 (Brain Tumor Segmentation) dataset represents a significant milestone in medical imaging resources, comprising multimodal MRI scans from 220 high-grade glioma (HGG) cases and 54 low-grade glioma (LGG) cases. Each case in the dataset contains four distinct MRI sequences: T1-weighted (T1), T1-weighted with contrast enhancement (T1ce), T2-weighted (T2), and Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR).

Rigorous preprocessing was undertaken on the dataset to ensure standardization across all cases of the dataset. All images were manually annotated by expert neuroradiologists. A key feature of the BraTS 2015 dataset is the inclusion of detailed segmentation masks and classification labels. Tumor regions were annotated using a hierarchical segmentation approach: label 1 for necrosis, non-enhancing tumor, and cyst; label 2 for edema; label 4 for enhancing tumor; and label 0 for all other areas. These annotations serve as a benchmark for developing and testing of automated segmentation algorithms. The unique advantage of the BraTS 2015 dataset lies in the inclusion of both HGG and LGG cases, making it invaluable for creating classification and segmentation algorithms that are both effective and robust.

Samples of the four MRI modalities are illustrated in Figure 8. Each modality includes 155 slices, resulting in 620 images per case. For the 274 cases, this results in a total of 169,880 MRI images, as detailed in Table III. The dataset is divided into 80% for training and 20% for testing. For this study, we categorized the dataset into three classes:

  • • Class 1 represents High-Grade Gliomas (HGG) and includes Necrosis (1), Enhancing Tumor (4), and extensive Edema (2), as these features indicate aggressive tumor behaviour.

  • • Class 2 represents Low-Grade Gliomas (LGG) and includes images labelled as Non-enhancing Tumor (3).

  • • Finally, Class 0, labelled as non-tumor.
