  • • High Efficiency with Limited Data: U-Net performs well even on small medical datasets. Its design allows for accurate segmentation with fewer labeled examples, which is crucial in medical imaging, where acquiring large annotated datasets can be challenging.

  • • Versatility Across Modalities: U-Net is widely used across different imaging modalities, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound, for tasks such as liver, brain, and cardiac segmentation.

Applications

  • • Tumor Segmentation: U-Net is commonly used to segment tumors in brain MRI scans, breast cancer mammograms, and lung cancer CT scans.

  • • Organ Segmentation: It is applied to segment organs like the liver, kidneys, and lungs in CT and MRI scans for surgical planning or volumetric analysis.

  • • Vessel Segmentation: U-Net is used to segment blood vessels in retina images for diabetic retinopathy diagnosis or in brain images to analyze cerebrovascular diseases.

4.2.2. ResNet for Improved Accuracy

ResNet (Residual Network), introduced in 2015, is another specialized CNN architecture that has achieved remarkable success in medical image classification tasks. Its key innovation is the introduction of residual connections, which help mitigate the problem of vanishing gradients in deep networks, allowing the model to be trained more efficiently while achieving higher accuracy Abdou, M. A. (2022).

Architecture

  • • Residual Blocks: ResNet consists of residual blocks, which include skip connections that bypass one or more layers. These connections allow the model to learn identity mappings, making it easier to train very deep networks without performance degradation.

  • • Deep Architecture: ResNet can have hundreds or even thousands of layers due to its residual design, which prevents the network from suffering from vanishing gradients, a common issue in very deep networks.

Enhanced Performance in Medical Applications

  • • Improved Classification Accuracy: ResNet’s deep architecture allows it to capture complex features in medical images, leading to improved classification accuracy. This is particularly useful in tasks like identifying subtle differences between healthy and abnormal tissues in histopathology images or classifying diseases from radiology scans.

  • • Reduced Overfitting: ResNet’s ability to prevent overfitting makes it ideal for medical datasets, which are often limited in size. The residual connections help the network generalize better, even with a smaller number of training examples.

  • • Transfer Learning: ResNet is widely used in transfer learning, where pre-trained models on large datasets (such as ImageNet) are fine-tuned for medical imaging tasks. This significantly reduces training time while maintaining high performance.

Applications

  • • Disease Classification: ResNet is used in tasks such as classifying chest X-rays for pneumonia, tuberculosis, and COVID-19 detection. Its high accuracy makes it suitable for identifying diseases with subtle visual cues.

  • • Pathology Image Analysis: In digital pathology, ResNet is applied to classify histopathology images, distinguishing between cancerous and non-cancerous cells. It is particularly effective in detecting breast cancer, lung cancer, and colon cancer from pathology slides.

  • • Retinal Image Classification: ResNet is used to detect diabetic retinopathy from retinal fundus images, helping to classify images into different severity levels of the disease.

4.2.3. Other Notable CNN Architectures in Medical Applications

VGG (Visual Geometry Group Network)

VGG is another popular CNN architecture used in medical imaging, particularly for classification tasks. It consists of a simple, sequential structure with multiple convolutional layers, followed by fully connected layers.

  • • Significance in Medical Imaging: VGG is used for tasks like classifying skin lesions in dermatoscopic images, detecting lung diseases from chest X-rays, and identifying different stages of diabetic retinopathy.

  • • Limitations: While VGG achieves good performance, it requires more computational resources and memory compared to ResNet, making it less efficient for very deep networks.

DenseNet (Densely Connected Convolutional Network)

DenseNet introduces dense connections between layers, where each layer receives input from all preceding layers, enhancing feature reuse and improving gradient flow.

  • • Advantages in Medical Imaging: DenseNet’s densely connected layers allow it to learn complex representations, making it highly effective for medical tasks like segmentation and classification. DenseNet has been used to detect abnormalities in brain MRI scans and classify breast cancer in mammograms.

  • • Improved Efficiency: DenseNet achieves better performance with fewer parameters than ResNet, making it more efficient in terms of memory and computation.

4.3 Explainable AI in CNNs

As the adoption of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and other deep learning models in medical applications continues to rise, the need for explainable AI (XAI) has become increasingly critical. The opaque nature of CNNs—often referred to as “black boxes”—poses significant challenges, particularly in high-stakes fields like healthcare. The importance of interpretability in medical AI systems cannot be overstated, as it directly impacts clinical decision-making, trust in AI systems, and patient safety (Van der Velden et al.,2022).

4.3.1. The Importance of Interpretability in Medical AI Systems

  1. a) Trust and Acceptance

    • • Building Trust: Clinicians must trust AI systems to integrate them effectively into clinical workflows. If healthcare professionals cannot understand how a model arrived at a specific conclusion or diagnosis, their willingness to rely on these systems diminishes.

    • • Enhancing Acceptance: The interpretability of CNN decisions fosters greater acceptance of AI tools among healthcare providers. Clinicians are more likely to adopt AI systems that provide clear reasoning behind their recommendations.

  2. b) Clinical Decision Support

    • • Supporting Clinical Judgments: Explainable AI aids clinicians in understanding the rationale behind model predictions, enabling them to make informed decisions. When a CNN suggests a diagnosis based on an image, clinicians need insights into which features influenced that decision.

    • • Augmenting Human Expertise: Interpretability helps integrate AI insights with human expertise, allowing clinicians to validate and contextualize AI recommendations. This synergy can lead to more accurate diagnoses and treatment plans.

  3. c) Compliance and Accountability

    • • Regulatory Requirements: The growing use of AI in healthcare brings scrutiny from regulatory bodies. Many regulatory frameworks demand a level of transparency in AI systems. Demonstrating how a model makes decisions is essential for compliance with ethical and legal standards.

    • • Accountability: In the event of a misdiagnosis or adverse outcome, understanding the decision-making process of an AI system is crucial for accountability. Explainable AI helps delineate responsibilities between AI systems and healthcare providers.

4.3.2. Ongoing Research into Making CNN Decisions Explainable

Recognizing the challenges posed by the black-box nature of CNNs, researchers are actively exploring various methodologies to enhance the interpretability of these models in medical applications. Here are some key areas of focus:

  1. a) Visualization Techniques

    • • Saliency Maps: Techniques like saliency maps and gradient-weighted class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) visualize the areas of an image that most influence a model's prediction. By highlighting important regions in medical images, such as tumors in radiology scans, clinicians can better understand the basis for a CNN's decision.

    • • Feature Visualization: Researchers are developing methods to visualize the features learned by CNN layers. By examining the features that contribute to certain predictions, clinicians can gain insights into the underlying processes of the model.

  2. b) Model-Agnostic Approaches

    • • Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME): LIME is a technique that generates interpretable models around individual predictions. By perturbing input data and observing changes in predictions, LIME helps to create a local model that explains the behavior of complex models like CNNs.

    • • SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP): SHAP values provide a unified measure of feature importance by quantifying the contribution of each feature to the model's predictions. This approach aids clinicians in understanding which aspects of medical images are pivotal for diagnoses.

  3. c) Integration of Clinical Knowledge

    • • Incorporating Domain Expertise: Research is exploring the integration of clinical knowledge into AI models to enhance interpretability. By aligning model predictions with established medical guidelines and expert opinions, systems can offer more interpretable outputs.

    • • Symbolic AI and Logic-Based Approaches: Combining CNNs with symbolic AI can facilitate the creation of more interpretable models. These approaches can provide human-readable rules and explanations based on the model's decisions.

  4. d) Human-Computer Interaction

    • • User-Centric Interfaces: Developing user-friendly interfaces that present model predictions alongside interpretive information can enhance clinicians' understanding of AI decisions. Effective visualization and communication of AI insights are crucial for seamless integration into clinical practice.

5. CHALLENGES AND LIMITATIONS OF CNNS IN MEDICAL IMAGING

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become a transformative tool in medical imaging, improving diagnostic accuracy and aiding treatment decisions. However, despite these advancements, there are several challenges and limitations associated with using CNNs in this domain.

5.1. Data Availability and Quality

Medical imaging datasets are often limited in size due to privacy concerns, the need for expert labeling, and complex regulatory requirements. CNNs are typically data-hungry, requiring vast amounts of labeled images for effective training. This lack of large, annotated datasets can lead to poor model performance, particularly in rare diseases where data scarcity is common. Moreover, data quality and consistency vary across institutions, affecting model generalizability. Differences in imaging equipment, protocols, and patient demographics introduce variabilities that CNNs struggle to handle without extensive domain-specific adjustments.

5.2. High Computational Costs

Training CNNs, especially deep networks with multiple layers, demands substantial computational resources. High-performance GPUs, specialized hardware, and significant energy consumption are necessary, making CNN implementation costly and inaccessible to resource-limited healthcare facilities. This computational complexity also makes real-time processing challenging, which is critical in clinical settings where timely diagnosis is crucial.

5.3. Interpretability and Trust

CNNs are often described as “black boxes” because they learn abstract representations that are not easily interpretable. In medical imaging, where trust and accountability are paramount, this lack of transparency poses a significant challenge. Clinicians and radiologists may be hesitant to adopt CNN-based systems if they cannot understand or explain the model's decisions, which can hinder integration into healthcare practices. Efforts to enhance model interpretability, such as using heatmaps to visualize areas of focus, only partially address this issue and do not provide complete insights into the decision-making process.

5.4. Risk of Overfitting and Generalization

Medical imaging datasets are often diverse in imaging modalities (e.g., MRI, CT, X-rays), and overfitting is a common problem when training CNNs on specific datasets. A model trained on data from a single hospital or demographic may not generalize well to other populations or imaging systems. Overfitting also limits the model's adaptability to new cases, especially those involving subtle variations or rare conditions that were underrepresented in the training data.

5.5. Ethical and Privacy Concerns

CNN models in medical imaging often require patient data, raising ethical and privacy issues. In some cases, the data used for training cannot be adequately anonymized, posing risks of data leakage and compromising patient confidentiality. Ethical considerations also arise regarding the use of AI in medical decision-making; questions around liability, accountability, and fairness remain largely unresolved.

5.6. Regulatory and Legal Barriers

Deploying CNN-based tools in clinical settings requires regulatory approval to ensure they meet safety and efficacy standards. However, the evolving nature of CNN models makes it difficult to standardize and gain approval, as any change or update may require a new round of evaluation and certification. This regulatory burden slows down innovation and integration into healthcare systems.

In summary, while CNNs have shown great potential in medical imaging, challenges such as limited data availability, high computational costs, interpretability issues, risks of overfitting, privacy concerns, and regulatory barriers hinder their widespread adoption. Addressing these limitations requires interdisciplinary efforts, combining advances in AI with improvements in data access, ethical frameworks, computational resources, and healthcare policies

6. FUTURE DIRECTIONS FOR CNNS IN MEDICAL IMAGING

The future of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in medical imaging promises significant advancements, with ongoing research aimed at overcoming current limitations and expanding CNN applications in healthcare. Several future directions hold potential for transforming CNNs into more robust, accessible, and effective tools in clinical environments.

6.1. Improved Data Availability and Synthetic Data Generation

One of the primary limitations in CNN-based medical imaging is the scarcity of large, labeled datasets due to privacy concerns and the need for expert annotations. A promising future direction is the use of synthetic data generation techniques, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), which can create realistic medical images to augment limited datasets. Synthetic data can be used to address data imbalance and improve model training for rare diseases, enhancing CNN performance without the ethical concerns associated with real patient data.

6.2. Transfer Learning and Pre-trained Models

Transfer learning has shown promise in medical imaging by allowing CNNs pre-trained on large general datasets to adapt to specific medical imaging tasks. This approach reduces the data requirements and training time, making it suitable for smaller datasets typical in healthcare. The development of dedicated pre-trained models specific to medical domains could further enhance the efficiency and accuracy of CNNs across various imaging modalities and diagnostic tasks.

6.3. Explainable AI (XAI) for Interpretability

Enhancing interpretability is essential for clinical acceptance, as clinicians need to understand CNN outputs to trust the technology. The future of CNNs in medical imaging includes integrating Explainable AI (XAI) methods to provide clear visualizations and explanations for predictions. Techniques such as attention maps, saliency maps, and Grad-CAM can help visualize which areas of an image influenced a CNN's decision, increasing transparency. More advanced interpretability tools that break down complex decision-making into understandable insights could bridge the trust gap between clinicians and AI systems.

6.4. Multimodal and Hybrid Models

Many medical diagnoses rely on information from multiple sources, such as imaging, clinical notes, and laboratory tests. CNNs could be combined with other AI models to analyze multimodal data, creating hybrid models that integrate various data types. This approach could improve diagnostic accuracy and enable a more holistic understanding of a patient’s health status. Future models may blend CNNs with natural language processing (NLP) for clinical notes or reinforcement learning for adaptive decision-making, paving the way for comprehensive diagnostic tools.

6.5. Real-time and Edge Computing Applications

As CNNs become more efficient, they can be implemented on smaller, more localized devices, enabling real-time analysis at the point of care. Future CNN models optimized for edge computing could process medical images directly on devices, such as portable ultrasound machines or smartphone-based diagnostic tools. This development could bring advanced diagnostic capabilities to remote or resource-limited settings, facilitating quicker diagnoses and broader healthcare accessibility.

6.6. Federated Learning for Data Privacy

Privacy concerns are significant in healthcare, making federated learning a promising direction. This approach allows CNN models to train on decentralized data across multiple hospitals or institutions without moving data off-site, preserving patient privacy while still providing high-quality training data. By using federated learning, CNNs could learn from diverse patient populations, increasing their generalizability without compromising data security.

6.7. Integration with Clinical Workflows and Regulatory Support

For CNNs to have a transformative impact on healthcare, they must be integrated into existing clinical workflows. Future CNN development will likely focus on seamless compatibility with clinical software and electronic health record (EHR) systems, ensuring that CNN outputs can be accessed and utilized easily by healthcare professionals. Additionally, advancements in regulatory frameworks specific to AI-driven healthcare tools could streamline the approval process, making it easier to bring CNN-based medical imaging solutions to clinical settings.

In summary, the future of CNNs in medical imaging is directed toward creating more accurate, interpretable, and accessible models through synthetic data, transfer learning, explainable AI, and privacy-preserving methods like federated learning. By addressing these areas, CNNs could play an increasingly vital role in global healthcare, making sophisticated diagnostic tools available in diverse clinical environments.

7. COMPARISON BETWEEN CNNS AND TRADITIONAL IMAGE ANALYSIS METHODS

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have revolutionized image analysis, outperforming traditional methods in numerous applications. The key differences lie in their approach to feature extraction, scalability, and adaptability.

7.1. Feature Extraction

Traditional Methods:

Traditional image analysis relies on hand-crafted features, such as edges, textures, or shapes, extracted using techniques like SIFT, HOG, or wavelet transforms. These methods require domain expertise to design effective features and are often limited to capturing low-level patterns.

CNNs:

CNNs automatically learn features from data through convolutional layers. They extract hierarchical features, from edges in early layers to complex patterns in deeper layers, without manual intervention. This adaptability eliminates the need for domain-specific feature engineering.

7.2. Scalability and Performance

Traditional Methods:

Traditional algorithms struggle with large datasets and complex patterns due to their fixed feature sets and computational constraints. Their performance often plateaus as data complexity increases.

CNNs:

CNNs scale effectively with larger datasets, improving performance as more data becomes available. Techniques like transfer learning allow CNNs to leverage pre-trained models, enhancing efficiency for new tasks.

7.3. Adaptability

Traditional Methods:

Customization for different tasks often requires redesigning features and algorithms, making traditional methods less flexible.

CNNs:

CNNs are highly adaptable, capable of fine-tuning for specific tasks with minimal reconfiguration. This makes them suitable for diverse applications, from medical imaging to autonomous driving.

While traditional methods offer simplicity and interpretability, CNNs provide superior accuracy, scalability, and adaptability, making them the dominant choice for modern image analysis tasks

8. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have significantly transformed the landscape of medical imaging, offering remarkable advancements in the diagnosis and treatment of various diseases. Their ability to automatically extract hierarchical features from complex medical images has made CNNs indispensable in tasks such as detecting tumors, classifying diseases, and segmenting anatomical structures. By leveraging large datasets and deep learning techniques, CNNs can outperform traditional diagnostic methods, delivering faster, more accurate, and sometimes even earlier detection of abnormalities.

The integration of CNNs into clinical workflows enhances not only diagnostic precision but also treatment planning, improving patient outcomes. As CNN models evolve with more sophisticated architectures and the availability of diverse medical imaging data, their potential continues to grow. However, challenges remain, such as the need for interpretability, regulatory approval, and addressing ethical concerns related to data privacy and bias.

Moving forward, collaboration between AI researchers, clinicians, and healthcare professionals will be crucial to ensuring the successful and responsible deployment of CNNs in medical imaging. With ongoing advancements, CNN-based systems are poised to revolutionize healthcare, empowering practitioners with more accurate tools for personalized medicine and ultimately transforming patient care on a global scale.

Chapter 10

Data Augmentation Techniques in Deep Image Processing

Fikriye Ataman

https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0257-7730

Van Yüzüncü Yıl University, Turkey

ABSTRACT

Image data augmentation is a technique for artificially expanding and diversifying existing image datasets. This method is beneficial when training data is insufficient for machine learning and deep learning models. It allows models to generalize better during training and reduces overfitting. The main techniques include geometric transformations, color and light changes, noise addition, optical distortions, and modern blending methods. These methods expose the model to more diversity by simulating real-world variations. Thus, data collection and labeling costs are reduced while the model's performance and generalization capacity increase. Data augmentation plays a role in the basis of success, especially in studies where medical images are processed. This study explains the techniques used for image augmentation in detail. It also reveals the performance results of the methods used on data sets and their effects on deep models. The study includes the most frequently used methods and provides a detailed literature review.

1. INTRODUCTION

The relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and medical imaging has become much more substantial. Medical imaging visualizes the body's internal structures to diagnose and treat disease. This process allows physicians to more accurately diagnose disease, personalize treatment plans, and track patient recovery (Aamir et al.,2023). Many diseases can be treated more successfully if they are diagnosed early (Carrasco Ramírez, 2024; Khalifa et al., 2024; Mahesh Batra & Reche, 2023; Pinto-Coelho, 2023; Rana & Shuford, 2024; Zatloukal et al., 2020). Medical imaging can detect disease earlier, allowing treatment to begin sooner (Guan et al., 2021). Medical images also give doctors detailed information about disease type, size, and location. This reduces the risk of misdiagnosis and allows the proper treatment to be chosen(Carrasco Ramírez, 2024; Khalifa et al., 2024; Mahesh Batra & Reche, 2023; Pinto-Coelho, 2023; Rana & Shuford, 2024). This is especially important for rare diseases (D. He et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024). In addition, imaging results can enable detailed preoperative planning for surgical procedures. This can shorten surgery time and reduce the risk of complications. During the treatment process, medical imaging also helps evaluate the treatment's effectiveness and modify the treatment plan if necessary. Medical imaging can perform many procedures with more minor or even no incisions. This means less pain, faster recovery, and fewer complications for patients (Carrasco Ramírez, 2024; Khalifa et al., 2024; Rana & Shuford, 2024). Many different techniques are used to produce medical images. Standard imaging techniques include positron emission tomography, x-ray, magnetic resonance imaging, computed tomography, and ultrasound (Aamir et al., 2022). The processing of medical images, which impact people's lives, is naturally of great importance.

Medical image processing faces numerous challenges, including the complex nature of images (Zheng et al., 2024), the scarcity of high-quality data for specific diseases, the cost of accurately labeling medical images, and ethical concerns about data privacy and security (Jalal et al., 2021; Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Sen et al., 2020; Tripathi & Musiolik, 2022). The reliability and transparency of AI models are crucial, and the distribution of data used for model training affects their ability to generalize to real-world data. The lack of data also negatively impacts model performance, as it can lead to overfitting and impairing the model's ability to generalize to new data. To address these challenges, research is being conducted to develop more extensive data sets, advanced algorithms, and powerful computational approaches (Jalal et al., 2021; Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Sen et al., 2020; Tripathi & Musiolik, 2022).

Regardless of how big the problems are, the power of the advancement of medical image processing is straightforward (Jalal et al., 2021; Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023). In recent years, the impact of deep neural networks on medical image processing has increased significantly. However, it is well known that medical data is often under-observed by nature, and the low volume of image data is a significant constraint on model training and performance. One important approach to address this is to increase the data sample size using image data augmentation (DA) methods. This study provides in-depth information on DA techniques developed in recent years. It also provides a detailed comparison of experimental results obtained by applying the models to state-of-the-art datasets. This study will provide researchers in the field with detailed information about DA techniques. By comparing the experimental results, it will help researchers to decide which technique or model is more appropriate for their data.

1.1. Image Data Augmentation (IDA)

IDA is a technique that increases the size and diversity of image data by creating new images from an existing dataset (Gao et al., 2019; C. Zhang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023). It is used in computer vision fields like object recognition, classification, model training (Goodfellow et al., 2020), abstract visual reasoning (S. Hu et al., 2021), and segmentation(Lee et al., 2023). IDA methods improve classification performance in limited training data and can prevent overfitting by learning about statistical noise in the training data. It also enhances generalization performance in object detection and makes models more robust to changes in input data. DA is also used in abstract visual reasoning to create new models consistent with task rules(Goodfellow et al., 2020).

1.2. The Importance of Data Augmentation

DA is important because ML models contribute to performing several image processing tasks, including segmentation, object detection, and classification.

DA is used in an abstract visual reasoning task to create new visual models consistent with the underlying rules. Thanks to the DA technique, the model learns the task's rules more efficiently and adapts to new data at a more acceptable rate (W. He et al., 2023)

Situations may arise where the available data is missing, making it necessary to take action against rare events and run ML models. DA is a preferred technique for filling the data gaps in rare events and effectively utilizing ML algorithms (Min et al., 2023).

Deformations and variations in the data can hinder the desired result in object detection problems. The DA technique can solve these obstacles (H. Lee et al., 2023).

DL has achieved significant success in various computer vision tasks, such as segmentation, object identification, and image classification. However, inadequate datasets are utilized to train DL models, which can result in overfitting and poor generalization. Increasing the data sample size is an important measure to counter these problems.

There are many areas, like abstract visual reasoning (C. Zhang et al., 2023), image-to-image translation, hyperspectral image classification (Gao et al., 2019), where DA is applied(Xu et al., 2023).

Image classification is challenging because natural images have high intra-class and low inter-class diversity (Aamir et al., 2019). Cross-class learning aims to improve classification performance by learning the features that distinguish different classes. DA is a common approach used to improve the performance of cross-class learning. DA generates new data points that are consistent with the task's ground rules. DA will help the model learn features that distinguish between different classes more effectively (Tokozume et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2017).

Another application area where DA is effective is Federated Learning (FL). FL and DA are two complementary technologies. FL is a collaborative ML method where user data never leaves users' devices, and the training process is distributed among many users (Hao et al., 2021; B. Hu et al., 2023; H. Zhang et al., 2023; J. Zhang & Jiang, 2022).

FL prevents sensitive data from being collected on a central server. DA methods can be integrated with FL and applied on local devices, and the model can be updated with augmented data from local data. The model is trained without sending data to a central server, and data privacy is protected(Hao et al., 2021; B. Hu et al., 2023; J. Zhang & Jiang, 2022).

FL brings together heterogeneous data sources from different institutions or devices. DA increases diversity by being applied to each of these heterogeneous data sets and makes the model more generalizable than DA alone. For example, DA performed with data from different demographic groups can reduce the model's biases(Hao et al., 2021; B. Hu et al., 2023; Menegatti et al., 2023; H. Zhang et al., 2023; J. Zhang & Jiang, 2022).

In some institutions, DA may have limited data sources. DA can be used locally to expand these small data sets and allow FL to benefit from these devices. For example, a few images on a mobile device can be used to train the model by augmenting them with augmentation methods(Hao et al., 2021; Menegatti et al., 2023; J. Zhang & Jiang, 2022).

DA can be included in FL processes by creating synthetic data with generative models. Using this synthetic data, FL can increase the performance of models without accessing sensitive data.

DA can increase anonymity in FL, especially in sensitive data scenarios. For example, anonymizing images with geometric transformations increases data privacy. FL trains the model securely with this anonymized augmented data. For example, FL and DA can be used together on medical images from different hospitals. Each hospital increases the overall success of the model by augmenting local data. However, there may be some disadvantages. DA and FL processes may require high computational resources on local devices. Some devices or institutions may have less or low-quality data, this data imbalance situation may limit the effect of FL. Also, in FL, each device should perform DA operations synchronously. FL and DA form a strong collaboration, especially in scenarios with sensitive and small data sets. FL and DA improve model performance while ensuring data privacy. Further integration of these technologies may provide more effective healthcare, finance, and mobile application solutions(Hao et al., 2021; B. Hu et al., 2023; Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Menegatti et al., 2023; H. Zhang et al., 2023; J. Zhang & Jiang, 2022).

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have attained considerable success in image classification, object detection, and many other diverse computer vision tasks. DNNs often struggle to provide accurate uncertainty estimates, which can be important for jobs such as diagnosing disease and autonomous driving(D. He et al., 2024; Jalal et al., 2021; Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Sen et al., 2020). DA is a common approach used to improve the robustness and uncertainty estimates of DNNs. It helps the DNN learn to generalize to new data, including competing examples. DA encourages the DNN to learn more informative features, allowing the model to make more accurate uncertainty estimates (Hendrycks et al., 2020).

DL is vital in computer vision and represents state-of-the-art results in many tasks, such as object detection, segmentation, and classification (Aamir et al., 2023). DL models need enormous amounts and various training data. DA can help fulfill this need by generating new instances from current data sets. Collecting enough diverse images for DL models could be difficult and expensive. Generating artificial image data creates an excellent comfort zone.

1.3. The Challenges of Data Augmentation

The accountability of the model to be used plays a critical role in the diagnosis and treatment processes. It is necessary to explain why and how the models' outputs are formed. Otherwise, making a wrong diagnosis can have fatal risks (Altaf et al., 2019; Chlap et al., 2021; Hesamian et al., 2019; Razzak et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2023).

The model's decision-making processes should be transparent. That is, model errors should be traceable, and in the event of an error, the problem should be more easily detected and corrected. Ethically, applications must comply with international standards. Therefore, accountability is also a necessity for legal compliance(Chlap et al., 2021; Garcea et al., 2023; Razzak et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2023).

Patient image data is anonymized during augmentation, but certain image features can reveal the patient's identity. When synthetic data is produced, a sample like the original data can be created, leading to privacy violations(Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Tripathi & Musiolik, 2022).

Black box models can create ethical problems in clinical decisions. For example: A model may classify a tumor as benign but ignore the presence of an abnormality in a certain area. In this case, it becomes difficult for physicians to question or verify model decisions.

In addition, if DA processes are based on incorrect or biased data, models can make biased decisions (Carrasco Ramírez, 2024; Khalifa et al., 2024; Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Rana & Shuford, 2024; Tripathi & Musiolik, 2022).

Patients should be informed whether their medical images will be used for augmentation or synthetic data production. Explaining data use processes and obtaining patient consent are ethically imperative. The lack of accountability and transparency in the models on which medical decisions are based can reduce physician and patient trust (Koohi-Moghadam & Bae, 2023; Tripathi & Musiolik, 2022)

Despite all these limitations, explainable AI methods should be used. Quality control mechanisms should be implemented in DA processes. Legal regulations regarding data privacy should be considered in augmentation processes. Ethics committees should play an active role in clinical AI projects. In addition, clinical teams should be trained on the advantages, risks, and limitations of augmented data and AI models.

2. RELATED DATA AUGMENTATION METHODS

2.1. Mixup

Mixup is a DA technique used to improve performance in image classification tasks. It seeks to improve the model's capacity for generalization and robustness by generating random mixtures of images belonging to different classes (H. Zhang et al., 2018a).

When it is desired to combine an image pair such as (xi,yi) and (xj,yj), where the one-hot labels in an image data are denoted by y and the data itself is denoted by x, Equation 1, also called Vanilla Mixup and Mixup, is used (H. Zhang et al., 2018b). Here, λ is a hyper-parameter determining how to mix the two images. The blended images assist ML models in steadily improving their performance by understanding certain hidden relationships in the uncharted search area.

2.2. CAM-Mix

The CAM-Mix algorithm is a new method designed to improve DA and model generalization for images (He et al., 2023). The algorithm consists of two main components. First, CAM uses a DL model to identify the most important regions and objects of the image. This allows the model to focus its attention on meaningful visual information and ignore background noise. Secondly, Mixup is a DA technique used to create new synthetic images by randomly mixing two images (He et al., 2023). CAM-Mix integrates Mixup with CAM modules to focus the mixing process on visually important regions.

CAM-Mix blends the visual attributes of two images without specifically extracting the visual attributes, unlike Mixup, which creates images with new visual attribute values outside the current limited set. This is accomplished by using Equation 2 and Equation 3 to define the following grey-level morphological procedures for a pair of grey-scale pictures I1 and I2 of size n×m. No new visual feature values are generated during the proposed image mixing process. The characteristics of the generated images are taken from each of the two original photos without the attributes being explicitly removed, and new images are created without the need for extra scalars or interpolation functions like vanilla mixup. By varying the candidate responses, the goal is to expand the training data. For this purpose, A = {ac} ∪ AN, where ac is the set containing correct answers, Q is the set to be eliminated, and AN is the set containing incorrect (negative) answers. 2.3. Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN)

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is a DL algorithm consisting of two neural networks (Chen & Chan, 2023; I. Goodfellow et al., 2020; I. J. Goodfellow et al., 2014; Stankovic et al., 2024). The GAN model tries to generate new data by giving the training data set to the deep network, training the network, estimating a probability distribution for this data, and generating new data based on this distribution. In general, they are game-theoretic models based on optimization-based generative modeling. They are best known for their success in image data generation. In a competitive setup, two models are developed simultaneously: a discriminative D and a generative G. The generative model G learns the data distribution. In contrast, model D assesses the likelihood that a given sample comes from the training dataset. The goal of G is to maximize the chances that D will incorrectly classify the samples. This framework corresponds to a minimax two-player game. G and D are MLPs, and the whole system is trained by back-propagation. The proposed G and D networks are opposing networks. A discriminative network is designed to determine whether a sample originates from an actual data distribution or a generated model distribution, and it is compared to the generator network G. In this analogy, the discriminative network resembles law enforcement attempting to identify counterfeit currency. In contrast, the generative network represents a group of counterfeiters striving to produce fake currency and use it discreetly. The competitive nature of this “game” compels both sides to continuously improve their strategies until the generated data becomes indistinguishable from authentic data as shown in Figure 2. The model’s algorithmic steps explain how the model operates with Algorithm 1 is shown in Figure 3.

The input noise variables pz(z) are pre-defined to learn the generator's distribution pg over the data x. G(z; θg) is a mapping function to be applied to the data domain. In this case, an MLP with parameters θg represents the differentiable function G. The second MLP that produces a single scalar is the discriminant network D. D(x; θd) is the definition. The probability that x originates from the training data rather than the pg distribution is given by D(x). The training process is not a one-time event but an iterative one when continuously optimizing the likelihood of correctly labeling training and G instances. When D is trained, G is trained to minimize log(1 - D(G(z))) at the same time. Equation 6 provides the two-player minimax game D and G play with value function V(G, D).

In reality, there might not be enough slope in Equation 6 for G to learn effectively. Since the samples differ from the training data, D may reject them with high confidence in the early stages of learning, while G is weak. Log(1 - D(G(z))) is saturated in this instance. It is suggested that G be trained to maximize logD(G(z)) rather than to minimize log(1 - D(G(z))) (I. J. Goodfellow et al., 2014). The dynamics of G and D reach the same fixed point with this objective function, but it offers much larger gradients at the beginning of learning. For gradient-based updates, it was proposed that any other common gradient-based learning rule might be applied; In the model, a momentum learning rule is applied.

2.4. CycleGAN

CycleGAN is a DL algorithm for visual style transfer between two different datasets (Zhu et al., 2017). It can work especially on mismatched datasets. It has two GANs (Goodfellow et al., 2020) and two discriminators, one for each GAN, and uses a cycle consistency loss function to transfer visual style from one image to another (Zhu et al., 2017). CycleGAN is given two datasets consisting of images from two different areas. The images in these sets do not need to match each other. It contains two generative layers, denoted by F and G. The first generating layer, G, transforms an image from one domain into another domain, while the second generating layer, F, tries to reverse this transformation. There is a separator for each area. These discriminators aim to differentiate between authentic images and fake ones the generators produce. An image is first transformed into the other domain with G and then returned to the first domain with F. The distance of the resulting image from the original image is called the cyclic coherence loss. The model is trained to minimize these losses. Thus, producers learn how to produce realistic images and, at the same time, reconstruct back to the original image.

In the model, X= {x1,…,xN} and Y= {y1,…,yM} are training data, and the variables x and y come from the same distribution. There are two distribution functions in the model, F and G which are defined as F: X→Y and G: Y→X. In addition, two contrasting discriminators, Dx and Dy are defined. Dx learns the difference between {x} and {F(y)}, which is the result transformed to Y, while Dy learns the difference between {y} and {G(x)}. Basically, two losses are calculated here. The first is the loss in each transformation, called the opposite loss, and the second is the loss between the generated data and the actual data when the functions F and G complete a full cycle. Here, the counter loss is calculated using Equation 9 for function G and Equation 10 for function F. The loss of cyclic consistency at the end of the loop is calculated by Equation 11. The total loss of the model is considered the sum of these losses. The total loss is calculated with Equation 12, with the hyper-parameter λ of the G and F function losses representing the relative importance of the two models. The objective is to minimize the total loss.

2.5. Robust Data Augmentation GAN (RDAGAN)

RDAGAN is a variant of GAN developed to increase the diversity of data and strengthen the generalization capability of the model. This model is particularly robust to limited data sets and changes in data distribution. It is used for tasks such as image synthesis, image translation and image editing (H. Lee et al., 2023).

The model is essentially based on the GAN model. Differently, it consists of two separate networks. The first one is the image object generator network and the second one is the image transformation network. The object generating network model uses the InfoGAN (X. Chen et al., 2016) architecture. The images produced by the object generating network model are given as input to the object transforming network and a loss function is calculated. Since the InfoGAN architecture has Info and GAN modules, which are the information layer, it calculates two different loss values. While the loss in the GAN module is calculated with Equation 13, the loss value of the Info module is calculated with Equation 14. The total loss of the producer network module is the sum of the losses of these two modules and is given by Equation 15. Equation 16 shows the total loss function of the model.

The image transformation network combines clean images (ic∈C) with target parts Gobj(z,c) generated from the InfoGan model. It is very similar to the CycleGAN architecture. It is an encoder-decoder architecture containing ResNet blocks. The difference is that the generator keeps the sampling frequency flexible. Therefore, it provides flexibility to the size variance of the images. This generator module has two different discriminators, local(Dtrlocal) and global(Dtrglobal), which calculate the loss value of the module. The global allocator evaluates the image produced by the generating network. It does not use the whole image, but only a patchy part of it. Equation 17 gives a measure of how similar the image is to the target area image. The loss of the Info layer is calculated by Equation 18. The loss between the input image (ic) and the generated image (Gtr(ip,ic)) is considered as the background loss and is calculated by Equation 19. 2.6. Pix2Pix (PatchGAN)

The Pix2Pix algorithm is a model proposed by (Isola et al., 2018). A similar model is given in another study (Wang et al., 2021) under the name PatchGAN. Since the two models are the same, they are given under one title. PatchGAN is a DL algorithm for tasks such as image synthesis, translation, and editing. It is a discriminative architecture used when generating data with GAN. It divides images into small pieces called patches and processes each patch separately. In this way, it can produce higher quality and more realistic images (Isola et al., 2018). While in classical classification problems, the whole image is reduced to one class, in patchGAN, each patch of the image is classified. Then, the average value of all the classified results is taken or combined by applying maximum pooling and given as a result. GANs are generative models that learn by minimizing a loss function and are designed to classify whether the output image is real or fake. Blurry images are unacceptable, as they can appear fraudulent. GANs are utilized for various tasks that typically require different loss functions since the loss function, they train with can adapt based on the data. In contrast, conditional GAN models have been produced in which an image is given as input as a condition (Goodfellow∗ et al., 2014). The conditional GAN model differs in that it learns a structural loss value. This structural loss penalizes the joint reconstruction of the output. Conditional GAN models provide a suitable architecture for picture-to-picture transformation. In the work by Isola et al. for PatchGAN, a U-Net and Encoder-Decoder architecture are used separately in the generator part. As a discriminator, it uses a convolutional network model and a classification model that penalizes image fragments rather than the whole image. GAN models here are generative models that create a new image from an image. G represents the generator and D the discriminator, cap G: z goes to y where z is the noisy input image vector, and y is the output image. The conditional GAN model is different because it tries to produce an outcome with the observation vector x and the noisy input image vector z. Therefore, the production function in the conditional GAN model is defined as G: {z,x}→y. The generator G's goal is to create phony images that are identical to authentic ones. To assess the degree of difference between these phony and authentic photos, discriminator D is trained. Equation 20 provides the conditional GAN model's objective function. Equation 21 shows the total loss. While G tries to minimize the objective function, discriminator D discriminates by trying to maximize it. When x is not given as a condition, this loss is calculated as shown in Equation 22. In previous studies, these loss functions have been tested by adding the loss of L1 (Isola et al., 2018) and L2 (Pathak et al., 2016). (Isola et al., 2018) calculated the total loss by adding the L1 norm shown in Equation 23 as in Equation 24. What is essentially done in this model is that instead of training the generator G to minimize the error log(1 - D(x,G(x, z)), the network is trained to maximize the error logD(x, G(x, z)). This means the discriminative network (D) has a lower learning rate than the generative network (G). The model uses SGD as the activation function, learning rate 0.0002, ADAM as the optimization function, and β1 = 0.5, β2 = 0.999 as momentum parameters (Isola et al., 2018). PatchGAN's algorithm is shown in Figure 6. The Pix2Pix architecture is shown in Figure 7.

2.7. Pre-Activation Residual Attention Network (PRAN)

PRAN is a DL algorithm combining residual network principles and attention mechanisms. It is built to perform well on tasks like object detection, image reconstruction, and classification (Gao et al., 2019). The model was developed to classify hyperspectral images. A set of hyperspectral images is represented as D∈RHxWxB where H is the height, W is the width, and B is the hyperspectral bandwidth. Images are given to the model in segments. Each image is composed of SxS neighborhoods woven around the central label pixel. Therefore, a segmented image is of size SxSxB. Assuming that an image contains N label pixels, the dataset of fragment images will be X={ x1,…,xn}∈RSxSxB. Their corresponding actual classes are defined as Y= {y1,…,yn}∈{1,2,…,Q}. Q here represents the classes of interest. What is emphasized in the model are the residual blocks that are replaced. The residue blocks are supplemented by two convolutional and a residue network, also called a hopping layer. This is called pre-activated residue. The modified residue block and the normal residue block used in the model are shown in the following Figure 8.

Figure 8. Normal residual block(a), pre-activated residual block (b)(Gao et al., 2019)

A residual block's output is calculated as follows: H(x)=f(F(x)+x), where f is the activation function, F(x) is the convolutional layer's pre-aggregation output, and F is the residual learning function. Before the convolutional layers, the residual blocks are pre-activated by applying a batch norm and RELU. In this instance, H(x)=F(x)+x will be the outcome of the pre-activated residual blocks.

Since the suggested network uses data from all spectral bands as inputs, needless redundant information lowers the classification accuracy. To solve this problem, a channel attention mechanism for recalibration is incorporated into the pre-activation residual block shown in Figure 9, comprised of the PRAN model.

Figure 9. Pre-activated residual attention block (PRAB) architecture (Gao et al., 2019)

Assume that the attention mechanism has s × s × d and c input feature maps, where c and d represent the channel and depth dimensions, respectively. C 1×1×1 channel feature tensors are produced by compressing the global spatial information in each feature map using a 3-B global average pooling (GAP) layer. The channel dimensionality is then decreased by feeding the feature tensors as input to a 1×1×1 3-B convolutional layer. Specifically, the channel dimension of the feature tensor becomes c/r during convolution, where r is a reduction ratio. The value of r in the suggested network is 4.

After that, a ReLU function is used to enhance the channel responses' nonlinearity, a second 1×1×1 3-D convolutional layer is used to expand the channel's size, and c feature tensors are produced. The attention mechanism's final output is rescaled to cs × s × d feature maps by multiplying the output by the pre-activation residual's feature maps using a sigmoid function. This implementation allows each feature map to be adaptively recalibrated by assigning it a channel weight. Additionally, the 2∗c2/r parameters obtained from the two 3-D convolutional layers inside provide an attention mechanism.

2.8. BC Learning

Between-class learning (BC Learning) is a DL algorithm that aims to improve performance in image classification tasks by maximizing class discrimination. The algorithm focuses on learning the differences between images belonging to different classes and thus provides more accurate classification results (Tokozume et al., 2018). Standard learning for classification issues involves selecting one training sample from the dataset and feeding it into the model. A single-label output is used to train the model. On the other hand, with BC learning, two training samples from distinct classes are chosen randomly from the dataset and combined. After that, the model is trained to provide the mixing ratio for each class using the mixed data fed into it. The typical loss function, as opposed to cross-entropy loss, is the difference between the model's outputs and the ratio labels. Mixing is not performed in the test phase. In the model, let {x1,t1} and {x2,t2} be datasets belonging to two different classes labeled from the training data. τ ∼  ∪ (0,1) being a random variable from a uniform distribution, the image datasets are shuffled by this random rate. Labels are shuffled as 𝜏t1+(1 – 𝜏)t2. The data are similarly shuffled simply as 𝜏x1+(1 – 𝜏)x2. However, to make the data more appropriate, it was divided by a coefficient, and as a result, the confused data was corrected to !!CFG-ERROR!! 2.9. CutMix

CutMix is a DA technique used to improve performance in image classification tasks. It aims to increase the generalization ability and robustness of the model by combining random fragments of images belonging to different classes (Yun et al., 2019). It is pretty similar to the Mixup model. In Mixup, data and labels of two images are mixed for all pixels, while in Cutmix, patches of two different images are mixed. This allows the model to produce more natural images. Where x∈RWxHxC is the training data and y is the label of the data, the aim is to generate the image $\left( \overset{\sim}{x},\overset{\sim}{y} \right)$ from two different training data (xA,yA) and (xB,yB). A combination process for this generation is given by Equation 31. Here M ∈ {0, 1}W×H is a binary mask with ones denoting the mask filled with ones indicating the place to be extracted and filled from the two images. ⊙ is element-wise multiplication. λ is a sample taken from the beta distribution that represents the combination ratio between two data points (𝜆~𝛽(𝛼,𝛼)). In the original study, α=1 in all experiments. In other words, λ is sampled from a uniform distribution (0, 1). Compared to Mixup, CutMix can create a locally natural image by substituting a patch from another training image for the image region. To take a sample of M, first, a boundary box Boundary=(rx,ry,rW,rH) is defined, which determines the size of the image to be copied from image A to image B. The box coordinates are set as in Equation 32. The samples are taken as rectangles in accordance with the original dimensions of the images (Yun et al., 2019).


$$\overset{\sim}{x} = M \odot x_{A} + \left( 1 - M \right) \odot x_{B},M \in \left\{ 0,1\}^{WxH}~and~\overset{\sim}{y} = \lambda y_{A} + \left( 1 - \lambda \right)y_{B} \right.$$
(31)


$$r_{x} \sim U\left( {0,W} \right),r_{w} = W\sqrt{1 - \lambda}~and~r_{y} \sim U\left( 0,H \right),r_{h} = H\sqrt{1 - \lambda}$$
(32)

2.10. AugMix

Augmix is a simple yet effective data processing method designed to make image classification models more robust and resilient to uncertainty. Basically, it works by mixing versions of an image augmented in different ways (Hendrycks et al., 2020b). It creates augmented versions of the original images by various methods such as rotating, cropping, adding noise, and changing color. Thus, these augmented versions make the model more sensitive to different visual variations. Then, the augmented version images are mixed with a certain ratio. This blending process allows the model to focus on more general and abstract features. The blended images are given the same labeling as the original image. In this way, the model learns to correctly classify both different visual variations and their mixtures. In this way, the model gains robustness by becoming more resilient to unexpected changes in real-world images, such as lighting conditions. The model can better predict how confidently it classifies an image. This helps to reduce the risk of misclassification. This emphasizes the uncertainty estimation feature of the model. The model is a generalizing model that performs better on different data sets by focusing on more general and abstract visual features. The model is processed by data pre-augmentation, composite data generation from augmented data, and error calculation using Jensen-Shannon Divergence Consistency Loss. In data pre-augmentation, the data is augmented with three consecutive chains of 3 randomly selected operations. These augmentation results are then merged. The model is then trained by minimizing the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the original image xorig and the posterior distributions of its augmented variants. Where !!CFG-ERROR!! 2.11. PuzzleMix

3. CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION

This study focuses on DA methods based on deep network models. It aims to examine new approaches that can deeply overcome the shortcomings of classical DA models. Image processing is widely used in medical data. Especially in medical data, it is vital for early diagnosis and early intervention in critical areas such as rare diseases. However, the low sample size of medical images is one of the most important limitations of this field. DA is one of the solutions that can be taken as a precaution. There are many methods used for DA. However, which of these methods should be preferred is usually a big question mark for researchers. In this study, current methods are explained in detail, and the comparison of the experimental results of the models with the state-of-the-art datasets to give researchers an idea is given in Table 1. In addition, model performances on the datasets are shown in Table 2. When we look at the literature, while a 99.7% success rate was achieved for Mixup in the studies conducted on the MNIST dataset, the GAN model reached a 98% success rate. Therefore, it is seen that Mixup is more successful than the GAN model in DA. As a result, it can be said that CAM-Mix has also contributed to the success of the CoPINET model. In the experimental results with CIFAR10, one of the frequently preferred current data sets, SuperMix comes with 97.2%, AugMix 96.4%, Co-Mixup 96.3%, CutMix 95.2%, BCLearning 93.7% and GAN 70% accuracy. Similarly, in the studies conducted with the Celeb-A data set, it is clear that the PatchGAN algorithm gives better results than the GAN model. In general, it is seen that the size and structure of the dataset directly affects DA performance and model training performance. Therefore, selecting the model to be used in DA is very important. However, although accepted datasets are used, whether real-life datasets will show the same success can only be revealed through experimental studies. Therefore, it should be known that there is still a significant gap in the field of medical image processing. This study gives a detailed framework of current and frequently used DA models.

3.1. Discussion of Ethical Issues

Augmented image data in clinical settings is a powerful tool for improving the performance of AI and ML models, especially in areas such as medical image analysis. DA techniques increase model performance in cases where medical image data is limited, prevent over-learning, and contribute to the model's generalization ability. Provides better representation in rare cases. In addition, imbalances in image data belonging to different age groups, genders, or ethnic groups can be eliminated with augmentation techniques, reducing model bias. However, besides these positive effects, there are ethical problems and risks related to model accountability, data privacy, and model transparency. For example, augmented image data may not fully reflect the characteristics of real-world clinical images. This can lead to misleading and pose great risks. Applications must be carefully designed to solve ethical issues such as data privacy, model transparency, and accountability. If this balance is achieved, DA can be used safely, ethically, and effectively in clinical decision-support systems.

3.2. Conclusion with Future Directions

The use of augmented data in medical imaging and AI is rapidly developing as a critical area shaping the future of clinical decision support systems. Potential developments in this area and the adoption of new technologies and emerging trends promise a major transformation in medical practices. It can provide more interactive diagnostic and medical education methods by integrating with Augmented Reality and Virtual Reality. In addition, more holistic clinical decision support can be provided by developing multimodal systems by combining them with large language models. Advanced models such as diffusion can create data that is almost indistinguishable from real medical images. This offers a significant opportunity, especially for simulating rare diseases, protecting data privacy, and reducing anonymity risks. With Federated Learning, model training can be done from many different sources without violating patient privacy, thus complying with data privacy regulations. It can enable the customization of medical models in the future. In the future, personalized diagnostic algorithms that consider individual risk factors for each patient can be created. More accurate results can be obtained by integrating the patient's genetic structure, lifestyle, and past medical images. Moreover, it will significantly contribute to algorithmic justice by reducing bias. Another contribution of DA will be to real-time continuous medical systems. It will help provide fast and effective model adaptation and make more accurate decisions in emergencies such as epidemics. Medical use of augmented data and AI models will be supported by stricter standards and regulations. This will ensure that the technology is used ethically and safely. The future of augmented data use in medical imaging offers multifaceted opportunities and challenges, both technologically and ethically. Advanced algorithms can potentially provide better diagnostic tools and personalized health solutions. However, the progress of these processes within the framework of reliable, transparent, and ethical principles will be critical for successfully adopting these technologies in the healthcare sector. Ongoing research will continue to add value to human health while expanding the boundaries of medical AI. Comparison of models according to features and specifications is shown in Table 3.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for Medical Imaging:
