ABSTRACT

In the recent past medical imaging has emerged as a tool for better diagnosis of patients. The diagnosis mechanism includes Non-invasive methods and further treatment of various diseases viz., pneumonia cancer and other neurological disorders. To address the challenges in the existing methods, this chapter introduces a novel Multi-Stream Attention-Based Convolutional Neural Network (MSA-CNN) technique which is a deep learning architecture. The main component of the proposed architecture is an Attentional mechanism that dynamically assigns prominence to the features of each modality, concentrating on the most relevant regions of the images that are of interest, to improve the models interpretability. Further, a Noise-Aware Loss Function is introduced to handle noise in the images to enhance model performance. Results show that the proposed technique is observed to have an accuracy of 95.7% on the Chest X-ray dataset, outperforming the existing benchmarking techniques to have 89.3% using AlexNet, 92.4% using ResNet-18 respectively.

1. INTRODUCTION

The present-day scenario of medical imaging techniques viz., Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), Computed Tomography (CT), and X-rays are used mostly and are considered as prime tools in modern healthcare system. Healthcare professionals will be using such tools to non-invasively visualize the internal body structures and further use to diagnose several conditions of the body pertaining from cancer to several infectious diseases. These technologies have revolutionized the way the diseases are detected, monitored and further treated. However, the interpretation of medical images has become complex and has remained till date, further making it a time-consuming task. Such a task can be done only through a skilled radiologist. The risk of human error is always present that depends on several factors such as fatigue or the overwhelming voluminous data that they acquire for processing. Recent studies show that radiologists can miss up to 30% of abnormalities when interpreting scans under pressure that leads to delay in the treatment or sometimes missed diagnoses (Wang et al., 2017).

Artificial Intelligence (AI), Deep Learning (DL), particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), is observed to be having better results in automation of the analysis of medical images that further assists technicians in making faster, for accurate diagnoses. CNNs have become a standard in image classification, segmentation and object detection as they can automatically learn hierarchical features from raw image data, removing the need for manual feature engineering (Litjens et al., 2017). These techniques can also be successfully applied to detect pneumonia in chest X-rays (Lakhani and Sundaram, 2017), segment brain tumors in MRI scans (Ronneberger et al., 2015), and diagnose COVID-19 from CT scans (Isensee et al., 2021). Many applications were developed in the recent past to demonstrate the potential of CNNs that reduce the workload on technicians and improve diagnostic accuracy.

However, in real-word clinical settings, several challenges remain unresolved in deploying CNNs for medical imaging. One of the major challenges is generalization. CNNs are trained on a specific dataset that often perform poorly when applied to images from different sources, viz., hospitals that use different imaging protocols or machines. For instance, a model that is trained on chest X-rays from one hospital may not generalize well to X-rays from another hospital. This is because of the resolution, noise level, or contrast that may differ from one hospital to another (Rajpurkar et al., 2017). This lack of generalization poses a critical problem for CNN-based models in healthcare, where variability between datasets is common. Guan et al. (Guan et al., 2021) presented an innovative framework for brain tumour classification using MRI images. This study achieved an overall accuracy of 98.04%, outperforming existing methods. The proposed model addresses challenges posed by low-quality MRI images. Additionally, the study employs effective data augmentation strategies, such as image rotation and flipping, to expand the training dataset and mitigate overfitting, thereby enhancing the model’s generalisation capability and reliability in tumour classification.

Another significant challenge in medical imaging lies in its multi-modal nature. Clinicians frequently need data from multiple imaging modalities for making a comprehensive diagnosis (Zhou, Greenspan, and Shen, 2017). For instance, MRI scans are highly effective in distinguishing soft tissues having varied contrast, while CT scans are better for visualizing bone structures. However, traditional CNN architectures, that are designed to handle single-modality data, struggle to integrate the complementary information that multi-modal inputs provide. Such an integration is essential to create comprehensive view of the patients condition particularly in diagnosing complex ailments such as cancer, where each modality uncovers unique aspects of the disease. Muhammad Aamir et al. (Aamir, M., et al., 2023) addressed the need for fast and improved brain tumor detection and the need for the computationally less complex approach to diagnose the diseases, achieved an accuracy of approximately 98.98%. Aamir, M. et al. (Aamir, M. et al., 2022) suggested that by combining EfficientNet-B0 and ResNet50 for feature extraction, along with innovative techniques like refinement, and alignment, the model demonstrates remarkable efficiency and diagnostic reliability.

In addition, the interpretability of CNN models poses a substantial alarm in the case of medical applications. These models are often considered as “black-box” models as their internal decision-making processes cannot be easily understandable. This lack of transparency makes it challenging for the healthcare professionals to cognize why the model has made a particular decision or prediction, which is critical in building AI-assisted diagnostic tools (Caruana et al., 2015). In general, in clinical practice, it is quite essential that the models that are developed need to provide accurate results and also explain the reason behind such result or prediction.

Furthermore, medical images are often affected by noise that is induced from several factors viz., movement of patient while acquiring the signal or during scanning or differences in imaging source / equipment. In general, CNNs (Tallapragada, V. S., et al., 2024). are trained on datasets that are free from noise, and will be perform poorly when trained on real-word data that may contain noise resulting in false positives or negatives (Ghafoorian et al., 2017). Therefore, models that are developed and designed for medical imaging must be robust to noise and must be capable of handling images of varying quality. Aamir, M. (Aamir, M. et al., 2019) evaluated the performance of a simple CNN architecture for image classification and demonstrated superior accuracy when compared to existing methods on CIFAR-10 dataset.

Moreover, medical images are often affected by noise. This will be the result of several factors such as patient movement during scanning or differences in imaging equipment. In general, CNNs trained on clean datasets. This hinders the performance as they are exposed to noisy, real-world data, resulting in false positives or negatives (Ghafoorian et al., 2017). Hence, models are designed for medical imaging that must be robust to noise and must have the capability of handling images of varying quality. In order to tackle these challenges, this chapter proposes a novel Multi-Stream Attention-Based CNN (MSA-CNN), architecture that processes Multi-Modal Data. The proposed technique uses multiple CNN streams. Each stream is dedicated to process that will be handling a different imaging modality (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray). This ensures that the features that are extracted will be unique to each modality that is captured.

In addition to the MSA-CNN an Attention Mechanism is added. The proposed architecture incorporates an attention mechanism that dynamically assigns weights to the features. These features are extracted each modality, making it to focus on the most relevant features. This process enhances the interpretability of the model, highlighting which parts of the image contributed most to the final prediction (Xu et al., 2016). Further, to handle noisy inputs, the proposed architecture incorporates a noise-aware loss function that penalizes the model more heavily for incorrect predictions on noisy data, thereby making the model more robust for real-world applications (Zhang et al., 2018).

Pujari, S. D., et al. (Pujari, S. D., et al. 2024) introduced a deep learning network for classifying histopathological images. Using Multi-Sclace architecture combined with an attention mechanism, the proposed or the developed model is effectively distinguishes the normal and cancerous cells and achieved an accuracy of 98.07%.

Figure 1 shows the generalised block diagram of the MSA-CNN architecture. The process begins with the acquiring of the multiple modalities or the multiple types of images (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray), which are simultaneously processed using separate CNN streams. Each process in the CNN (Simonyan and Zisserman, 2014) stream is dedicated for extraction of features that are unique to the input modality. The advantage of such process will capture full range of information for the input modality. The Attention Mechanism will assign weights to the feature maps that are generated from each stream which highlights the most relevant features. These features which are weighted will be combined or fused together to form a single unified feature representation that will be passed through final fully connected layers for classification (e.g., disease detection) or segmentation (e.g., tumor boundary identification).

Figure 1. Generalized block diagram of MSA-CNN architecture

Figure 2 shows the workflow of the MSA-CNN model. The input images acquired from multiple modalities (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray) are pre-processed through steps like resizing, normalization, and data augmentation. The pre-processing is done to ensure consistent input. Each modality is then processed through its own modality-specific CNN stream, where features are extracted for further processing. The next step is the Attention Mechanism, which assigns weights to the features from each modality. This focuses on the most important regions of the images. These weighted features are combined in the Feature Fusion Layer and are further passed through the output layer for either classification (e.g., detecting pneumonia) or segmentation (e.g., identifying tumor regions).

The remaining sections are categorized as: Section 2 introduces a brief literature survey, Section 3 highlights the research gaps in medical imaging, Section 4 details the proposed architecture, section 5 outlines results and discussions, followed by conclusion and future scope.

2. LITERATURE SURVEY

2.1 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for Medical Imaging

In the recent past, researchers have observed advancements In the field of medical imaging. The most prominent deep learning technique used is Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).

This section provides a brief overview of various methodologies, architectures, mathematical formulations. Basically, CNN performs a convolution operation and is defined by


$$(f*g)(x) = {\sum\limits_{a}{f(a).g(x - a)}}$$

… (1)

Where

fis the input image, gis the convolution filter or kernel, x is the current position in the image, ais the filter size.

From equation (1), the output is a convolution operation that extracts the features by sliding the filter g across the input imagef, resulting in a feature map. This feature map highlights the prominent patterns viz., edges or textures. In medical imaging certain conditions prevails such as identification of tumors or lesions which can be captured using these prominent patterns. Further, pooling layers in CNN reduce the spatial dimensions of the feature maps and are typically applied after the operation of the convolutional layers. These pooling layers downsample the data and is given in equation (2).


y = max (xi, xi + 1, ..., xi + k)

… (2)

Such a pooling operation selects the maximum value from a group of neighboring pixels thus retaining the most important information. This further help in reducing the computational load. Table 1 shows the comparison of the recent works carried out in the field of medical imaging using CNN.

2.2 U-Net for Medical Image Segmentation

In the recent past U-Net architecture has evolved and has shown better performance for medical image segmentation tasks. This is proposed by Ronneberger et al. (2015) [3]. It uses an encoder-decoder structure, where the encoder extracts features through successive convolution and pooling layers, while the decoder reconstructs the image by up-sampling. The unique feature of U-Net is the skip connections that combine feature maps from the encoder to the corresponding decoder layers. This process ensures that fine-grained details are preserved during reconstruction. The U-Net operations are mathematically defined by equation (3).


$$y^{(l)} = \sigma\left( {\sum\limits_{k}{W_{k}^{(l)}*x_{k}^{(l)} + b^{(l)}}} \right)$$

… (3)

Where xk(l)is the input to the l-th layer, Wk(l)are the convolutional weights, b(l)is the bias term, σ is the activation function (typically ReLU). The next process is the upsampling which is defined by


x(l + 1) = upsample(x(l))

… (4)

This architecture is widely used for the medical imaging tasks due to its ability to learn precise segmentation boundaries and is widely used in brain tumor segmentation, liver segmentation, and cell segmentation using microscopic images. Figure 3 shows the UNet architecture diagram.

Figure 3. Generalised diagram of U-net architecture

This architecture follows symmetric encoder-decoder structure. The former is often called as the contracting path, that captures high-level features from the input image through convolutional and max-pooling operations. This is shown as layer 1 in the figure 3. This process of having convolutional and max-pooling operations at layer 1 reduces the spatial dimensions while also preserving the prominent features that are required for the feature representation. On the other hand, the later, also known as the expanding path, reconstructs the spatial resolution of the input image using upsampling layers which are mentioned at layer 5 and 6 in the figure 3. Such an inclusion of upsampling mechanism ensures accurate localisation of the features which is more essential for the segmentation tasks. The most important property of U-Net is the skip connections that link corresponding layers in the encoder and decoder. These connections allow the network to retain the spatial information that is lost during the downsampling process in the encoder. By combining the feature maps from the encoder with the upsampled features in the decoder, the network effectively combining the low-level spatial details with high-level information, resulting in the improvement in the segmentation accuracy. This architecture completely relies on convolutional layers. This avoids the use of fully connected layers ensuring flexibility with the variable input data sizes. The architecture uses repeated convolutional operations with ReLU activation functions and batch normalisation shown in layer 1 is used to extract and refine features at each layer. This design ensures efficient learning and high quality segmentation.

2.3 DenseNet for Classification in Medical Imaging

DenseNet (Huang et al. 2017) (Zhang et al. 2021) uses dense connections between the layers which is different from the existing CNN architectures wherein each layer received input from only from the previous layers. This is defined by


xl = Hl([x0,x1,...,xl − 1])

… (5)

Where Hlis the composite function of convolution, batch normalization and ReLU. The output of each layer is combined or concatenated with the inputs that are processed from all the previous layers, resulting in a more efficient feature propogation and mitigating the vanishing gradient problem. The dense connections that are established in the network provides better flow of gradients during training that results in faster convergence and higher accuracy. From the literature it is observed that DenseNet has shown superior performance in classification tasks concentrating mainly on medical image classification. Such a classification includes chest X-rays and CT scan datasets.

Figure 4. Architecture of DenseNet.

DenseNet ich is also called as Densely Connected Convolutional Network, is one of the modern deep learning architecture that is designed to improve feature reuse and alleviate the problem of varnishing gradients. This architecture is proposed by Gao Huang in 2017. This architecture uses layer connectivity. Besides, traditional CNNs, each layer receives input from the previous layer and is processed before passing it to the next layer. This architecture establishes direct connections between all layers within a dense block. In other words, each layer receives the feature maps of all the previous layers as input and passes the feature maps to all the subsequent layers. This structure ensures that all the information flow remains robust throughout the network, thus leading to more efficient gradient propagation during the training phase. The dense connectivity in this architecture enables substantial feature reuse. This process reduces the problem of redundancy in the deep networks. The architecture allows each layer to access all the previously computed feature maps making this DenseNet architecture useful for both low- and high-level features. This leads to an effective learning mechanism and better feature extraction. Furthermore, the architecture is highly parameter efficient compared to other deep networks. Instead of learning the redundant features, DenseNet maximises its use of each feature map. This inturn reduces the number of parameters and the computational cost required for training.

DenseNet produces highly differentiating features without requiring over tthe existing complex models. This architecture shown in figure 4 employs batch normalisation, activation functions and convolutional layers to process the feature maps within each layer. The utilisation of combination or the concatenation layer is to combine the feature maps ensuring that each layer has direct access to the gradients from the loss function. This process reduces the likelihood of the vanishing gradients. This makes DenseNet particularly useful for deep learning architectures wherein the traditional architectures often face challenges in terms of training, stability and convergence. It is to be noted that DenseNet has good ability to produce highly discriminative features when compared to other complex models. This architecture employs batch normalisation, activation functions and convolutional layers to process feature maps within each layer. The use of the combine block shown in figure 4 provides direct access to the gradients from the loss function at each layer. This process reduces the likelihood of the vanishing gradients. This property also makes DenseNet particularly suitable for very deep networks, where traditional architectures often face challenges in training, stability and convergence. DenseNet is observed to have better application in computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection and semantic segmentation. Its architecture is flexible and can be adjusted to meet specific application requirements. For illustration purpose some of the lines shown in figure 4 are drawn from image to combine block, which means that it uses transition layers to control the size of the feature maps and further reduce the computational overhead in deeper networks. These layers include operations such as pooling and 1 x 1 convolutions to compress feature maps, maintaining efficiency while preserving critical information.

2.4 Generalization Across Modalities

Generalisation across imaging modalities has remained as an important confront in deep learning applications. This can be dealt in particular in the field of medical imaging. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) trained on data from a specific imaging modality, viz., X-rays, often strive to accomplish analogous performance when applied on or over the other types of modalities like MRI or CT scans. This issue comes or arises due to inherent differences in image resolution, contrast levels, noise patterns, and imaging protocols. Such properties may vary across modalities and institutions and the imaging equipment that the user choose to. Such variations make it difficult for models to learn representations that are robust and transferable across different types of medical images.

2.5 ResNET

ResNet(Residual Network) is basically a deep Convolutional Neural Network(CNN) based design that addresses the problems of training in very deep network. This primarily vanishes the gradient problem. This was introduced in 2015 by Kaiming He . This architecture is built based on the concept of residual learning that allows information to bypass intermediate layers through shortcut connections, finally improving the gradient flow during the backpropagation mechanism. The basic building block of this network is the residual block that consists of few convolutional layers and a shortcut connect. The later adds the input of the block directly to the output after passing through the convolutional layers. This allows the network to learn residual mappings. Instead of learning the full transformation from input to output, the network focuses on learning the difference or residual that simplifies the optimization process. A residual block in general consists of two to three convolutional layers, followed by batch normalization and activation functions which are commonly referred to as ReLU (Rectificatioin Linear Unit). The shortcut connections bypass these layers either may be directly provided the dimensions match or through a 1 x 1 convolutional layer if the dimensions differ as shown in figure 5. This structure is repeated throughout the network, enabling the construction of highly deep architectures viz., ResNet-50, ResNet-101 etc. where the numerals indicate the number of layers.

Figure 5. Architecture of ResNet.

This architecture is structured hierarchically with multiple stages. Each stage contains several residual blocks with reliable feature map sizes, that are separated by down sampling layers. Such a down sampling reduces the spatial resolution while increasing the feature depth. This approach of hierarchical structure ensures that the network captures both low-level and high-level features effectively. With the introduction of bottleneck blocks that are introduced in this architecture reduces the computational costs by compressing the feature maps with a 1 x 1 convolution before performing the main 3 x 3 convolution and then expanding them back using another 1 x 1 convolution. This design enables deeper networks with reduced computational overhead while preserving the accuracy. Hence, this architecture is proved to be versatile, serving as a backbone for numerous advanced models and tasks beyond standard image classification. The architectures ability to train very deep networks while maintaining performance has made this architecture influencing the design of subsequent models like DenseNet and EfficientNet.

The vanishing gradient problem, which frequently impedes the training of very deep neural networks, is addressed by the ResNet (Residual Network) design, which is a ground-breaking architecture in the field of deep learning technology. Initially presented by Kaiming In 2015, he and his team were able to accomplish a key milestone by winning the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC). They did this by achieving a top-5 error rate of 3.57%, which was higher than the performance of humans. The residual block is the most important innovation associated with the architecture. It enables information to flow straight across shortcut links, which in turn makes it possible to train networks that have more than one thousand layers. Because of its scalability, ResNet is suited for a wide range of computer vision tasks, which is one of the most significant advantages of this network. The ResNet-50, ResNet-101, and ResNet-152 variants are among the most widely utilised versions because they provide a balance between the depth of the network and the computational efficiency of the network. Image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation are just some of the tasks that have seen widespread adoption of these networks.

2.6 Attention Mechanisms

Attention Mechanisms allows CNNs to concentrate on the most prominent areas in the images which are having information content so that they can be processed for further analysis. This improves the performance in handling challenging tasks such as tumor detection in noisy images. The attention function is mathematically defined by


$$\alpha_{i} = \frac{\exp(e_{i})}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}{\exp(e_{k})}}$$

… (6)

Where αiis the attention weight of the feature weight hi, υand Ware learnable parameters.

Attention mechanisms enhance or improve the interpretability by concentrating or focusing on the specific regions of the images. This process improves the model performance, particularly in the cases where abnormalities occupy in a smaller region of the image in particular in the cancer detection. Figure 6 shows the architecture of the attention mechanism used in deep learning.

In the field of deep learning, attention mechanisms have emerged as a game-changing breakthrough that offers significant advantages. This can be applied in various tasks that require sequential data processing. The attention mechanisms were initially implemented in the field of machine translation. These mechanisms enable models to distillate on particular segments of input sequences. Hence, this technique has shown improving their capacity to handle long-term dependencies. The potential of attention in Natural Language Processing (NLP) based works or such tasks is observed to be having recent development by the addition of transformer-based designs. Some examples of such designs are the widely used BERT and GPT models. These advancements have allowed the state-of-the-art performance in language production, summarisation, and translation. Attention mechanisms have become more prominent in the field of computer vision. This was the results of the efforts to overcome the limitations of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), where in the drawbacks of the CNNs are exploited. Vision transformers, also known as ViTs, have changed the phase of the image processing mechanism by the virtue of their ability to use self-attention. This is further used to acquire global contextual information. ViTs, in contrast to conventional CNNs, do not require kernels of a fixed size. But, they use the advantage of attention to dynamically alter focus across spatial dimensions. Using this technique, significant advancements has resulted in the fields of classification, object detection, and analysis of the video.

Figure 6. Architecture of attention mechanism

An additional area that has seen major advancements is multi-modal learning. This is one form of learning in which attention mechanisms allow for the integration of several sorts of material. This includes text, visuals, and audio. The purpose of models such as CLIP and DALL-E is to develop linkages between visual and textual representations by combination of the self-attention with cross-modal attention. Applications in content production, labelling of images, and human-computer interaction have been improved. This created a path way to develop new methodologies, which has opened up new paths for study and applications in the real world.

Recent study has also focused on the scalability of attention mechanisms as a specific area of investigation. Self-attention computations that are traditionally used scale quadratically with the size of the input. This presents challenges when dealing with large datasets and high-resolution images. In order to reduce the overhead in computation or to reduce the computational complexity over the side to maintain the performance of the model, various innovations have been proposed. These innovations include sparse attention, linear attention, and hierarchical attention. These developments are absolutely necessary for the successful deployment of attention-based models in scenarios such as the system with limited resources. In addition, attention mechanisms have been used in reinforcement learning, that has made it possible to improve decision-making in scenarios that are computationally complex, complicated and real-world scenarios. The efficiency and effectiveness of learning policies are improved by attention-driven models. Since they make it possible for agents to concentrate on the most pertinent aspects of their state spaces. In fields such as robotics, autonomous systems, and gaming, it is quite important to have a solid grasp of dynamic surroundings. These methodologies have demonstrated their potential in such applications where there are dynamic changes in the scenarios. A further inquiry has been driven by concerns over the ethical implications and interpretability of these models. Despite the fact that attention offers insights into the decision-making process of models, new research has called into question whether or not attention accurately reflects causality. Methods are being investigated by researchers in order to improve the interpretability of attention weights so that the model should be fair enough in particular for the applications that have a significant impact on society. The establishment of trust and accountability in artificial intelligence systems is dependent upon these initiatives.

The field of medical imaging has been completely transformed by the introduction of Convolutional Neural Networks, which provide state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks including segmentation, classification, and detection. Recent developments, such as U-Net for segmentation, DenseNet for classification, and attention methods, have significantly increased the accuracy and robustness of the system. However, there are still obstacles to overcome in terms of the availability of data, generalisation across different modalities, and the costs of computation. In the future, research should concentrate on establishing models that are capable of efficiently generalising across a variety of imaging modalities and increasing the interpretability of those models.

3. RESEARCH GAPS IN MEDICAL IMAGING

Based on the literature survey, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and its derivative techniques or models have shown noteworthy improvements when applied over medical imaging applications. These applications vary from classification to detection. This can also be used for segmentation. However, several challenges and limitations continue and it is the need of the hour to address these challenges to use the complete potential of CNNs in the medical field. Such challenges arise from factors such as data availability, model interpretability, generalizability across different datasets, computational costs, and the complexity of real-world medical applications. This section elaborates the key problems and research gaps in CNN-based medical imaging.

3.1 Data Scarcity and Annotation Challenges

Data scarcity is one of the prominent challenge that every researcher face. This offers a significant challenge in using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for medical image analysis. Unlike other domains, finding large and diverse datasets in the medical field is often not suggestable and is also hindered by strict regulations and privacy concerns. Ethical approval and patient consent requirements are required to collect the data. This limits the speed in which the process is carried out. This also further limits the availability of publicly accessible medical datasets. Additionally, rare diseases or conditions prone to be another level of difficulty, as their infrequent occurrence poses a challenge. This means that datasets for such cases are inherently small and lack diversity. This scarcity can negatively impact the generalisability of CNN models. This further leads to overfitting and reduced performance on unseen data.

Annotation challenges increase the difficulties in medical image analysis. Labelling such medical images typically require an expert who have got trained or any person who have expertised in the field of radiation therapy. Such task seems to be time-consuming and costly, but quite necessary as annotations and labelling offer some groundtruth to the existing data. Moreover, even among experts, there may be variability in annotations. This occurs due to the differences in interpretation, especially for complex or ambiguous cases. High inter-observer variability can introduce noise into the training data. This affects the reliability of CNN models. Additionally, creating annotations at a granular level, such as segmenting tumours or other abnormalities, demands significant effort, further increasing the burden on annotators. These challenges underscore the importance of developing innovative solutions to address both data scarcity and annotation limitations in medical image analysis.

3.2 Lack of Large Annotated Medical Datasets

One of the most significant barriers to the successful deployment of CNNs in medical imaging is the limited availability of large, annotated datasets. Medical data is often scarce, particularly in fields such as radiology, where images must be annotated by expert clinicians. Manual annotation is time-consuming and expensive, requiring highly specialized knowledge. For example, in tumor segmentation tasks, precise delineation of tumor boundaries requires clinical expertise, which makes it difficult to scale the creation of large training datasets.

Many CNN architectures, such as U-Net and DenseNet, require vast amounts of labeled data to avoid overfitting and to generalize well across different datasets. In contrast to natural image datasets such as ImageNet, which contains millions of labeled images, medical datasets are typically much smaller. For instance, the BRATS (Brain Tumor Segmentation) dataset used by Shen et al. (2017) for 3D CNN training contains only a few hundred examples, which poses significant limitations for training deep networks effectively.

3.3 Imbalanced Datasets

The current research mainly concentrates on the medical image analysis. In this juncture, medical datasets often have a challenge on the class imabalance on the data that they get or acquired via an agent. This is very particulary observed in the condition of rare diseases that are underrepresented when compared to others. For example, in the case of chest X-ray datasets, pneumonia images are represented by a much smaller portion of the datasets when compared to healthy images. It can also be noted that Wang et al. (2018), trained CNN models on such datasets that are poorly or underrepresented classes, which may lead to biased predictions. This is very essential in the healthcare sector where it is quite important to detect rare but seriously effecting conditions as well.

3.4 Limited Publicly Available Multi-Modal Data

Medical imaging often involves multiple modalities (e.g., CT, MRI, Ultrasound). These modalities provide unique insights into the analysis of medical images as these serve to be the labels for the particular ailments. However, due to the constrains in the medial filed the use of the scarcity of publicly available multi-modal medical datasets have become increasingly more and thus making it difficult to train models that are developed in the recent past for analysis. These models concentrate on the fusing the data from different modalities, thus creating a novel architecture for the immediate prediction of the disease. Due to the lack of the publicly available datasets the development of robust models have become limited and poste a challenge.

3.5 Model Interpretability and Trustworthiness

CNNs, while powerful, are often referred to as black-box models because their decision-making process is not easily interpretable by humans. In medical imaging, where the stakes are high, this lack of transparency presents a significant barrier to clinical adoption. Clinicians need to trust and understand the predictions made by AI models to use them in critical decision-making processes.

For instance, Esteva et al. (2017) developed a CNN that achieved dermatologist-level accuracy in classifying skin cancer but did not explain how or why certain decisions were made . In the clinical environment, this lack of interpretability can be problematic, as doctors are often required to justify diagnoses to patients and other healthcare providers.

While attention mechanisms and techniques such as Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) have been introduced to provide visual explanations for CNN predictions, these approaches are still far from providing full interpretability. Most of these methods highlight which areas of an image the CNN focuses on but do not offer insights into the higher-order reasoning behind the decision.

3.3. Generalization Across Different Medical Datasets and Modalities

One of the key issues identified in the literature is the lack of generalization of CNNs across different medical datasets and imaging modalities. CNNs trained on specific datasets often perform well within those datasets but struggle when applied to images from different sources, institutions, or imaging devices.

For example, Lakhani and Sundaram (2017) demonstrated that their CNN model achieved high accuracy in detecting pneumonia from chest X-rays on the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, but the model's performance degraded significantly when tested on data from different hospitals . This highlights the challenges posed by variations in imaging protocols, equipment, and patient demographics. For CNNs to be clinically useful, they must generalize across diverse populations and imaging environments, which is currently a major limitation.

Based on these research gaps, now let us define the problem definition and the solution approach. In the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Deep Learning (DL) there is a remarkable progress that can solve the complex real world problems. As the in crease in the technological advancements persists, many tasks still require handling diverse and multi-modal data streams, that challenge the traditional CNNs and other benchmark techniques. Hence, in this context Multi Stream Attention Based CNN (MSA-CNN) has emerged and is observed to address the shortcomings by combining the strengths of multi-stream processing and attention mechanisms. This section elaborates the core challenges and limitations in current approaches and defines the specific problem that MSA-CNN seeks to solve.

One of the most prominent and significant challenges in the modern machine learning is the effective integration of multi-stream data, that refer to the datasets that contain diverse modalities or various types of images having diversified features. For example, in tasks such as video classification, a system must process both spatial information and temporal information that is from the sequence of frames. Similarly, in multi-modal learning, data might be acquired from different sensors and will be of different types. These vary from images, text, audio etc., each carrying complementary but distinct information. Handling this diversified data is challenging as each modality or the feature type has its own unique characteristics requiring a special preprocessing technique and further analysis algorithms that provide better accuracy by the handling such data.

The existing benchmark techniques excel in extracting the spatial features from the images but they lack the flexibility to accommodate the heterogeneous input data streams. They process the data through a single pipeline, that results in the loss of valuable information when multiple modalities are involved. Without a defined approach, the model might treat all the input features that are extracted to be uniform, resulting in a suboptimal learning and reduced accuracy. Therefore, a critical aspect of this problem is developing an architecture capable of parallel processing, where each stream focusses on a specific type of data, ensuring that the unique attributes of each modality are preserved.

Another challenge at the central or global level is the differentiation or differing or distinguishing learning of the relevant features from the noisy or irrelevant data that is acquired. As the complexity of the input data increases, model face difficulties in prioritizing the most important elements for a given task. It is also a known fact that as the dataset size increases classification error also increases. For example, in the case of object detection with noisy or cluttered images, many regions in the input may not contribute meaningfully to the detection task. Similarly, in multi-modal data scenarios, all the modalities may not hold equal relevance for the output. In this context, attention mechanisms have proven to be a powerful tool for addressing these challenges which is used in the proposed technique. By dynamically assigning weights to features that are extracted or to the segmented regions of the input attention mechanism allows models to focus on the most critical regions or features while suppressing irrelevant ones. Still another problem exists. Incorporating attention mechanisms within a mult-stream framework introduces additional complexities. These mechanisms must operate across streams and within individual streams that requires careful design to ensure that the attention system aligns with the overall objectives of the network. Furthermore, the added computational overhead or computational complexity due to this combination of attention mechanisms can hinder their practicality in resource-constrained environments like mobile devices or embedded systems. Hence, the problem comprises of creating an attention framework that is both effective in focusing on relevant features and by the side efficient in computation. Besides feature selection, a critical challenge in multi-stream learning is the acquisition of contextual dependencies. Various tasks, including as video analysis, speech recognition, and sentiment analysis, require an understanding of the relationships among data points inside a single stream and across multiple streams. In video analysis, understanding the sequence of actions requires modelling temporal relationships, whereas in a multi-modal context, the alignment between text and images is crucial for tasks such as caption generation. Traditional CNNs are inherently limited in their capacity to capture such correlations since they primarily perform local operations that focus on restricted portions of the input. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers alleviate certain limitations by modelling temporal and sequential links, incorporating these capabilities into a multi-stream architecture is intricate. The objective is to create a model that can concurrently handle multi-stream data, capture long-range dependencies inside each stream, and align inter-stream relationships. This complexity underscores the need for a new approach that combines the benefits of CNNs, attention mechanisms, and advanced sequence modelling techniques. A vital aspect of the matter is aligning model efficacy with computational efficiency. Multi-stream architectures inherently increase computing complexity due to the integration of many processing pipelines. The integration of attention processes intensifies this complexity by introducing additional layers for the computation and utilisation of attention weights. Despite the availability of significant computational resources in research settings, many practical applications, including as autonomous vehicles, real-time video processing, and wearable technology, require models that operate within strict resource constraints. The objective is to optimise the MSA-CNN architecture to achieve a balance between accuracy and efficiency. This includes the design of lightweight attention mechanisms, the reduction of redundancy in multi-stream processing, and the implementation of techniques such as model pruning or quantisation. Ensuring scalability is essential, as the model must adapt to varying levels of input complexity without requiring substantial modifications. Despite significant progress in neural network architecture, considerable shortcomings remain in addressing the intricacies of multi-stream and attention-based learning. Traditional multi-stream models often demonstrate inadequate techniques for integrating information across streams. They independently process each stream and include their outputs in later stages, which may result in the loss of critical inter-stream dependencies. Similarly, several attention-based models are designed for single-stream data, and their adaptation to multi-stream situations requires additional advancements. An additional limitation is the generalisability of existing models. Many techniques are tailored for certain purposes or datasets, making them less effective when applied to new or diverse problems. A paradigm designed for image-text integration may exhibit suboptimal performance in a video-audio situation without significant re-engineering. This rigidity highlights the need for a flexible framework capable of handling various tasks and data types.

By addressing the limitations of the traditional CNNs and the influence of the strengths of multi stream and attentiona based learning, the MS-CNN, the proposed technique or framework provides a robust solution for the complex, multi-odal data processing tasks. It is particularly well-suited for applications such as video analysis, multi-modal sentiment detection and sensor data fusion where handling of diversified data is crucial and critical for success.

4. MULTI-STREAM ATTENTION-BASED CNN (MSA-CNN)

This section outlines the proposed novel architecture Multi-Stream Attention-Based CNN (MSA-CNN), that is designed and developed to address the key issues identified in the previous sections. This architecture integrates multi-modal medical image processing (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray) using separate convolutional streams. This is followed by an attention mechanism to combine the most relevant features from each modality. The proposed technique is designed to Improve generalization across diversified datasets and medical imaging modalities, address the issue of noisy or low-quality images by incorporating a noise-aware loss function, enhance interpretability through an attention mechanism that identifies the most important image regions which are contributing to the model’s predictions, mitigate the need for large annotated datasets through transfer learning and attention mechanisms.

The Multi-Stream Attention-Based CNN (MSA-CNN) signifies a important development in the field of deep learning. This addresses the challenges related to the effective processing of multi-modal and multi-stream data. Unlike the Traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) which are observed to be highly effective in extracting spatial features have often fall short in handling heterogeneous data. Such data comes from multiple modalities or feature types, such as images, audio, text, or temporal data. These limitations arise because conventional CNNs process data through a single pipeline. This leads to a loss of unique characteristics and dependencies that exist within and between different streams of data. MSA-CNN addresses these shortcomings by introducing a multi-stream architecture integrated with attention mechanisms. This allows the model to dynamically focus on the most relevant features for the task at hand.

An essential innovation of MSA-CNN lies in its multi-stream design. This design uses multiple data streams and will be processed in parallel. Each stream is customised to handle a specific type of input. These inputs may be of spatial features from images or temporal sequences from videos. For example, in video processing, one stream might focus on extracting spatial details from individual frames while the other another captures temporal dynamics between successive frames. This ensures that the unique characteristics of each modality are preserve and also and processed independently, hence preventing interference or loss of information that might occur in single-stream architectures. As each stream autonomously processes, MSA-CNN enhances the model’s ability to extract meaningful patterns and features from diverse inputs.

Besides feature selection, a critical issue in the proposed technique is the acquisition of contextual dependencies. Various tasks, including as video analysis, speech recognition, and sentiment analysis, require an understanding of the relationships between the input data or among data points inside a single stream and across multiple streams. In video analysis, understanding the sequence of actions requires modelling temporal relationships. This is different in multi-modal context where the alignment between text and images is crucial for tasks like caption generation. Traditional CNNs are inherently have limited capacity as their capturing ability such as linkages because of their mostly local operations that focus on restricted portions of the input.

While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers alleviate certain limitations by modelling temporal and sequential links, incorporating these capabilities into a multi-stream architecture is intricate. The aim is to develop a model capable of simultaneously processing multi-stream data, capturing long-range dependencies within each stream, and aligning inter-stream relationships. This complexity underscores the need for a new approach that combines the benefits of CNNs, attention mechanisms, and advanced sequence modelling techniques. A vital aspect of the matter is aligning model efficacy with computational efficiency. Multi-stream designs inherently increase computing complexity due to the engagement of many processing pipelines. The integration of attention processes intensifies this complexity by introducing additional layers for the calculation and utilisation of attention weights. Despite the availability of significant computational resources in research settings, certain practical applications, such as autonomous vehicles, real-time video processing, and wearable technology, require models that operate within strict resource constraints. The objective is to optimise the MSA-CNN architecture to achieve a balance between accuracy and efficiency. This includes the development of lightweight attention methods, the reduction of redundancy in multi-stream processing, and the implementation of techniques like model pruning or quantisation. Ensuring scalability is essential, as the model must adapt to varying levels of input complexity without requiring substantial modifications. Despite significant progress in neural network architecture, considerable shortcomings remain in addressing the intricacies of multi-stream and attention-based learning. Traditional multi-stream models often demonstrate inadequate techniques for integrating information across streams. They independently process each stream and include their outputs in later stages, which may result in the loss of critical inter-stream dependencies. Similarly, several attention-based models are designed for single-stream data, and their adaptation to multi-stream situations requires additional advancements. An additional limitation is the generalisability of existing models. Many techniques are tailored for certain purposes or datasets, making them less effective when applied to new or diverse problems. A paradigm designed for image-text integration may exhibit suboptimal performance in a video-audio situation without significant re-engineering. This rigidity highlights the need for a flexible framework capable of handling various tasks and data types. Figure 7 shows the block diagram of the proposed MSA-CNN.

Figure 7. Block diagram of the proposed technique.

The proposed technique consists of multistream input scuh as MRI, CT and X-ray that often provide complimentary information. For examples, stream 1 processes high resolution images like MRI and stream 2 processes low resolution or noise images like X-rays. Then these are processed using CNN which are called here as Multi-Stream Convolutional layers. These layers extract modality specific features by processing inputs from different imaging modalities. These are further processed using attention mechanism. This attention mechanism dynamically assigns weights to the feature maps produced by each stream, highlighting the most relevant parts of the image.

Let X1, X2, ..., Xnrepresent the input images from different modalities. Each input image Xiis passed through a separate CNN stream CNNi, which consists of convolutional layers, activation functions, like ReLU and pooling layers to extract modality specific feature maps and is defined by


Fi = CNNi(Xi)

… (7)

These feature maps Fiare learned through the convolution operation, which is mathematically expressed as


$$F_{i}^{(l)} = \sigma\left( {\sum\limits_{j}{W_{i,j}^{(l)}*X_{j}^{(l)} + b^{(l)}}} \right)$$

… (8)

Where

Fi(l)is the feature map at layer l

Wi, j(l)represents the filter weights for feature map i

Xj(l)is the input from the previous layer

b(l)is the bias term and σis the activation function.

Each modality's feature map contains the most important information from the input image, ready for the fusion through the attention mechanism.

After the attention mechanism has assigned importance to each stream, the weighted feature maps are combined and passed to fully connected layers for classification or segmentation. The attention mechanism calculates the importance of each feature map Fiby generating an attention weight αi for each modality stream. This weight is computed using a softmax function and is given by


$$\alpha_{i} = \frac{\exp(W_{i}^{T}F_{i})}{\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}{\exp(W_{i}^{T}F_{i})}}$$

… (9)

Where Wi are learnable parameters that determine the contribution of feature map Fito the final decision. The feature maps are weighted and combined as


$$F_{final} = {\sum\limits_{k = 1}^{n}\alpha_{i}}F_{i}$$

… (10)

The fused feature map Ffinalis then passed through a fully connected layer for classification or segmentation. For classification, a softmax layer is applied to predict the class probabilities given by


P = softmax (WfcFfinal + bfc)

… (11)

Where Wfcand bfcare the wights and biases of the fully connected layer respectively and P represents the probability distribution over the possible classes. The next process is the component that adds a penalty to the loss function based on the noise levels in the input images, improving the robustness to noisy ad low resolution medical images. To handle noisy and low quality medical images, a noise aware loss function is introduced here. Traditional CNNs often struggle with noise in medical images, thus leading to poor generalization. The proposed loss function adds a noise penalty term N(Xi). This estimates the likelihood that the input image Xicontains noise. The modified loss function is


$$L = - {\sum\limits_{i}{y_{i}\log(P_{i}) + \lambda N(X_{i})}}$$

… (12)

Where yi is the true label for the input i, Pi is the predicted probability for the class i, N(Xi) is a function that estimates the noise level in image Xi, λis a hyperparameter that controls the importance of noise penalty. This loss function penalises misclassifications more heavily when they occur on noisy images encouraging the model to become more robust to variations in image quality. Table 2 shows the algorithm for the proposed technique.

Table 2. Algorithm for the proposed technique

Algorithm for MSA-CNN

Input: Multi-modal medical images (e.g., MRI, CT, X-ray)
Output: Predicted class or segmentation map

1. Initialize CNN parameters for each modality-specific stream (Stream 1 for MRI, Stream 2 for CT, etc.)
2. For each modality i in {1, 2, ..., n}:
a. Extract feature map F_i from CNN_i for input X_i:
F_i = CNN_i(X_i)
b. Store feature maps {F_1, F_2, ..., F_n}

3. Apply attention mechanism to compute attention weights {α_1, α_2, ..., α_n}:
For each feature map F_i:
α_i = softmax(W_i^T F_i)

4. Compute the final fused feature map F_final:
F_final = Σ(α_i * F_i) for i in {1, 2, ..., n}

5. Pass F_final through fully connected layers for classification:
P = softmax(W_fc * F_final + b_fc)

6. Compute noise-aware loss:
L = CrossEntropyLoss(P, y) + λ * NoisePenalty(X)

7. Update CNN weights using backpropagation and gradient descent.

8. Output predicted class or segmentation map.

6. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

The results obtained from the implementation of the Multi-Stream Attention-Based CNN (MSA-CNN) over the diversified datasets demonstrate its robustness and effectiveness. This also address the key challenges in medical image classification and segmentation. On the Chest X-ray Pneumonia dataset, the proposed model achieved 95.7% accuracy, outperforming the existing benchmark techniques. This can be attributed to the model's architecture that allows simultaneous processing of different aspects of the image. This also ensures that the most relevant features were highlighted. The attention mechanism played a crucial role which focusses on the prominent areas of the X-rays, leading to improved detection particularly in noisy and low-resolution images. The increased sensitivity of 94.1% demonstrates the model’s ability to correctly identify a higher proportion of pneumonia cases, minimizing the risk of false negatives. Results on the BRATS Brain Tumor MRI dataset underline the efficacy of the proposed model with an accuracy of 93.4% and 91.5% Dice score for tumor segmentation outperforming other benchmark techniques. Moreover, the specificity of 94.9% highlights the model's reliability in correctly identifying healthy tissue, reducing the risk of false positives, which could lead to unnecessary treatments or interventions. For the COVID-19 CT dataset, the proposed model showed a similar trend and achieved an accuracy of 94.6% and 92.9% sensitivity. The model was particularly effective in identifying COVID-19 positive cases from lung CT scans, even in cases where the scans were noisy or of lower quality. Hence, the proposed technique MSA-CNN not only advances the state-of-the-art in medical image analysis but also addresses some of the fundamental challenges associated with noisy data, lack of interpretability, and generalization across different imaging modalities. The results clearly demonstrate the model’s potential for integration into clinical workflows, where its high accuracy, combined with its robustness to noise and interpretability, can assist healthcare professionals in making faster, more accurate diagnoses and treatment decisions.
