Despite these advances, challenges remain in ensuring the reliability, interpretability, and experimental validation of AI-generated molecules. Concerns about the potential for these models to generate toxic or controlled substances have led to discussions about ethical guidelines and regulatory frameworks for their use (Urbina et al., 2021). As the field progresses, the integration of generative models with experimental validation pipelines, including rapid synthesis and testing methodologies, will be crucial to realizing their full potential in accelerating drug discovery and materials development. The ongoing refinement of these models, coupled with increasing computational power and expanding chemical databases, promises to revolutionize the way we explore chemical space and discover new therapeutic agents and functional materials.

Integration of Multi-Omics Data For More Comprehensive Drug Response Prediction

The integration of multi-omics data for more comprehensive drug response prediction represents a significant advancement in personalized medicine and pharmacogenomics, offering a holistic approach to understanding the complex biological mechanisms underlying drug efficacy and toxicity. This approach combines diverse molecular data types, including genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and epigenomics, to create a more complete picture of cellular processes and their interactions with pharmaceutical compounds (Hasin et al., 2017). Machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques have been pivotal in handling the high-dimensional, heterogeneous nature of multi-omics datasets, enabling the discovery of intricate patterns and relationships that are not apparent when analyzing single omics layers in isolation (Chaudhary et al., 2018, Shakil et al.,2024). Network-based methods have proven particularly effective in integrating multi-omics data, capturing the complex interactions between different molecular entities and providing insights into the systemic effects of drugs (Yan et al., 2018). Deep learning architectures, such as multi-modal deep neural networks and autoencoders, have demonstrated superior performance in integrating diverse data types and predicting drug responses across various cancer types and other diseases (Sharifi-Noghabi et al., 2019). The incorporation of single-cell multi-omics data has further refined drug response predictions, accounting for intratumoral heterogeneity and enabling more precise targeting of specific cell populations (Pratapa et al., 2021). Pathway-based approaches to multi-omics integration have provided mechanistic insights into drug action and resistance, facilitating the identification of novel drug targets and combination therapies (Huang et al., 2019). The integration of pharmacological data with patient-derived multi-omics profiles has enhanced the ability to predict individual drug responses, supporting the development of personalized treatment regimens in oncology and other therapeutic areas (Paré et al., 2018). Moreover, the inclusion of microbiome data in multi-omics integration has shed light on the role of host-microbiome interactions in drug metabolism and efficacy, opening new avenues for improving drug response predictions (Wilmanski et al., 2019). Time-series multi-omics data have enabled the study of dynamic drug responses, providing insights into the temporal aspects of drug action and resistance development (Banaei-Esfahani et al., 2020). The integration of imaging data with molecular multi-omics has further enhanced drug response predictions by incorporating spatial information and tissue-specific effects (Perlasca et al., 2019). Despite these advancements, challenges remain in harmonizing diverse data types, managing batch effects, and developing robust statistical methods for high-dimensional data integration (Rappoport & Shamir, 2018). Efforts to standardize multi-omics data collection and analysis protocols are ongoing, aiming to improve reproducibility and facilitate cross-study comparisons (Suhl et al., 2019). As the field progresses, the integration of multi-omics data with electronic health records and real-world evidence is expected to bridge the gap between molecular-level predictions and clinical outcomes, further refining drug response models (Karczewski & Snyder, 2018). The ethical implications of using comprehensive molecular profiles for drug response prediction, including issues of data privacy and potential discrimination, are also being actively discussed (Townend, 2018). Looking forward, the continued development of advanced computational methods, including quantum computing approaches, promises to further enhance our ability to integrate and interpret complex multi-omics datasets, ultimately leading to more accurate and personalized drug response predictions that could significantly improve patient outcomes and revolutionize drug development processes.

While AI Shows Great Promise In Medicine, Several Challenges And Ethical Considerations Must Be Addressed:

While artificial intelligence (AI) shows great promise in medicine, several challenges and ethical considerations must be addressed to ensure its responsible and effective implementation. Data privacy and security concerns are paramount, as AI systems require vast amounts of sensitive patient data for training and operation. The risk of data breaches, unauthorized access, and potential misuse of personal health information pose significant threats to patient confidentiality and trust in healthcare systems (Cohen et al., 2018). Robust data protection measures, including encryption, anonymization, and secure data storage protocols, are essential to mitigate these risks. Additionally, the development of privacy-preserving AI techniques, such as federated learning and differential privacy, offers promising solutions for maintaining data confidentiality while enabling collaborative AI model development across multiple institutions (Rieke et al., 2020). Algorithmic bias and fairness in AI models represent another critical challenge, as biased datasets or algorithms can perpetuate or exacerbate existing health disparities. AI models trained on non-representative data may perform poorly for underrepresented populations, potentially leading to misdiagnoses or inappropriate treatment recommendations (Gianfrancesco et al., 2018). Efforts to address this issue include developing diverse and inclusive datasets, implementing fairness-aware machine learning algorithms, and conducting rigorous bias audits of AI systems before deployment (Rajkomar et al., 2018). Regulatory challenges in approving AI-based medical devices pose significant hurdles to the widespread adoption of AI in healthcare. The rapid pace of AI development often outstrips the ability of regulatory bodies to establish appropriate guidelines and approval processes. The FDA's efforts to create a regulatory framework for AI/ML-based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) represent a step towards addressing this challenge, but ongoing collaboration between regulators, industry stakeholders, and healthcare providers is necessary to ensure that AI technologies are safe, effective, and continuously monitored post-market (Gerke et al., 2020). The integration of AI systems with existing healthcare workflows presents both technical and cultural challenges. Healthcare organizations must invest in infrastructure upgrades, data interoperability solutions, and staff training to effectively incorporate AI tools into clinical practice. Resistance to change among healthcare professionals and concerns about AI replacing human judgment must be addressed through education, clear communication of AI's role as a supportive tool, and the development of human-AI collaboration frameworks (Topol, 2019). Liability and responsibility in AI-assisted medical decisions raise complex legal and ethical questions. As AI systems become more involved in diagnosis and treatment recommendations, determining accountability in cases of medical errors or adverse outcomes becomes increasingly complicated. Clear guidelines for the appropriate use of AI in clinical decision-making, ongoing monitoring of AI system performance, and the development of legal frameworks that address the unique challenges posed by AI in healthcare are necessary to navigate this evolving landscape (Price et al., 2019). Ensuring transparency and explainability of AI models in healthcare is crucial for building trust among patients, healthcare providers, and regulatory bodies. The “black box” nature of many advanced AI algorithms, particularly deep learning models, can make it difficult to understand how decisions are made, potentially leading to skepticism and reluctance to adopt AI technologies. Developing interpretable AI models, implementing techniques for post-hoc explanations of AI decisions, and establishing standards for AI transparency in healthcare are essential steps in addressing this challenge (Holzinger et al., 2019). The potential for AI to exacerbate health inequities must also be carefully considered and mitigated. AI systems that rely on data from predominantly affluent or urban populations may not generalize well to underserved communities, potentially widening existing health disparities. Efforts to collect diverse, representative data and to develop AI models that explicitly account for social determinants of health are crucial for ensuring equitable access to the benefits of AI in medicine (Obermeyer et al., 2019). The ethical implications of AI in healthcare extend beyond technical considerations to fundamental questions about the nature of the patient-provider relationship and the role of human judgment in medicine. As AI systems become more sophisticated, there is a risk of over-reliance on automated recommendations, potentially eroding the human elements of care and empathy that are central to the practice of medicine. Developing frameworks for the ethical use of AI that prioritize human values, patient autonomy, and shared decision-making is essential for maintaining the integrity of healthcare practice (Char et al., 2018). The rapid pace of AI development in healthcare also raises concerns about the potential for premature adoption of unproven technologies. The pressure to implement cutting-edge AI solutions must be balanced against the need for rigorous validation and evidence of clinical benefit. Establishing standards for the evaluation of AI technologies in healthcare, including requirements for prospective clinical trials and real-world performance monitoring, is crucial for ensuring that AI truly improves patient outcomes (Liu et al., 2019). The global nature of AI development in healthcare presents challenges related to data sharing, cross-border collaborations, and the harmonization of regulatory approaches. Differences in data protection laws, ethical standards, and healthcare systems across countries can hinder the development and deployment of AI solutions on a global scale. International cooperation and the development of global governance frameworks for AI in healthcare are necessary to address these challenges and ensure that the benefits of AI are equitably distributed worldwide (Cath et al., 2018). As AI continues to evolve and permeate various aspects of healthcare, ongoing ethical deliberation and public engagement are essential. The societal implications of AI in medicine extend beyond technical and regulatory considerations to fundamental questions about the future of healthcare, the nature of medical expertise, and the values we prioritize in our health systems. Fostering interdisciplinary dialogue among AI researchers, healthcare professionals, ethicists, policymakers, and patient advocates is crucial for navigating the complex landscape of AI in medicine and ensuring that its development aligns with societal values and priorities (Vayena et al., 2018). Addressing these challenges and ethical considerations will require sustained effort, collaboration, and innovation from all stakeholders in the healthcare ecosystem. By proactively engaging with these issues, we can harness the transformative potential of AI in medicine while safeguarding patient rights, promoting equity, and maintaining the human-centric nature of healthcare.

5. FUTURE OUTLOOK

The future of AI in medicine is poised for transformative growth, with increased integration across the entire healthcare ecosystem expected to revolutionize patient care, research, and health system management. This integration will likely extend beyond clinical applications to encompass areas such as supply chain management, resource allocation, and public health surveillance, creating a more interconnected and efficient healthcare landscape (Topol, 2019). As AI systems become more deeply embedded in healthcare processes, we can anticipate the emergence of “learning health systems” that continuously improve based on real-world data and outcomes, enabling more agile and responsive healthcare delivery (Rajkomar et al., 2019). The development of more sophisticated, multi-modal AI models represents another key trend, with future systems capable of integrating diverse data types such as genomics, imaging, electronic health records, and wearable device data to provide more comprehensive and nuanced insights (Xu et al., 2020). These advanced models will likely leverage techniques such as transfer learning and multi-task learning to improve performance across a wide range of medical tasks, potentially leading to more generalizable and robust AI systems in healthcare (He et al., 2019). The integration of natural language processing with computer vision and other AI modalities may enable more human-like interactions between AI systems and healthcare providers, facilitating smoother adoption and more intuitive use of AI tools in clinical settings (Esteva et al., 2021). As AI becomes more pervasive in healthcare decision-making, there will be a greater emphasis on explainable and trustworthy AI. The development of interpretable AI models and advanced techniques for post-hoc explanations will be crucial for building trust among patients, healthcare providers, and regulatory bodies (Holzinger et al., 2019). This focus on explainability will likely extend beyond technical solutions to encompass new frameworks for AI governance in healthcare, including standards for model transparency, auditability, and continuous monitoring of AI system performance (Amann et al., 2020). The concept of “algorithmic stewardship” may emerge as a key principle in healthcare organizations, with dedicated teams responsible for overseeing the ethical and responsible use of AI across various clinical and operational contexts (Char et al., 2018). The expansion of AI applications in personalized and precision medicine is expected to accelerate, driven by advances in genomics, proteomics, and other -omics technologies. AI-powered systems will likely play an increasingly important role in interpreting complex molecular data, identifying novel biomarkers, and predicting individual patient responses to treatments (Würstle et al., 2021). This may lead to more tailored therapeutic approaches, optimized drug dosing regimens, and early detection of diseases based on subtle molecular signatures (Schork, 2019). The integration of AI with emerging technologies such as CRISPR gene editing and synthetic biology could open new frontiers in personalized medicine, potentially enabling the design of bespoke cellular therapies and targeted genetic interventions (Fellmann et al., 2017). As AI continues to demonstrate its potential in drug discovery and development, we can expect to see increased adoption of AI-driven approaches throughout the pharmaceutical R&D pipeline, from target identification to clinical trial design and post-market surveillance (Vamathevan et al., 2019). The continued evolution of regulatory frameworks to keep pace with AI advancements will be crucial for ensuring the safe and effective deployment of AI in healthcare. Regulatory bodies such as the FDA are likely to develop more sophisticated approaches to evaluating AI/ML-based medical devices, potentially including real-time monitoring of AI performance and frameworks for regulating continuously learning systems (Babic et al., 2019). International collaboration on AI governance in healthcare may increase, aimed at harmonizing regulatory approaches and facilitating global development and deployment of AI technologies (Cath et al., 2018). The concept of “regulatory sandboxes” for AI in healthcare may gain traction, allowing for controlled testing of innovative AI applications in real-world settings while managing risks and gathering evidence on their impact (Ginsberg et al., 2021). The future of AI in medicine will likely see a greater focus on addressing health disparities and ensuring equitable access to AI-driven healthcare innovations. This may involve the development of AI models specifically designed to account for diverse populations and social determinants of health, as well as initiatives to improve data representation and reduce algorithmic bias (Obermeyer et al., 2019). The potential for AI to extend high-quality healthcare to underserved areas through telemedicine and mobile health applications may help bridge gaps in healthcare access, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (Wahl et al., 2018). As AI systems become more advanced, the nature of medical education and clinical practice is likely to evolve. Future healthcare professionals may need to develop new skills in data science, AI interpretation, and human-AI collaboration to effectively leverage these technologies in patient care (Kolachalama& Garg, 2018). The role of healthcare providers may shift towards more complex decision-making, emotional support, and oversight of AI systems, potentially leading to new specialties focused on the intersection of medicine and AI (Topol, 2019). The integration of AI in medical education, including AI-powered simulation and training tools, may enhance the learning experience and better prepare future healthcare professionals for a technology-driven healthcare landscape (Chan &Zary, 2019). The future of AI in medicine is also likely to see increased convergence with other emerging technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT), 5G networks, and quantum computing. This convergence may enable real-time, continuous health monitoring and interventions, more sophisticated predictive modeling of disease outbreaks, and the ability to process and analyze vastly larger and more complex datasets (Deo, 2015). The development of edge computing and AI-enabled medical devices may allow for more distributed and responsive healthcare delivery, reducing latency and improving the ability to provide care in remote or resource-limited settings (Azam et al., 2022). As these technologies mature, we may see the emergence of highly integrated, AI-driven health ecosystems that seamlessly connect various aspects of individual and population health management. While the potential benefits of AI in medicine are immense, the future will also bring new ethical challenges and societal implications that will require ongoing dialogue and careful consideration. Issues such as AI's impact on human autonomy in healthcare decisions, the potential for AI to exacerbate or create new forms of healthcare inequities, and the long-term effects of AI on the healthcare workforce will need to be addressed (Vayena et al., 2018). As AI becomes more deeply integrated into healthcare systems, ensuring the resilience and security of these systems against potential cyber threats or AI failures will be paramount (Rigby, 2019). The future of AI in medicine holds great promise for improving patient outcomes, increasing healthcare efficiency, and advancing medical knowledge. However, realizing this potential will require sustained collaboration among stakeholders, ongoing innovation in technology and governance, and a commitment to ethical and equitable deployment of AI in healthcare.

6. CONCLUSION

AI is set to revolutionize medical practice by enabling more accurate diagnoses, personalized treatments, and improved patient outcomes. From early disease detection to drug discovery, AI holds the potential to transform every aspect of healthcare. However, this power comes with significant challenges. Safeguarding patient data, addressing algorithmic bias, and ensuring fairness are critical concerns that need careful management. Building trust through explainable AI models and transparent decision-making processes will be key to integrating AI into healthcare effectively. As AI systems advance, the balance between human judgment and machine recommendations will require ongoing ethical consideration. Regulatory frameworks must evolve to keep pace with technological advancements, ensuring both safety and innovation. Furthermore, the role of healthcare professionals will shift, with greater emphasis on human-AI collaboration, necessitating new skills in data interpretation and AI oversight. Medical education will need to adapt to prepare future professionals for this tech-driven landscape. To ensure equitable benefits across all populations, especially in resource-limited settings, AI must be developed and deployed thoughtfully. As AI converges with other emerging technologies like genomics and the Internet of Things, it will likely drive new advancements in personalized and predictive medicine. Realizing AI’s full potential in healthcare will require a commitment to responsible innovation, interdisciplinary collaboration, and an ongoing focus on ethical reflection to ensure that AI aligns with human values and benefits society as a whole.

ABSTRACT

The field of neuroradiology has advanced significantly with the implementation of 3D Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) technology. This imaging modality enables early-stage tumor diagnosis by detecting minute tumors and subtle abnormalities with high precision. Brain tumors are classified into three primary categories: benign, premalignant, and malignant. A brain tumor is defined as an abnormal proliferation of cells and tissues, with malignant tumors being characterized by rapid growth, irregular surfaces, lack of encapsulation, and deep attachments to surrounding structures. These tumors can exert substantial pressure on adjacent tissues and spread rapidly. The proposed method leverages 3D MRI scans for precise brain tumor detection. Users can choose between two advanced classification approaches: the Support Vector Machine (SVM) or Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) classifiers. The preprocessing phase, which includes contrast enhancement, noise reduction, and grayscale conversion, optimizes image quality. Segmentation techniques are then applied to isolate the tumor region, followed by feature extraction to identify vector-based characteristics. These features are input into the classifier to accurately determine the tumor type. Tumor-affected MRI images are visualized through various graphs generated by a Self-Organizing Map (SOM), enhancing interpretability and aiding in diagnostic decision-making.Keywords: 3D brain Model, Detection, Tumour Stages, 3D MRI, segmentation.

1. INTRODUCTION

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a technology that uses magnetism, radio waves, and a sophisticated system to produce detailed images of internal body parts that are not visible to the naked eye. MRI images are highly detailed and can detect subtle changes in the body's internal structures. In some cases, specialized algorithms are applied to enhance the quality of MRI images. An MRI scanner operates based on the principles of electromagnetic waves and consists of two primary magnets that generate the required magnetic fields (DeAngelis, 2001).

The initial giant circular magnet aligns water molecules in the body to orient them in the same direction. The second magnet causes each hydrogen atom (H-atom) in the body to adjust its alignment under the influence of the magnetic field. When the magnetic field is removed, sensors detect the energy released as protons return to their original alignment. The patient is positioned inside the scanner using a sliding bed. After the entire process, the internal MRI mechanism processes the data, and an image is constructed (Liang & Lauterbur, 2000).

MRI images can be viewed on a computer screen and transmitted electronically. There are several reasons why MRI scans are performed. In addition to brain imaging, neurosurgeons use them to assess the spinal cord after trauma and to examine the vertebrae or intervertebral discs of the spine. MRI provides valuable information about the entire body and is also used to evaluate the structure of the heart. The precise results of an MRI scan can often help improve the accuracy of surgical procedures (Gordillo et al., 2013).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is an advanced method for detecting brain malignancies. A brain tumor is any intracranial tumor caused by abnormal cells, typically located inside or near the brain. Automated brain tumor identification is one of the most challenging tasks in modern medical imaging. It requires image segmentation, a process that divides an image into distinct regions based on specific characteristics. However, removing noise from MR images without compromising fine anatomical details is a complex task. These challenges make obtaining accurate MRI images difficult, yet precise tumor detection relies heavily on accurate brain image segmentation (Gondal & Khan, 2013).

Various algorithms are available for brain image segmentation, which is crucial for tasks such as surgical planning and post-surgical evaluation. Despite the availability of numerous automated methods, many of them fail due to challenges such as noise and low contrast in the images (Borole et al., 2015).

A brain tumor refers to any intracranial tumor caused by abnormal cell and tissue proliferation. In the human body, cells and tissues function as fundamental building blocks. Normally, cells proliferate and then die in an orderly manner as part of their life cycle. However, tumors form when these cells fail to undergo programmed cell death (apoptosis) and instead grow uncontrollably, replicate excessively, form blood vessels, and invade surrounding tissues in an unnatural manner.

The size, shape, and other physical characteristics of cancerous cells differ significantly from those of normal cells. For example, their nuclei are often larger and darker than those of normal cells. Cancerous cells may also form clusters without a defined cell wall or outer boundary, and they exhibit an abnormally high number of disorganized chromosomes compared to normal cells. Cancerous tumors are typically classified into benign and malignant .

A benign tumor is a slow-growing primary tumor that is unlikely to spread because it does not invade surrounding tissues or metastasize to other parts of the body. It is typically small, has a regular surface, is encapsulated, and may be attached to deeper structures. While it may exert slight pressure on nearby organs, it is generally not serious unless it transitions to a malignant state or reproduces secondary (malignant) tumor cells. However, there is a potential for recurrence of the tumor after surgery.

On the other hand, malignant tumors (secondary tumors) are fast-growing, large, cancerous cells that can spread easily. They are life-threatening, have irregular surfaces, are non-encapsulated, and are attached to deep structures, exerting significant pressure on neighboring tissues. These tumors can also reproduce after surgery. Tumors that originate in other parts of the body and spread to the brain via the bloodstream are known as secondary tumors or metastases (Pereira et al., 2016).

According to a recent research, the survival rate for individuals with brain cancer is 36% for women and 34% for males (Pereira et al., 2016). The type of cancer and the stage at which it was diagnosed are two of the many variables that may affect the survival rate.Our researchs goal are to promptly diagnose tumours and categorise them into two groups: benign (primary) and malignant (secondary) in three dimensions. The object can be seen in detail in the 3D perspective.

Using 3D MRI scans as input; our algorithm performs key tasks such as segmentation and feature extraction before identifying the tumor and its stage. This approach could potentially improve the survival rates of future brain tumor patients by enabling timely and appropriate treatment.

The structure of this document is as follows: Section 2 presents a literature review on brain tumor detection, Section 3 outlines our proposed method and classifier, and Section 4 provides an analysis of the results and discussion. The paper concludes with a summary of our research and findings in Section 5, followed by the conclusions in Section 6.

2. LITERATURE REVIEW

The identification of brain tumors using MRI scans is a crucial task in medical imaging, aimed at improving diagnostic precision and ensuring timely treatment. As medical imaging technology advances, researchers have developed various techniques to enhance the detection and classification of brain tumors.Various algorithms have been proposed by researchers to detect tumors. In 2020, some researchers developed algorithms that use an adaptive K-means clustering approach to enhance contrast and fill in gaps in MRI brain images. After receiving an MRI scan as input, the algorithm applies a threshold to eliminate undesirable pixels. The left portion of the processed image is then overlaid onto the original image to detect tumors.The left region is then mapped onto the original image for tumor detection. Tumor detection is performed in two stages: first, segmentation, and second, mapping onto the original image. After detection, classification is carried out using a Support Vector Machine (SVM). The tumor-detected image is input into a Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), which decomposes the image into four components: Low-Low (LL), Low-High (LH), High-Low (HL), and High-High (HH). The Low-Low (LL) coefficient is further processed through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to extract stronger features (Zulpe & Pawar, 2012).

The features are further characterized using the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM). Finally, a Support Vector Machine (SVM) is trained on the dataset, using a linear kernel for classification and Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM)-derived features for tumor type determination. By doing so, they achieved an accuracy rate of 93% (Zulpe & Pawar, 2012).

The preprocessing techniques applied to an image in their study include various methods collectively referred to as convolution filtering. These methods encompass RGB to grayscale conversion, edge detection, and 2D convolution masking. The images are utilized to train the system, during which their features are systematically extracted. Morphological techniques are applied to remove unwanted pixels, enhancing image quality for further processing. Segmentation is performed by generating a Signed Distance Map (SDM), which aids in accurately delineating regions of interest. For the final classification, MATLAB's Classification Learner application is utilized, resulting in an achieved accuracy rate of 80% (Chander et al., 2020).

In this paper an automated technique was proposed to detect brain tumours using 3d MRI images. This technique involves around preprocessing of 3d MRI images using Bias field correction. The N4ITK (N4ITK Bias Field Correction) technique is used and Histogram matching in which histogram of each image is adjusted with image means histogram. After the preprocessing Otsu algorithm is applied for extracting the desired region of brain tumour cells. For classification or identification feature extraction is an important step, so they extracted Local Binary Patterns (LBP) features and Histogram Orientation Gradient (HOG) features of thebrain's MRI image. Inthe end, classification is carried out with the help of the random forest algorithm with the help of that proposed methodology; they got maximum accuracy of 83% (Abbasi & Tajeripour, 2017).

In this paper (Sharmila et al., 2019), the researchers proposed a technique for classifying brain tumors using a Support Vector Machine (SVM). Images from the dataset are input into the system, which begins by extracting features. First, the system uses the Wavelet-based Fractal Texture Analysis (WSFTA) technique, which includes Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) and Segmentation-Based Fractal Texture Analysis (SFTA). Second, Dimensionality Reduction is applied using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

The system is then trained using the Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm, and two images are mapped for similarity checking. With this approach, they achieved an accuracy of 90.67%. In this methodology proposed in paper (Sharma et al., 2018), preprocessing techniques including grayscale conversion, binary thresholding, morphological operations, contour tumor region identification, and watershed segmentation are applied. Features are then extracted using the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM). Finally, classification is performed using K-means clustering and an Artificial Neural Network (ANN). For this purpose, a neuro-fuzzy system is utilized. The proposed algorithm was compared with a single K-means clustering and neuro-fuzzy system.

In a separate study, researchers focused on extracting and identifying gliomas from MRI images. In their work (Selvapandian & Manivannan, 2018), they first applied preprocessing techniques to prepare the images. Afterward, features were extracted using the Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) method. The four extracted features were then input into an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS) classifier to determine whether the tumor was glioma.

Kapoor and Thakur (2017) compared various image segmentation techniques, including threshold-based segmentation, region-based segmentation, and unsupervised learning algorithms (such as fuzzy clustering, C-means, and k-means). They assessed the advantages and disadvantages of each technique, highlighting that threshold segmentation is the easiest to implement, but it fails to provide all the necessary information and cannot be applied to images with low contrast. Although fuzzy clustering, C-means, and k-means are learning-based techniques, they do not produce accurate results when applied to noisy images. In contrast, region-based segmentation is more accurate, though slightly slower than the other methods.

In their 2018 study, S.M. Kamrul Hassan and Mohiuddin Ahmad et al. implemented a two-step verification process for brain tumor segmentation and brain status evaluation. The image datasets were sourced from the BRATS 2012 dataset, containing MRI scans from 30 patients with gliomas—20 with high-grade gliomas and 10 with low-grade gliomas. The segmented regions were then matched with the ground truth images using a watershed algorithm (Hasan & Ahmad, 2018).

Recent studies highlight the growing role of machine learning in brain tumor classification and medical imaging. Aamir et al. (2023) developed a method for classifying brain tumors by utilizing deep features derived from high-quality regions of MRI images, improving accuracy in detecting tumors.

In a previous study, Aamir et al. (2022) proposed a deep learning approach for brain tumor classification using MRI images, focusing on improving classification performance. The hybrid approach for object proposal generation by Aamir et al. (2017) also contributes to the field of medical imaging by enhancing image analysis techniques. Additionally, a framework developed by Guan et al. (2023) offers an efficient method for classifying brain tumors using MRI data. Finally, Aamir et al. (2023) explored the broader applications of machine learning in medicine, emphasizing current trends and future prospects in the context of medical technologies like MRI-based tumor classification.

Recent studies have demonstrated significant advancements in brain tumor detection using deep learning and machine learning techniques applied to MRI images (Zulpe & Pawar, 2012). Abdusalomov et al. (2023) explored deep learning approaches, emphasizing their ability to improve tumor detection through the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and magnetic resonance imaging (Chander et al., 2020).

Anantharajan et al. (2024) further enhanced MRI-based brain tumor detection by integrating both deep learning and machine learning approaches, resulting in more robust tumor classification and detection. In 2021, Brindha et al. applied deep learning techniques, specifically CNNs, for automatic brain tumor detection from MRI scans, showcasing their capability to effectively analyze medical images. Ahmed et al. (2024) proposed a hybrid model combining Vision Transformer (ViT) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with explainable AI to improve classification performance and provide transparency in the decision-making process for tumor classification.

Martínez-Del-Río-Ortega et al. (2024) contributed to the field by utilizing CNNs for brain tumor detection, demonstrating their potential in enhancing MRI analysis for precise diagnosis. Lastly, Khaliki and Başarslan (2024) compared transfer learning techniques with traditional 3-layer CNN models, offering insights into their comparative efficacy in tumor detection. These studies collectively highlight the progressive shift towards AI-driven methods in brain tumor detection, promising more accurate, reliable, and efficient diagnostic tools for clinical applications.

The state-of-arts have demonstrated significant advancements in brain tumor detection using deep learning and machine learning techniques applied to MRI images. Abdusalomov et al. (2023) explored deep learning approaches, emphasizing their ability to improve tumor detection through the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and magnetic resonance imaging.

3. METHODOLOGY

3D MRI brain tumour scans acquired from BRATS (2015-2019) are sliced into (150) slices inside a volume. The 3D slice is preprocessed using contrast enhancement to make the contrast of the image bright and bring visibility to scan and highlight the regions in the image. Now the scan is segmented using K-means for tumour detection and then self-organizing map representation is drawn for 3D MRI scan. Feature extraction is performed and the appropriate feature set is chosen using PCA that maximizes the accuracy result, at last, the tumour is classified into high-grade glioma and low-grade glioma, and the user is given an option that the user can choose either SVM for tumour classification or ANFIS.

The 3D MRI BRATS (2015 and 2019) brain tumor datasets are utilized, with each 3D volume containing approximately 150-155 slices. From these slices, only the key slices are extracted for further processing. These key slices include the full brain along with the tumor regions, which are then fed into the preprocessing step for the subsequent detection of brain tumors.

After slicing the 3D volume, the next step is improving and eliminating extra information from the data. 3D MRI brain tumor datasets (BRATS) are used for training as well as testing of data as the datasets choose are standard datasets that are already processed for noise removal so only contrast enhancement technique is applied on the 3D volumes. Contrast enhancement is useful here and when it is applied to each 3D slice, we get a balanced image in which the input pixel intensities are mapped to new values such that 1% of the values are saturated at low and high-intensity values resulting in increasing the contrast of the image. As the data is standard dataset, so no noise removal step is performed, see Figure 1.

Figure 1. Original image (left side), enhanced image (right side image)

The key task is to segment the image in order to extract the desired region from the entire 3D slice. For this purpose, the K-means algorithm is employed with three clusters. The K-means algorithm initially assigns random positions to the cluster centers in a multidimensional feature space. Each point is then assigned to the cluster whose center is closest. This process continues iteratively until there is no significant change in the location of the class mean vectors between successive iterations. The segmentation is performed using three clusters: one for the brain region without the tumor, one for the non-brain area, and one for the tumor. Each pixel is assigned to the cluster it belongs to (See Figure 2).

Figure 2. Showing cluster formed in the image

K-Means [29] clustering is applied to separate different clusters in the brain. For this purpose, three clusters are used that is one for one cluster is for the non-brain part, one for the brain with no tumour, and one for tumour. The steps of this method are described below in the algorithm:

Let suppose an image (x * y) having coordinates as ‘x’ and ‘y’ and the image will be divided into ‘L’ clusters and k(x, y) illustrate all the disorganized pixels and ‘CL’is the cluster formed.Divide the image into ‘l’ no of clusters Then Estimate the Euclidean distance of each pixel from the cluster in equation (1)


Distance = ||k(x, y)−CL||
(1)

Assign the pixel to the cluster having minimum distance from that cluster.After grouping every pixel recalculate centroid by calculating data mean given by equation (2) (Guan et al., n.d.).


$$C_{L} = \frac{1}{L}{\sum\limits_{x \in C_{L}}{\sum\limits_{y \in C_{L}}{k\left( {x,y} \right)}}}$$
(2)

Repeat all the above steps until the centroids values stop changing.Now map the remolded clusters picture element on the image.

Figure 3 will show the detailed working of the K-Means Algorithm.

Figure 3. K-Means Algorithms

Morphological operations are carried out when the input pixel in the input image is compared to its neighbourhood for acquiring desired output results in the output image. Irrespective of the other types here in the proposed system opening is chosen according to the scenario. The morphological opening is useful when the objective is to eliminate the small objects carrying unnecessary information while preserving the shape and causing no disturbance to its size. The opening involves erosion and dilation that are the key types of morphological operations, erosion shrinks the region and dilation dilate it, so opening operation is a combination of erosion and dilation, same structuring element is utilized in both operations.

4.1 Self-Organizing Map (SOM)

Self-organizing maps are neural networks that are trained purely to perform the clustering of data. The structure included in a network so that the net is forced to decide as to which one unit will respond and learn to classify input vectors according to how they are grouped in the input space. In our case, an image size of 10*10 is used, having a neuron value of 25*25. Different graphs are given as an output by the system after the SOM training, which shows the position of different neurons at different locations. Self-organizing feature map network identifies a winning neuron i* using the same procedure as employed by a competitive layer. However, instead of updating only the winning neuron, all neurons within a certain neighbourhood Ni* (d) of the winning neuron are updated, using the Kohonen rule. Specifically, all such neurons i ∊ Ni* (d) are adjusted as follows:


iw(q) = iw(q−1) + α(p(q)−iw(q−1))
(3)

Or


iw(q) = (1−α)iw(q−1) + αp(q)
(4)

Here the neighborhood Ni* (d) contains the indices for all of the neurons that lie within a radius d of the winning neuron i*.


Ni(d) = {j,dij≤d}
(5)

Thus, when a vector p is presented, the weights of the winning neuron and its close neighbors move toward p. Consequently, after many presentations, neighboring neurons have learned vectors similar to each other.

In every representation of SOM, the dimensions are

% Create a Self-Organizing Map

dimension1 = 25;

dimension2 = 25;

Which shows that the neurons are taken as 25*25.

While training the batch weight algorithm is used with the iterations of 200. Each graph shows the taken dimension of the neuron on the x-axis and y-axis describing the position of the first neuron to the last neuron.

Darker colors represent larger distances, while lighter colors represent smaller distances. The Self-Organizing Map (SOM) hit tells us how many data points are associated with each neuron. 4.2 Feature Extraction

The figure below is giving a complete understanding of the feature extraction techniques used and what features are being extracted by using these techniques.

Figure 10. Feature extraction methods and feature labels

GLCM (Martínez-Del-Río-Ortega et al., 2024) is used to obtain the statistical textural second-order features (these features are generated using first-order statistics and provide information on the distribution of gray level in an image). The GLCM function is used to outline the texture (information of color arrangements in the picture) of the image to measure repeatedly certain pixels are appearing in a pair and distinct relationship for this purpose GLCM is created and then required texture features are extracted by utilizing the statistical calculations from the GLCM matrix.GLCM is a 2D histogram in which (m,n)th element s are the frequency of how usually an event m occurs with n. It is a function of distance D =1, calculated at four different angles that are 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees resulting in values calculated from four different orientation for each of the below, and also calculate how regularly a pixel having intensity value m occurs in relation with another pixel n at a specific distance D and on these orientation.

Contrast: Measure the contrast between a pixel and its neighbor in equation (6)


$$Contrast = {\sum\limits_{a = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum\limits_{b = 0}^{q - 1}{\left( {a - b} \right)^{2}f\left( {a,b} \right)}}}$$
(6)

Correlation: Measure of how much a pixel is dependent or associated to its neighbor pixel in the entire equation (7)


$$Correlation = \frac{\sum_{m = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum_{n = 0}^{q - 1}{\left( {m \cdot n} \right)f\left( {m,n} \right) - P_{m}P_{n}}}}{\sigma_{m}\sigma_{n}}$$
(7)

Energy: It is the squared sum of all reoccurring pixel pairs in GLCM equation (8)


$$Energy = \sqrt{\sum\limits_{m = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{q - 1}{f^{2}\left( {m,n} \right)}}}$$
(8)

Homogeneity: It measures the proximity of the element scattered in GLCM matrix to that of present in diagonal in GLCM equation (9)


$$Homogeneity = {\sum\limits_{m = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum\limits_{n = 0}^{q - 1}{\frac{1}{1 + \left( {m - n} \right)^{2}}f\left( {m,n} \right)}}}$$
(9)

Laplacian of Gaussian is applied, and four features are obtained mean, standard deviation, skewness,kurtosis where p is length and q is width and C(x,y) is log value at the location stated by a and y, sigma (σ) is the variance, and Mu (μ) is average.

Mean: The mean calculate the part of each pixel intensity value in the whole image


$$\mu_{x} = \frac{1}{p \cdot q}{\sum\limits_{x = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum\limits_{y = 0}^{q - 1}{C\left( {x,y} \right)}}}$$
(10)

Standard deviation: It is the measure of how much the data is dispersed from its mean value

Skewness: It is the measure of lack of balance of inequality equation (11)


$$Skewness = \frac{1}{p \cdot q}\frac{\sum_{x = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum_{y = 0}^{q - 1}\left( {C\left( {x,y} \right) - \mu_{x}} \right)^{3}}}{\sigma_{x}^{3}}$$
(11)

Kurtosis: Kurtosis is the term used to describe the circulation of data equation (12)


$$Kurtosis = \frac{1}{p \cdot q}\frac{\sum_{x = 0}^{p - 1}{\sum_{y = 0}^{q - 1}\left( {C\left( {x,y} \right) - \mu_{x}} \right)^{4}}}{\sigma_{x}^{4}}$$
(12)

Local binary patterns are feature descriptors used to the texture properties of the surface. It is a mixture of earlier used divergent statistical features and structural models to examine and investigate the texture properties of the surface. These feature descriptors are prioritized due to its stiffness power to confront the monotonic grayscale images and its computational efficiency. Its algorithm threshold the adjoining neighborhood pixels on the ground of existing value. They mainly store grayscale contrast information and image patterns spatially. The following is description of features calculation procedure. Initially, several pixels are selected in the neighborhood of every pixel in radius R’ then Intensity difference is calculated for the selected current pixel and its neighboring pixels .Now all the differences that have negative values will become 0, and all others are set to 1 by applying thresholding. At last the vector acquired will be changed into decimal value and is assumed as new intensity value for that current pixel

The following is the equation that calculates LBP for each pixel in equation (13)


$$LBP_{({A,R^{\prime}})} = {\sum\limits_{a = 1}^{A}{s\left( {g_{A} - g_{B}} \right) \cdot 2^{({a - 1})}}}$$
(13)

And


s(x) = {1,x≥00,x<0
(14)

Where A represents the number of neighboring pixels and R’ shows the radius respectively. While gA and gB are intensity values of the present and neighborhood pixels respectively

Wavelet packet transform Image is decomposed using the wavelet packet transform by using different frequencies of the pixels range in the image. Here 2D-DWT is used that is truly constructive in defining and evaluating the features and the DB5 wavelet is used. By using region of interest four Sub bands that are HH(high-high), LL(low-low),HL (high-low) and LH (low-high) are achieved that will output 40 features having 20 values of mean and 20 values of standard deviationMean is the average of each decomposed level. It shows the data distribution in each decomposed level. Different features are extracted that is contrast, energy, correlation, and homogeneity from four different angles 0, 45,90, and 135, also the mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis is calculated, these features are called as Local Binary Patterns.

The second 40 features are extracted from Wavelet Based Features and their mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis are also calculated. LOG based features are 40 because images are decomposed to 40 levels so from every level one feature is extracted. Feature reduction is the process of reducing features to desired use from obtained features so for better accuracy; a matrix is formed of these features to be given as an input to classifiers for the process of classification. This step is performed using Principal Component Analysis Algorithm.

4.4 Implementation and Result Analysis

Training time usually requires 20-30% of development time it can be longer up to months and as low as days or weeks, depending on the datasets we train the system on.The Computation time and response time could not be predicted as early yet complete implementation is not done but definitely, the aim of the system will be increase performance and enhance results by increasing efficiency and decreasing time.The previous systems developed were not able to describe the tumor stage they only focused on the tumor extraction from the image, its detection and some were also discussing the tumor location. The classifier implemented will be able to specify tumor stage that whether its malicious or not. An error always affects the system results and usability of the system. They had a bad impact that the actual requirement is not fulfilled, As errors will be reduced, there will be better results which also affect the quality of the system and better performance directly.

It consist of at first 3D standard dataset containing brain tumor, magnetic resonance images are found and then downloaded from brats (brats2015). These images were present in .mhaformat that is not visible; a special code is needed in Matlab to read these images. Further, the image is processed using different noise removal and image quality improving functions and techniques as these are standard datasets so they are already processed for noise removal and also image quality is much better but to increase contrast, contrast adjustment is applied. The key 3D slice obtained from 3D MRI is the input to the proposed method.

Further, it is processed using contrast adjustment; it increases the pixel values difference by improving the contrast of the image, it applied for stretching the pixels gathered at the middle of the image, then to diagnose the tumor region and extract it from the required image, k-means clustering is applied making 3 clusters for the data one for the non-brain part, one for the brain with no tumor and last for tumor.

K-means estimates the Euclidean distance of each point or pixel from its centroid. It then assigns the pixel to the centroid with the smallest distance. This process continues for all points. After assigning each cluster to its respective points, the centroids are re-calculated by taking the mean of the data in each cluster. This iterative process is repeated until the stopping criteria are met, i.e., when the centroids' values no longer change.

Once the clustering is finalized, the clusters are mapped onto the image, resulting in a binary image as the output of the K-means algorithm.

Next, a morphological opening operation is applied to the binary image. This involves first eroding the image and then dilating it using the same structuring element. The opening operation smooths the object and removes small unwanted details that could interfere with the results.

After the opening operation, objects smaller than 200 pixels are removed from the image to eliminate any remaining noise or irrelevant objects. The final output is the segmented image, with unwanted objects successfully removed.

Feature extraction involves retrieving useful quantitative information from the image. A total of 64 features are obtained in this process. Several techniques are applied for feature extraction: GLCM, LBP, Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), and Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG).

In GLCM, four features are extracted from four different orientations (0°, 45°, 90°, and 135°). These features include contrast, correlation, energy, and homogeneity, each with four corresponding values.

Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) is applied to calculate the mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis. LBP is used to extract mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis as well.

Finally, Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) is applied, and the mean and standard deviation are calculated. Each of these values has twenty different measurements, providing a comprehensive set of features for analysis.

The principal component analysis is applied for feature reduction to have the most relevant data from the given data, after using PCA when a tumor is classified using SVM its accuracy decreased from 83% to 80% and when PCA applied features are used in classification using ANFIS its accuracy increased from 92% to 97.76% then their results are compared and resulted as ANFIS with higher accuracy and som weight positions are presented in Table 1 (See Figures 13-16).

Perform validation using external datasets from different sources to ensure the model can handle diverse patient demographics, tumor types, and clinical conditions. This demonstrates the model’s applicability across different clinical environments and enhances its clinical utility.Apply cross-validation techniques using independent subsets of the BraTS 2015 dataset or other datasets to check the model’s performance consistency. This helps us identify overfitting or biases towards specific data characteristics, ensuring the model’s robustness.

Finally, test the model in clinical environments with real-world MRI scans, which may contain artifacts, noise, or other variations not present in training data. This provides insights into the model's performance and reliability in routine clinical use.

5. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, MRI remains a vital tool for the identification of abnormalities and diseases across various organs. The proposed brain tumor identification model, evaluated on BraTS 2015, demonstrates significant improvements in accuracy, precision, and recall compared to earlier models on BraTS 2012 and 2013. These advancements highlight its potential for reliable tumor classification and clinical applications. Future work could integrate advanced deep learning techniques and real-time implementation to further enhance accuracy and efficiency in tumor diagnosis.

Her recent research focuses on ultra-wideband antennas, traffic flow prediction using deep learning, and driver assistance systems.

A. Swetha Rani completed B.TECH in ECE and MT.ECH with specialization in DECS from JNTU Anantapuram.Now pursuing Ph.D in JNTU Anantapuram and her area of interest is Image processing.Qualified UGC NET as assistant professor.Worked as assistant professor in BITS,ADONI.Present Working as assistant professor in Gpcet kurnool.

T. V. V. Satyanarayana is currently working as Professor in the Department of ECE, Mohan Babu University, Tirupati. He completed his Graduation and Post Graduation from Acharya Nagarjuna University in 2002 and 2007 respectively. In 2015, he obtained Ph.D from Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Hyderabad. His research contributions include development of novel techniques for Iris Recognition. He has improved the existing Iris Recognition System by improving the accuracy to 99.63% and reduced the time in recognition from 31 seconds to 3.1 seconds, which is a ten-fold improvement. One of his research papers entitled “Multilevel Network Security Based on Iris Biometric” is listed as Iris Image Quality reading materials by NIST Laboratory under U.S. Department of Commerce. His research interests include IoT, Machine Learning and allied fields. Currently he is the reviewer of various International Journals. He has 45 International publications and 4 patents to his credit.

Kalyanasundaram V is an Integrated MTech student in Computer Software Engineering at Vellore Institute of Technology, with a passion for exploring cutting-edge technologies and their real-world applications. In addition to my studies, I am actively engaged in research focused on artificial intelligence, machine learning, cloud computing, and blockchain. These pursuits aim to address complex challenges and drive innovation at the intersection of these transformative fields, shaping a future where technology empowers progress and growth.

Veena V.S., B.E., M.E., MBA, is an accomplished academic professional with extensive experience in electrical engineering education and administration. Holding degrees in Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Power System Engineering, and Human Resources Management, she serves as an Assistant Professor at St. Peter’s College of Engineering and Technology. She specializes in power systems, renewable energy technologies, and instrumentation, with notable contributions including authoring a book, publishing papers in conferences, and holding leadership roles such as President of the Institution Innovation Council and AICTE Campus Ambassador. An Anna University rank holder and a life member of the International Association of Engineers (IAENG), she is dedicated to fostering academic excellence, mentoring students, and ensuring successful placements. Proficient in MATLAB and an advocate for continuous learning, she has completed many courses, attended faculty development programs, and actively promotes innovation and entrepreneurship in her field.

Aparna VB is an undergraduate neuroscience student at Yenepoya University, India, with a strong interest in research, particularly in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and neurological disorders.

Deepika Yadav is working with SRM University as an Assistant Professor in Electrical and Electronics Engineering since August 2017. She did her Master of Engineering from LIMAT (affiliated to M.D.U), Faridabad with specialization in Power electronics, Electrical Machines and Drives. She has been awarded doctorate degree on topic “Optimal Operation and Scheduling of Hydro Power Plant” by NIT Hamirpur (H.P) in 2014. She has presented her work at national and international levels. Her research work has been published in the form of papers in international journals and conferences and is duly recognized. She has reviewed various papers for International journals such as Elsevier Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, Taylor and Francis and Springer plus. She is a Life Member of ISTE. She has more than 8.5 years of teaching experience in various institutes. Earlier, she has also worked at Adama Science and Technology University, Ethiopia in Electrical and Computer Science Department. Her research area is Soft Computing Techniques application in Power System and Renewable Energy.

Hewa Majeed Zangana is an Iraqi lecturer and assistant professor in computer science and information technology. He holds a Bachelor's degree from Nawroz University, a Master's degree from the International Islamic University Malaysia, and an Honorary Doctorate from the British Accreditation EB - JAS, and currently studying PhD of ITM at DPU. With expertise in network systems and teaching experience, Hewa has taught various subjects and held positions such as Curriculum Division Director and Head of the Computer Science Department at Nawroz University. He has also published research articles in prestigious journals and presented at conferences.
